It makes me wonder about the metric a bit.Anyway, here's my interpretation of the results: At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image is 14–17% larger than the AVIF image for the same quality. jixel is the better JPEG XL encoder at medium/high quality, and libjxl is slightly better at very high quality. At maximum efforts, the best JPEG XL image (jixel 'extraslow') is 6–15% larger than AVIF (s0).jixel at its slowest setting slightly beats AVIF's default effort, with files 1–10% smaller. The biggest gain is at very high quality. At default efforts, jixel is 12–36% faster than AVIF, but its files are 14–18% larger. To match the file size of AVIF's default, jixel needs its 'extraslow' setting, which takes 18–27x as long as AVIF. libjxl's default takes 1.5–2x as long as AVIF's default, and still produces bigger files. At default efforts, jixel uses around half the memory of AVIF, but again, its files are 14–18% larger. To match the file size of AVIF's default, jixel 'extraslow' uses ~10x the memory. libjxl's default uses 2–3x the memory of AVIF, and its higher efforts use ~7x. JPEG XL takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, narrowing to ~1.5–1.8x at very high quality. Safari's JPEG XL decoder is the slowest.Higher effort is worth it for AVIF. AVIF's s5 gets you ~10% smaller files for ~3x the encode time.Higher effort is worth it for jixel too, up to 'slow'. 'slow' gets you 9–13% smaller files than its default 'fast', for ~3.7x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 3–8%, but takes ~8x longer than 'slow' and uses ~9x the memory. Even so, AVIF still wins when given the same encode time: AVIF s5 takes about as long as jixel 'slow', and its files are ~13% smaller.Higher effort isn't worth it for libjxl. libjxl's maximum effort is barely any better than its default, but takes ~18x longer.AVIF's 4:2:0 mode doesn't help much. It's slightly faster to encode/decode, and uses less memory, but the files aren't meaningfully smaller, and it struggles to reach higher qualities.Here's the full data, so you can make up your own mind:I've heard people say that AVIF's tendency to smooth out details makes it bad for human faces, so I picked this image from Unsplash.The results of the benchmark for this image: At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image is 17–24% larger than the AVIF image for the same quality. jixel is the better JPEG XL encoder across the whole quality range this time. libjxl is 30–50% larger than AVIF, which is a much bigger gap than the F1 image. At maximum efforts, the best JPEG XL image (jixel 'extraslow') is 12–17% larger than AVIF (s0).jixel at its slowest setting doesn't quite match AVIF's default effort this time. It's a few percent larger at medium/high quality, and only edges ahead at very high quality. At default efforts, jixel is 18–33% faster than AVIF, but its files are 17–24% larger. Even jixel's 'extraslow' setting, which takes 25–39x as long as AVIF, only matches AVIF's default file size at very high quality. libjxl's default takes 1.5–2.2x as long as AVIF's default, and still produces bigger files. At default efforts, jixel uses around half the memory of AVIF, but again, its files are 17–24% larger. jixel 'extraslow' gets closest to AVIF's default file size, but uses ~10x the memory. libjxl's default uses 2–3.3x the memory of AVIF, and its higher efforts use ~7x. JPEG XL takes 2–2.9x as long to decode at medium quality, narrowing to ~1.3–1.7x at very high quality. At the very top of the quality range, libjxl images decode as fast as AVIF in Chrome, but not in the other browsers.Higher effort is worth it for AVIF. AVIF's s5 gets you 5–8% smaller files for ~3x the encode time. That's a smaller gain than the F1 image.Higher effort is worth it for jixel too, up to 'slow'. 'slow' gets you 7–14% smaller files than its default 'fast', for ~3.9x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 4–6%, but takes ~10x longer than 'slow' and uses ~9x the memory. AVIF still wins when given the same encode time: AVIF s5 takes about as long as jixel 'slow', and its files are 8–17% smaller.Higher effort is somewhat worth it for libjxl on this image. Unlike the F1 image, libjxl's maximum effort gets you 4–11% smaller files than its default. But it takes ~10x longer, and it still produces much bigger files than AVIF at its default effort.AVIF's 4:2:0 mode doesn't help much. Same as the F1 image. ColorVideoVDP gives it a small (~4%) advantage, but SSIMULACRA2 doesn't.At lower qualities, you can see the smoothing on the face, but it's the same for both AVIF and JPEG XL.I threw this one in because it's the default image in Squoosh, but I guess the sharp lines of the hairs make it different to the previous images. In fact, even at medium quality, the difference from the original is much less perceptible to my eyes compared to the other images.The results are much closer than the previous two:File size: , narrowly. At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image (jixel) is only 2–6% larger than the AVIF image for the same quality. libjxl does much worse, at 10–18% larger. At maximum efforts, jixel 'extraslow' and AVIF s0 are roughly tied, with jixel up to 5% smaller at very high quality. However, ColorVideoVDP disagrees, and puts AVIF 5–12% ahead at maximum efforts.Encode time: , according to SSIMULACRA2. At default efforts, jixel is 19–35% faster than AVIF, and its files are only 2–6% larger. Comparing higher efforts, jixel 'slow' produces files the same size or slightly smaller than AVIF s5, in the same time or less. And jixel 'extraslow' matches or beats AVIF s0 while being 12–34% faster. But, since ColorVideoVDP gives AVIF more of a file size advantage, it isn't clear-cut. libjxl's default takes 1.3–1.9x as long as AVIF's default, and produces bigger files.Encode memory: , at lower efforts. At default efforts, jixel uses 37–48% less memory than AVIF, and its files are only 2–6% larger. jixel 'slow' uses about the same memory as AVIF s5 to produce a similar file size, but 'extraslow' uses ~9x the memory of AVIF s0. libjxl's default uses ~2x the memory of AVIF, and its higher efforts use 6–7x. JPEG XL takes 2–2.4x as long to decode at medium quality. But the gap closes at very high quality, where jixel's files decode about as fast as AVIF in Firefox and Safari, and ~25% faster in Chrome.Higher effort is less worth it for AVIF on this image. AVIF's s5 gets you 3–6% smaller files for 3–4x the encode time.Higher effort is worth it for jixel, up to 'slow'. 'slow' gets you 6–14% smaller files than its default 'fast', for 3.5–4.3x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 2–9%, but takes 9–14x longer than 'slow' and uses ~9x the memory.Higher effort isn't worth it for libjxl. libjxl's maximum effort gets you 1–2% smaller files than its default, but takes ~12x longer.AVIF's 4:2:0 mode doesn't help. The files are the same size as 4:4:4.I've played with both codecs a lot, and for photos, what I've shown so far is representative, where AVIF beats JPEG XL. However, every now and then there's an outlier, such as this image. At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image is 4–11% smaller than the AVIF image for the same quality. libjxl is the better JPEG XL encoder at medium/high quality, and jixel at very high quality. At maximum efforts, jixel 'extraslow' is 12–27% smaller than AVIF s0. This time, ColorVideoVDP agrees.jixel's 'medium' setting is a big step up on this image. Its files are 11–25% smaller than AVIF's default, and 4–18% smaller than AVIF s0, the maximum effort.Encode time: . At default efforts, jixel is 28–38% faster than AVIF, and produces files that are around the same size or smaller. At higher efforts, it's even more one-sided: jixel 'medium' is 37–65% faster than AVIF s5, and produces files 9–23% smaller. libjxl's default takes 1.5–2.2x as long as AVIF's default.Encode memory: . At default efforts, jixel uses 14–24% less memory than AVIF, and produces files that are around the same size or smaller. AVIF s0 uses even more memory (~1.55x its default), and still produces bigger files than jixel 'medium', which uses 41–55% less memory than AVIF s0. libjxl's default uses 2.4–3.6x the memory of AVIF, and the maximum efforts of both JPEG XL encoders use 10–18x.Decode time: , except in Chrome at higher qualities. JPEG XL takes 1.3–1.9x as long to decode in Firefox and Safari. In Chrome, JPEG XL takes ~1.25x as long at medium quality, but from high quality upwards, it's 11–36% faster than AVIF.Unlike the previous images, jixel images aren't particularly slow to decode in Safari. In fact, they decode slightly faster than libjxl images.Higher effort isn't really worth it for AVIF on this image. AVIF's s5 only gets you 1–3% smaller files for 3–4.5x the encode time. s0 gets you 7–8% smaller files, but takes ~50x as long.Higher effort is worth it for jixel, up to 'slow'. 'medium' gets you 6–14% smaller files than its default 'fast', for 1.9–4.1x the encode time. 'slow' gets you 9–19% smaller files than 'fast', for 3.9–6.5x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 5–9%, but takes 8–18x longer than 'slow' and uses ~11x the memory.Higher effort isn't worth it for libjxl. libjxl's maximum effort gets you 1–6% smaller files than its default, but takes 11–14x longer.AVIF's 4:2:0 mode doesn't help. The files are the same size as 4:4:4.All three encoders produce lower SSIMULACRA2 scores for this image. As in, with the same encoder quality value, they score lower. It seems like the encoders are pretty happy smoothing out some of the background noise, which seems fine.Ok, let's try something other than a photo:The results of the benchmark:File size: , by a lot. At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image is 73–89% larger than the AVIF image at medium/high quality (jixel), and 29–44% larger at very high quality (libjxl). At maximum efforts, the best JPEG XL image (jixel 'extraslow' with patches) is 23–73% larger than AVIF (s0).libjxl can't produce anything between SSIMULACRA2 ~45 and ~78 at its default effort (~45 and ~75 at higher efforts). jixel doesn't have this problem.jixel's patches feature helps a lot with this image, but it's off by default. With patches, jixel's files are 10–29% smaller at its higher efforts, from SSIMULACRA2 ~65 upwards. Patches have no effect at jixel's default 'fast' setting. At default efforts, jixel is ~50% faster than AVIF, but its files are 70–98% larger. libjxl's default takes 1.7–1.8x as long as AVIF's default, and still produces much bigger files. At default efforts, jixel uses ~40% less memory than AVIF, but again, its files are much larger. libjxl's default uses 1.2–2.2x the memory of AVIF. jixel 'extraslow' with patches gets closest to AVIF's file sizes, but uses ~7.5x the memory of AVIF's default.Decode time: , by a lot. Taking the faster of the two JPEG XL encoders' output, JPEG XL takes 2–3.8x as long to decode, depending on browser and quality.Higher effort is more worth it for AVIF on this image. AVIF's s5 gets you 6–13% smaller files for 2.5–3x the encode time, and s0 gets you 16–23% smaller files for 30–45x the encode time.Higher effort is worth it for jixel, as long as you enable patches. 'medium' with patches gets you 11–44% smaller files than its default 'fast', for 3–4x the encode time. 'slow' with patches saves another 7–16% for ~1.7x the time of 'medium'. 'extraslow' with patches saves another few percent, but takes ~5x longer than 'slow' and uses ~4.5x the memory.Higher effort is harmful for libjxl. At very high quality, libjxl's maximum effort produces files 33–40% than its default effort, and takes ~7x longer.AVIF's 4:2:0 mode helps at higher qualities. At SSIMULACRA2 70 and above, it produces files 7–18% smaller than 4:4:4. At lower qualities, it makes no difference.All three encoders produce higher SSIMULACRA2 scores for this image. Opposite to the weasel image. But, this seems correct. At SSIMULACRA2 70 the artifacts are pretty noticeable around the Firefox logo (to me, anyway), so I'd go with 80, which is where the codecs lean anyway.Some developers, especially those who've been around as long as I have, seem to think things like screenshots need to be delivered in a lossless format. But I think this is because they're used to formats like JPEG and WebP (and seemingly JPEG XL) which handle this kind of image badly, whereas lossy AVIF handles them really well.In many cases, for largely flat-colour images, you'd use SVG. But sometimes that isn't possible (it's a screenshot), or undesirable, such as this case. This image, also from Unsplash, is still 1.1 MB as a compressed and minified SVG. This is due to the complexity of the shaded areas. As a result, a raster format wins on file size and decode/draw time.At quality 50 in the demo above, the jixel has some pretty severe colour blocks, e.g. on the cat's face. Again, it makes me question the metric a bit.The results of the benchmark:File size: , by a lot. At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image (jixel) is 32–65% larger than the AVIF image up to SSIMULACRA2 80, and ~90% larger beyond that. At maximum efforts, the best JPEG XL image (jixel 'extraslow') is 22–55% larger than AVIF (s0) up to SSIMULACRA2 80, and more beyond that. ColorVideoVDP agrees, and puts the gap at 27–58%.libjxl performs particularly badly with this image. At default efforts, it's 71–106% larger than AVIF.Lossy AVIF can't reach SSIMULACRA2 90 with this image. Even at its maximum quality setting, it tops out at ~87, so the 90 example above isn't a totally fair comparison. JPEG XL can reach 90, but the result is 8–50% larger than JPEG XL's lossless version, so you may as well use lossless. At default efforts, jixel is 35–44% faster than AVIF, but its files are 32–65% larger, which is a bad trade. jixel needs its 'slow' setting to get within 7–27% of AVIF's default file size, which takes 2.4–2.6x as long as AVIF. libjxl's default takes 1.3–2.3x as long as AVIF's default, and produces much bigger files. At default efforts, jixel uses ~37% less memory than AVIF, but again, its files are much larger. jixel 'slow' uses about the same memory as AVIF, and 'extraslow' uses ~12x. libjxl's default uses 1.5–3x the memory of AVIF.Decode time: , by a lot. JPEG XL takes 2–4.6x as long to decode at medium/high quality, narrowing to 1.6–2.1x at very high quality.Higher effort is more worth it for AVIF on this image. AVIF's s5 gets you 5–8% smaller files for ~2.7x the encode time, and s0 gets you 14–21% smaller files for 35–48x the encode time.Higher effort is worth it for jixel, up to 'slow'. 'medium' only gets you 4–13% smaller files than its default 'fast', but 'slow' gets you 19–24% smaller files (up to 36% at very high quality), for ~4x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 2–3%, but takes 8–9x longer than 'slow' and uses ~11x the memory.jixel's patches feature doesn't help with this image. Unlike the screenshot, the file sizes are identical with and without it, but it does increase encode time and memory.Higher effort isn't worth it for libjxl. libjxl's maximum effort gets you 3–9% smaller files than its default, but takes 10–13x longer.AVIF's 4:2:0 mode doesn't help. SSIMULACRA2 rates it slightly worse than 4:4:4, and ColorVideoVDP rates it slightly better (~3–4%).So far, all the images have been mostly opaque. What about an image with transparency?There are a few things that make this one different:jixel always encodes the alpha channel losslessly. It doesn't have a setting for alpha quality. This puts jixel at a big disadvantage with this image. AVIF by default compresses the alpha channel lossily, tracking the main quality setting. libjxl compresses the alpha channel losslessly by default, so watch out for that. For this benchmark, I set libjxl's alpha quality to the same as the main quality.SSIMULACRA2 scores fully-transparent pixels as perfect, so with lots of transparency, the scores will be higher than they would be for an opaque image.The results of the benchmark:File size: , by a lot. At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image (libjxl) is 31–44% larger than the AVIF image for the same quality. At maximum efforts, it's 61–70% larger. Due to its lossless alpha, jixel is 1.9–3.1x the size of AVIF at default efforts. libjxl's default takes 1.2–1.35x as long as AVIF's default, and produces much bigger files. jixel's default is ~2x faster than AVIF, but its files are around 2–3x the size. libjxl's default uses 2.4–2.7x the memory of AVIF's default, although in absolute terms, that's ~120 MB vs ~46 MB. jixel's default uses about the same memory as AVIF, but again, its files are much bigger. libjxl's output takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, narrowing to 1.4–1.8x at very high quality. jixel's output decodes faster than libjxl's, and at very high quality it's around the same speed as AVIF. Although, it's slow in Safari at lower qualities, taking ~2.4x as long as AVIF.Higher effort is worth it for AVIF. AVIF's s5 gets you 4–7% smaller files for 2.3–2.9x the encode time, and s0 gets you 10–15% smaller files for 24–29x the encode time.Higher effort barely helps jixel on this image. 'extraslow' only gets you 5–8% smaller files than its default 'fast', for 21–26x the encode time.Higher effort is harmful for libjxl. libjxl's maximum effort produces files up to 8% than its default effort, and takes ~6.5x longer.AVIF's 4:2:0 mode is harmful. It produces files 4–27% larger than 4:4:4, and can't get beyond SSIMULACRA2 ~79.The images so far have been a similar resolution. Are the results different with smaller images?Not really. The results are pretty similar to the full-size F1 image:, by about the same margin. At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image is 13–18% larger. At maximum efforts, the gap is slightly bigger than the full-size image, at 12–20%.Encode time & memory: , although libjxl's default is now around the same speed as AVIF's default. jixel's default is ~2x faster than AVIF, but its files are 13–18% larger, and this time it uses ~30% more memory. In any case, at default efforts, everything encodes in under 50ms, using under 40 MB, so these differences don't really matter at this size., by a similar margin, but again, everything decodes in a few milliseconds.What about an 18 megapixel image?Mostly the same story as the regular F1 image, but with a few differences:File size: at medium/high quality, by more than the regular image. At default efforts, the best JPEG XL image is 18–46% larger, and at maximum efforts, 28–54% larger.But JPEG XL catches up at very high quality. Around SSIMULACRA2 85, libjxl's default matches AVIF's default, and at maximum efforts, jixel 'extraslow' is ~6% smaller than AVIF s0. jixel 'slow' is 10–13% smaller than AVIF's default from SSIMULACRA2 80 upwards.Encode time: at medium/high quality, but at very high quality. AVIF's default takes ~0.5 seconds, whereas libjxl's default takes 1–2 seconds. jixel's default is ~2x faster than AVIF, but at medium/high quality its files are 29–57% larger. At very high quality, that drops to 6–12% larger, which seems like a reasonable trade-off for the speed. And jixel 'slow' produces files around the same size as AVIF s5, while being 33–41% faster.Encode memory: , and the costs are now significant. AVIF's default uses ~560 MB. libjxl's default uses ~2.5 GB at medium/high quality. jixel's default uses ~35% less than AVIF, and 'slow' uses ~18% less than AVIF s5. At maximum efforts, libjxl uses 5–6.4 GB, and jixel 'extraslow' uses 6.8–8.3 GB. at medium/high quality, by a similar margin to the regular image. jixel images take over 5x as long as AVIF to decode in Safari at those qualities. At very high quality, JPEG XL decodes faster than AVIF in Chrome.Another criticism I've heard levelled at AVIF is that its quality is unreliable. As in, a single quality setting is great for some images, but no good for others, meaning for automatically encoded images, you need to pick a higher quality setting to be safe, resulting in larger file sizes than necessary for some images.For the images I've looked at so far, I encoded them with , , and jixel at quality 80, and recorded the resulting SSIMULACRA2 scores:The behaviour of the codecs here seems really similar. All produce a range of SSIMULACRA2 scores, and they all go higher or lower for the same images.And I think this is ok? Like, all three go for a lower quality for the Weasel picture, which removed noise without reducing quality of the image subject. With the screenshot, all go for a higher quality, which seems justified to my eyes.Obviously this is a small sample size, but I haven't seen anything that suggests using a single quality setting is a risk, for any of the three codecs.Both AVIF and JPEG XL are capable of showing something progressively as the image loads. Chrome and Firefox support progressive JPEG XL, whereas only Chrome supports progressive AVIF. So, and I say this through gritted teeth, this next demo is best viewed in Chrome (I have a Firefox patch in progress):This is the 18 megapixel image again, so if you're viewing this on a device with a smaller screen, you're not getting the full effect.Progressive AVIF and JPEG XL work very differently. With JPEG XL, you can opt into the data being stored in such a way that a decoder can render low resolution versions, before it brings in the higher resolution tiles. jixel recently (like, yesterday at time of writing) added support for this too. It's called "progressive DC", and it's the most important kind of progressive rendering for JPEG XL.With AVIF, progressions work more like frames of a video. You provide up to four frames, so that's three phases before the final image. Again, like a video, each frame can use data from the previous frame as an optimisation. An advantage of this is you can choose exactly how those frames look. In the example above, I went with a single preview frame: a 1/8th resolution version, with a bit of blurring. But, your preview frames can be completely different images if you really want.There's a lack of data when it comes to progressive images and user experience, so these are just my reckons:If you're on a bad connection, data doesn't arrive gradually like some throttling tools will have you believe. It tends to come in bursts. So, there's little benefit to progressive rendering on smaller images, and I'm not sure that many progressive phases is particularly useful.I think that it's nice to have a preview for images that may take some time to load. I've experienced this personally, where a site or app has given me something clearly not-loaded, but with enough detail to know what's coming. That's useful to me, as I can decide things like, if it's worth waiting for the whole thing. This is also why I think things like BlurHash are cute, but useless. They're not a preview, so there's little a user can do with the information provided.The preview frame I chose for the AVIF is enough to tell it's an open-wheel race car. If you know F1, you'll know what team it is. You might even know where the photo was taken. And it delivers that in ~11.5 kB.The JPEG XL gets a BlurHash-like preview on screen in ~2 kB, but it takes until ~63 kB to match the preview quality of the AVIF. After that, it continues to improve gradually, providing a more detailed and higher quality image as more data arrives.However, I'm not convinced this is a good user experience, as it presents the user with something they may mistake for fully-loaded, but poor quality. For example:Here's a crop of the JPEG XL, 80% loaded. It seems reasonable that someone would look at that, and just assume I took the picture badly, leaving parts out of focus. You could probably convince me that blurring the ApeCoin logo is a societal benefit, but it still feels like a suboptimal user experience.AVIF's system gives me more control, but it's also more complex.I encoded the large F1 image with and without progressive rendering enabled, adjusting the quality setting to keep the SSIMULACRA2 score around 70:With libjxl, progressive is basically free. In fact, it produced files 6–10% smaller. At default effort, it was also faster to encode, and used less memory. Decoding was ~10% faster in Firefox, but 12–20% slower in Chrome and Safari.With jixel, it depends on the effort. For jixel, I used progressive DC, with the centre of the image loading first. At jixel's default ('fast'), progressive made the file 12% bigger. At 'extraslow', it made the file 10% smaller, and 11% faster to encode, although it used 17% more memory. Decoding was barely affected, other than being 7–9% slower in Chrome.But ColorVideoVDP is less kind to progressive jixel. It rates jixel's progressive files slightly lower than the non-progressive versions, whereas it rates libjxl's progressive files slightly higher. Taking that into account, progressive jixel at 'extraslow' is only ~2% smaller than non-progressive, and at 'fast' it's around 18% bigger.Regular progressive AVIF has a bigger cost when it comes to encoding. It uses around twice the memory, and at default effort (s6), it takes twice as long to encode. At s0, encode time is only 9% longer, but the file is 14% bigger. And this is pure encode time - it doesn't factor in how you might generate the preview frame, e.g. adding some blur.Regular progressive AVIF is 29–44% slower to decode in Chrome, although the difference is smaller in other browsers (6–15%). Since Chrome is the only browser that supports rendering the progressive frames, that might explain it. Although Firefox and Safari are still having to decode the progressive frame, as the main image builds upon it.With AVIF, making the final frame a keyframe fixes the decoding overhead, at the cost of a longer encode time. At maximum effort, it results in a smaller file too, only 3–5% bigger than the non-progressive version. You could call this cheating, as there's now no 'progression' in terms of data - it's just two images in one. But, if it's a better user experience, who cares?Even with the overhead, progressive AVIF wins on decoding time, and usually on file size. The progressive AVIFs are 152–181 kB. jixel's 'extraslow' progressive JPEG XL is in that range at 166 kB, but jixel's default produces 252 kB, and libjxl's progressive files are 233–242 kB. The AVIFs decode 1.6–6x faster, with the biggest gap in Safari, which is particularly slow to decode jixel's files.Let's get back to lossy compression, but this time HDR! There are a few ways to encode HDR images, and we're going to look at two. (PQ) tells each pixel what to be. Each value maps to an absolute brightness, up to 10,000 nits, with the curve shaped so the data is spent where our eyes are most sensitive. If the image asks for colours and brightnesses the display can't show (no consumer display can hit 10,000 nits), the browser/OS has to tone-map it down, and how well that's done varies between platforms. are different. The main image is a regular SDR image (usually), and alongside it is a 'gain map', which applies a brightness and colour change to each pixel to achieve the HDR version.The same image will look exactly as you want on an SDR display - the gain map is simply ignored.If the display supports HDR, but maybe not as much as the image needs (for example, the screen is at low or maximum brightness), the browser/OS can apply as much of the gain map as it can handle.CSS and let us serve an SDR or PQ image to the user via the media query, but then you're relying on tone mapping in cases where the browser signals HDR support, but it doesn't support the full range.Although the JPEG XL format supports gain maps, no browser handles them, and the encoding story is messy.AVIF supports gain maps, and you encode them by providing two images: the SDR image and the HDR image. It uses those to calculate and encode the gain map.Your browser/screen doesn't support HDR, so the PQ images will look bad.At medium brightnesses, on an HDR screen, the gain map and PQ images look the same. At maximum brightnesses, on my Pixel 10 Pro and 2024 MacBook Pro, the PQ images get a bit blown out, and the gain map image looks better. At low brightness on my Pixel 10 Pro, again the gain map image looks better.This is because, at extreme brightness levels, the device doesn't have the full HDR headroom to display the image, and gain maps can handle these cases better. So, although gain maps seem to add a lot to the file size, I think it's worth it.Maybe there's a future where tone mapping gets much better, and the advantage of a gain map becomes less significant.Regular SSIMULACRA2 only understands SDR, so for this image, the scores come from an experimental HDR mode in fast-ssim2. That means these scores can't be compared to the SSIMULACRA2 scores elsewhere in this article. ColorVideoVDP handles HDR natively, and here it's modelling a 1,500 nit HDR monitor.The two metrics disagree a lot with this image. And they don't factor in the benefits of gain maps, so treat these results as a comparison between the PQ variants:File size: , but the metrics disagree on how much, and with which encoder.According to HDR SSIMULACRA2, jixel's default ranges from 8% smaller to 3% larger than PQ AVIF's default, and libjxl is 5–33% larger. At maximum efforts, jixel 'extraslow' is up to 15% smaller than PQ AVIF s0.According to ColorVideoVDP, libjxl is the clear winner. At default efforts, it's 28–53% smaller than PQ AVIF, and 17–37% smaller than gain map AVIF. At maximum efforts, it's up to 23% smaller than the best AVIF, but jixel 'extraslow' is roughly level with it, ranging from 12% smaller to 14% larger.The metrics also disagree about gain maps. HDR SSIMULACRA2 says gain map AVIF is 31–38% larger than PQ AVIF, but ColorVideoVDP says gain map AVIF is 11–25% than PQ AVIF.Encode time: . At default efforts, jixel is ~2x faster than PQ AVIF, and produces files around the same size or smaller, depending on the metric. libjxl's default is 5–47% slower than PQ AVIF, but given ColorVideoVDP's view of the file sizes, that's a reasonable trade. Gain map AVIF is the slowest, as it's calculating a gain map, then essentially encoding two images: ~3x slower than PQ AVIF.Encode memory: . At default efforts, jixel uses ~30% less memory than PQ AVIF. libjxl's default uses ~1.9x the memory of PQ AVIF, and gain map AVIF uses ~1.55x. At maximum efforts, libjxl uses ~6x the memory of PQ AVIF's default, and jixel 'extraslow' uses ~10x. PQ and gain map AVIF decode at around the same speed. JPEG XL takes 1.2–1.7x as long to decode in Chrome, although it's slightly faster at the top of the quality range. In Safari, it takes 1.6–3x as long. Firefox is particularly slow with these HDR JPEG XL images, taking ~4x as long as AVIF at all qualities. We're working on it.Higher effort is worth it for AVIF. For gain map AVIF, s5 gets you 9–12% smaller files for ~1.9x the encode time, and s0 gets you 14–20% smaller files for ~11x the encode time. For PQ AVIF, s0 gets you 14–19% smaller files, for 17–20x the encode time.Higher effort is worth it for jixel, up to 'slow'. 'slow' gets you 7–32% smaller files than its default 'fast', for ~3.8x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 1–9%, but takes ~10x longer than 'slow' and uses ~8.5x the memory. jixel only has a few data points for this image, so these numbers are rough.Higher effort isn't worth it for libjxl. libjxl's maximum effort gets you 2–7% smaller files than its default, but takes ~15x longer.It will be interesting to see how JPEG XL handles gain maps once they're fully supported.JPEG XL allows you to convert an existing JPEG to JPEG XL without additional loss. I tested this with the F1 image at a range of sizes and JPEG qualities:The JPEG XL is 9–20% smaller than the JPEG. The saving grows with resolution, from ~9% at 400 pixels wide to ~20% at 4,900 pixels wide. The saving is slightly smaller at higher JPEG qualities. libjxl and jixel produce practically identical file sizes.For small images, JPEG XL is slower to decode than JPEG, taking 1.4–2.7x as long, depending on the browser. But it's just a millisecond or two.For larger images, JPEG XL is faster to decode in Chrome and Safari. From ~1,000 pixels wide, it matches JPEG, and at the largest sizes, it decodes in around half the time. In Firefox, it ends up around the same speed as JPEG.jixel's output is slightly slower to decode than libjxl's in Chrome and Firefox, by up to ~25%. But again, these are small numbers, at most a few milliseconds.Of course, if you have the original, you'd be way better off creating a proper new lossy version with AVIF or JPEG XL, but it's pretty cool that the JPEGs end up smaller, and sometimes faster to decode. Although, I suppose this is just pointing to a missing optimisation in browser JPEG decoders.It is very rare to need lossless images on the web. As we've already seen, even for things like screenshots and illustrations, lossy AVIF handles them really well. Ironically, this page is one of the outliers, because I wanted to show the compressed versions vs their lossless counterparts. Thankfully, JPEG XL is great at lossless! At default efforts, libjxl produces the smallest files for every image except the illustration, where WebP matches it. WebP is 9–17% larger for photos, and AVIF is 33–122% larger. At highest efforts, libjxl and jixel are within a few percent of each other, WebP is 5–44% larger, and AVIF is 29–176% larger.Encode time: . libjxl's default takes 0.1–0.5 seconds, which is faster than WebP's default, and similar to AVIF's default, while producing smaller files than both.Encode memory: or , depending on the image. WebP's default uses around half the memory of libjxl's default (55–110 MB vs 110–250 MB), but libjxl's files are smaller. For photos, WebP can't match libjxl's default file size even at its maximum effort, which uses more memory than libjxl's default. For the screenshot, they use around the same memory, but libjxl's file is smaller. The illustration is the exception: WebP's maximum effort produces a file 20% smaller than libjxl's default, using the same memory.Decode time: or , depending on the image. WebP decodes photos in 17–39 ms in all browsers, and the screenshot in ~5 ms. libjxl's output takes 1–2.2x as long in Chrome, 1.4–2.7x as long in Firefox, and 2.1–3.2x as long in Safari. But for photos, JPEG XL's smaller files more than make up for this on a first load, unless the connection is really fast. For the screenshot and illustration, WebP's decode advantage wins. Lossless AVIF is particularly slow to decode, taking up to 4x as long as libjxl's output in Chrome. It's significantly larger than the others, and slower to decode.jixel's 'medium' setting is the sweet spot for file size. It beats libjxl's default on every image (0.5–23% smaller), and is within 2–3% of the best result for photos, taking 0.4–0.7 seconds. But it uses 470–670 MB of memory, and its output is slower to decode than libjxl's, particularly in Safari.jixel's 'slow' and 'extraslow' output is very slow to decode for photos. ~200–290 ms, compared to 22–95 ms for libjxl's output. That's 2–13x slower, depending on the browser. It's also slow for the alpha image, at 80–123 ms compared to 14–27 ms for libjxl's output. This doesn't happen with the screenshot and illustration. This means, for my use-case on this page, I'd avoid it.libjxl's maximum effort is very slow. It produces files 2–7% smaller than its default for photos, and ~25% smaller for the screenshot and illustration, but takes 9–46 seconds, which is 50–180x as long as its default. jixel gets the same results in a couple of seconds.jixel's default 'fast' setting isn't great for lossless. It's the fastest encoder by far (40–80 ms), but its files are 16–32% larger than libjxl's default for photos, and ~80% larger for the screenshot and illustration.jixel's patches feature helps a bit with the screenshot (4–9% smaller), but makes no difference to the illustration.Animated image formats are dumb and animated JPEG XL is no exception. Video formats are better at video. They're built for it. They're optimised for it. Not just in terms of encoding, but also in terms of playback.I encoded a short clip, and the animated AVIF was 725 kB, and the JPEG XL was 2.17 MB for the same ColorVideoVDP score (9.5).The JPEG XL is super noisy compared to the AVIF, because each frame is encoded individually, and arttifacts land in different places per frame.AVIF is basically the keyframe format of AV1 video, with a bunch of still-image-specific optimisations thrown in. Animated AVIF however, is pretty much just a repackaging of AV1 video. You can convert an AV1 MP4 to AVIF and back losslessly - it's just a container change. That's why it performs so much better, because it's built for motion.However, animated AVIF plays like shit in Chrome and Safari. It's fine in Firefox, so this is purely an implementation problem. But… is right there.No, I'm not adding a demo. I don't want it on my server. Use video formats for video.I already gave you my conclusions at the start, so I guess I'm ready to hit publish.I'm a little nervous about this, because discourse around JPEG XL can get a little… weird. I see a lot of conspiracy theories about Google trying to 'silence' JPEG XL, even though one of the leads of the project worked at Google, as part of a team that were working on JPEG XL. That same leader claimed that the post-COVID layoffs wouldn't have happened if companies simply used JPEG XL. I was recently called a racist for asking about JPEG XL use-cases. This kind of thing just doesn't happen with other technologies and standards I follow. So, urm, I'm kinda bracing for impact here.My first version of this article was very negative about JPEG XL, but then I heard about jixel, and honestly, I'm really excited about it. There's serious competition between AVIF and JPEG XL now, and whoever wins, we'll all benefit from better image compression.

item.title: US Rep Announces Congressional Legislation to Protect Video Game Ownership
item.author: DeepLogin
item.content:encoded: Today, (NY-15) announced he will introduce the , legislation that would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations protecting consumers’ ability to own and play the video games they purchase.Over the past few years, video game companies have moved toward digital-only games and consoles, removing the option to buy or use physical games. These digital games are often sold as revocable licenses rather than owned outright, leaving players dependent on the company’s continued support. NBA 2K25 is a clear example. The game, which retailed for $69.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the All-Star Edition, will be delisted from digital storefronts on October 30 and will have its online servers shut down on December 31, only two years after its initial release. No consumer should have a game they paid for pulled out from under them on a company’s arbitrary timeline.“When you pay for a game, you should own it,” said Rep. Torres. “Consumers must have the right to own, the right to play, and the right to transfer the games they buy. A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale. Families in the Bronx and across the country save up to buy these games, and they deserve better than a license that can vanish at any time. The Power To The Players Act ensures consumers own what they buy and can keep playing long after a company moves on.”Under the bill, buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it. Games with online functionality would also be required to provide an offline mode before the servers supporting them are shut down. The legislation aims to close the gap between buying a game and owning it. By preserving consumers’ ability to own and resell their games, the bill would ensure that players can keep playing the games they paid for with friends and family for years to come.

item.title: Postgres 19 delayed after AI reviewers find more bugs than humans can fix
item.author: magoghm
item.content:encoded: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has delayed the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest iteration of the popular open source database, and held back an unusual number of features. Once slated for release in late September or early October, PostgreSQL 19 is now expected to be generally available around November 19. Developers have also dropped between eight and 10 significant features.Explaining the number of reverts — features whose rollouts have now been postponed to next year's release, PostgreSQL 20 — Peter Eisentraut, veep at EDB, a PostgreSQL support and consultancy, said the reason could be at least in part attributed to the LLM code reviews used by developers. In a blog post, Eisentraut, who is a leading PostgreSQL committer, said some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix "quickly and during beta."However, the introduction of LLM-assisted code review also uncovered a long tail of “relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases” which, in past times, developers might not have noticed until much later, most likely issuing bug fixes in the five years following launch. “With LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring at a list of forty defect reports. Even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time.”When the big updates for PostgreSQL 19 were written, LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is now, we're told, but in the months leading up to the launch, the AI-supported reviews became better understood and more effective. “The effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future development cycles,” Eisentraut said. He was also at pains to point out that the reverts were not down to “vibe coding” in development, as the technique was not available when most of the new features were written. Postgres was first proposed by Michael Stonebraker in 1986. In 1994, Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen replaced the query language POSTQUEL with SQL, and in 1995 made the database freely available and modifiable under a more permissive license, renaming it PostgreSQL. It has since become the most popular database among professional developers owing to the services the big three hyperscalers built on it as well as the range of wire-compatible distributed systems available. Among the features pulled from the PostgreSQL 19 iteration is support for SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), which became part of the SQL standard in 2023. The feature provides syntax for exploring relationships between nodes connected by edges. PostgreSQL's implementation was removed over unresolved issues.At the time, PostgreSQL contributor Tom Lane warned: "At this point I'd be willing to bet dinner that if we ship it in v19 there will be post-release bug discoveries that are unfixable until v20."Despite the delay, Eisentraut promises PostgreSQL 19 will still be “a great release,” that includes , which avoids the table-lock operation used to reclaim disk space. “And it will be very robust, after all the additional scrutiny,” he said. The features reverted from PostgreSQL 19 will likely make it into PostgreSQL 20. Just a few months ago, developers expected PostgreSQL 20 to have no new features, just bug fixes. Now, it is likely to have the new features left over from the earlier release, Eisentraut said.®

item.title: Rendering pretty sky in Around The World game
item.author: ibobev
item.content:encoded: This post is part of a series about Around The World, a game of exploration and discovery at sea. The game is currently in early development. If you're new to this project, you can read up on it here.In the last post, I got the game’s clouds to look passable. But after looking at it during playtesting, I still wasn’t satisfied with the way the overall picture of how sea, sky and clouds came together. With some small tweaks, things started to look a lot better.Light scattering in cloudsI ended the previous post using a lookup table rendered out by povray, that contains the amount of light scattered out of clouds depending on light angle (horizontal axis) and cloud density (vertical axis):And I wrote about my dissatisfaction with this table:I am beginning to suspect that povray doesn’t actually simulate multiple scattering at all; the documentation does not say yes or no either way. No matter how many samples and intervals I configure, I can’t get the bottom of those spheres to become lighter.Once again I’m tempted to write my own recursive ray tracer to confirm my suspicions, but I resisted the urge […]In the end, curiosity got the better of me and I write my own multithreaded recursive Monte Carlo ray tracer in a few hundred lines of Rust. It’s extremely dumb and hard-coded for this specific situation, so it only renders one perfectly spherical cloud of uniform density. But it was enough to confirm that indeed, povray does not simulate multiple scattering. With multiple scattering, the lookup table looks very different:The comparison is not entirely apples to apples, because I also tweaked some parameters and the scaling of the axes. But overall, the effect is clear: the light coming out of the cloud is distributed much more uniformly, making the cloud appear lighter overall.At low density (thin clouds), the difference is not very apparent; the top rows of the lookup tables are very similar. After all, there isn’t much opportunity for a light ray to be scattered more than once when density is low. So let’s compare the look at a higher density, representing a thicker cloud layer. Here are some clouds rendered with the old LUT:The “metallic” look that I mentioned in the last post is now gone; cloud bottoms are brighter, and lighting is smoother overall.In reality, clouds aren’t just lit by the sun directly. They also receive, and scatter, indirect sunlight from the sky. Since this light is usually tinted blue, the clouds should take on a more blueish hue as well.I don’t want to add a constant “blue” term, since that is only correct during daytime; we’d want clouds to follow the current colour of the sky even at sunrise, sunset or night. How could I do that in Godot?The answer turns out to be simple, but requires some understanding of how Godot’s light rendering works. Besides direct light, which we already handle, Godot also takes into account indirect light from the environment. This all happens under the hood outside user control, so my understanding is vague, but good enough to be useful.As far as I understand it, indirect light is sampled from a cube map or two, containing radiance and irradiance from every direction. (I know radiance and irradiance are different things, but I don’t fully understand the distinction.) For diffuse materials like clouds, I’d expect the this cube map (these cube maps?) to be sampled in the direction of the surface normal, since that represents where most indirect light is coming from.At the bottom of clouds, this normal points downwards towards the ground, so the cloud is rendered with little indirect light here. In reality, it receive indirect light, but from above: it’s just scattered through the cloud. So, what would happen if we tweak the normal to point upwards to the sky instead? The effect is subtle but important; here’s before:The clouds have indeed gotten a blueish hue, making them blend in with the sky much better, and generally giving them a softer and more distant look, as clouds should have. I like this a lot!How about a sunset, when the sky is not almost uniformly blue? Here’s before:The bottoms of the clouds are tinted orange, because the incoming direct sunlight is orange due to heavy Rayleigh outscattering. Here’s the same sunset with tweaked normals:The clouds have turned pink! I think this is much closer to how real sunsets look; the pink hue is apparently the result of mixing red (direct sunlight) and blue (indirect sky light), with the green channel getting somewhat lost in between.Another thing that bothered me was that the sky looked unnaturally yellow near the horizon. This is fine and expected when the sun is low, but it was happening even with the sun straight overhead, like here:I suspected that this was due to applying too much outscattering during the raymarch compared to inscattering, so I tried various hacks like adding a fake multiple inscattering term. In the end, a better fix turned out to be changing the order in which operations happen during the ray march. Instead of:Add (blueish) light scattered into the ray segmentAttenuate by outscattering over the ray segment (reddening)Attenuate by outscattering over the ray segment (reddening)Add (blueish) light scattered into the ray segmentThe effect is that less attenuation happens along the way, compared to inscattering, and the result looks much better:This should theoretically be an artifact of the numerical integration approach, and so the difference should disappear when increasing the number of integration steps. But it doesn’t, so I suspect there’s still something wrong somewhere. But it’ll do for now and hopefully forever.To render a realistic sky, I have to use parameters of the real Earth, like atmospheric density, height and planet size. However, the planet in my game is about 75× smaller than Earth, and so it’s curved more strongly. So when we use Earth parameters for the sky, the sky’s horizon ends up above the actual horizon. In between the two horizons, the sky shader pretends that the atmospheric density continues to increase exponentially towards the centre of the planet, which causes a dark band that’s especially noticeable during sunrise and sunset:To make the two horizons meet, I applied a simple hack to the sky shader: add a small value to the y (vertical) component of the global view vector, then re-normalize it. The effect is to pull down the entire sky, most strongly around the horizon, causing the dark band to disappear behind the horizon:It’s a hack, but cheap and effective.Ah, the bane of every modern 3D game artist. Games are rendered in HDR (high dynamic range) nowadays, meaning their colour values can go brighter than the maximum of 1.0. If we display these on a typical monitor, the result has to be clamped, resulting in patches of oversaturated colours:To fix this, some formula is typically used to map the HDR values back into LDR space for display. Godot implements several tone mappers; I found Reinhard to be too dark, and ACES and AgX too desaturated. So in the end, I settled on Filmic tone mapper with a white point of 2.0:It gives especially the clouds a nice soft look, and makes them fade into the distance much better.The choice of white point is still fairly subtle since Godot itself recommends at least 6.0 for “photorealistic rendering”, but that just makes everything look darker.Tuning the tone mapping is a tricky endeavour, because changes to the tone mapper affect everything that came before. So in practice, this process was not as linear as I wrote it down here, and required some back-and-forth between adjusting the tone mapper and the scene lighting. For one, I literally reduced the brightness of the sky by a factor of 2, which gave much better contrast after tone mapping.If we want a proper day-night cycle, we need the sun to rise and set. And if we want our planet to feel Earth-like, the times of sunrise and sunset should depend on location and season. This dependence is due to the motion of the Earth around the sun and around its own axis. A similar thing happens with the motion of the moon through the sky, and the phases of the moon.It seemed complicated to figure out all the math to do these calculations properly. So I took an easier route: I modelled the entire situation in the engine, making the planet and its moon spin around like in an orrery:Then I let the engine figure out the inverse transformation to determine where things are in the sky, from the point of view of an observer somewhere on the planet’s surface. This worked well, and the rendered orrery turned out to be a useful debugging aid.After all that, I think I owe you another sunrise video, don’t I? And let’s find a scenic in-game spot for it, too!

item.title: Waymo in Toronto
item.author: ChrisArchitect
item.content:encoded: Waymo is officially heading to Canada! We’re laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, investing in local facilities and jobs, with the goal of welcoming our first riders in 2028.In the coming days, you’ll start to see Waymo vehicles on the streets of Toronto as we begin driving manually. We are taking a rigorous, phased, safety-first approach starting with high-definition mapping of local street networks and testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to Toronto’s distinct driving conditions.“Expanding into Canada marks an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey,” said Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana.“Toronto is one of the world’s great cities — innovative, diverse, and forward-looking. We’re proud to bring the Waymo Driver to Canada’s largest city and to partner with the vibrant business, arts and cultural communities that share our commitment to safer streets and more accessible mobility.”To serve Toronto, we’re partnering with Element Fleet Management, a Toronto-headquartered company and global leader in intelligent fleet and mobility solutions that will provide end-to-end fleet management services. Together with Element and our partners, we’ll invest in hundreds of roles over time spanning fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and other operations functions that support our service. This deep partnership builds on Waymo’s existing ties to Canada, which includes our long-term investor relationship with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and our manufacturing partner, Magna International."As a Canadian company, we are proud to be expanding our partnership with Waymo to help bring autonomous ride-hailing to Toronto,” said Laura Dottori-Attanasio, Chief Executive Officer, Element Fleet Management. Together with Waymo, Element will help create employment opportunities providing the fleet expertise, operational capabilities, and intelligent mobility solutions needed to support autonomous fleets reliably and at scale."As one of North America’s fastest-growing metropolitan regions, Toronto has both evolving mobility demands and a dynamic and growing number of tools. From bike lanes to public transit, Waymo’s all-weather Driver can provide an additional option that complements the city’s transportation ecosystem. The data from over 400 million fully autonomous kilometres driven shows the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) crashes involving serious injury or worse compared to humans in the cities where we operate.Safety and accessibility are fundamental to Waymo's mission to be the world's most trusted driver, and we're proud to collaborate with leading accessibility and mobility advocacy organizations, including BALANCE for Blind Adults, CNIB, Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians, and Epilepsy Ontario, among others.“Innovation that removes barriers to independence is at the heart of everything we do. Waymo’s history of partnering with the sight loss community to build accessible solutions is encouraging and their decision to engage with us early reflects the kind of approach that leads to real results,” said Michelle McQuigge, CEO, BALANCE for Blind Adults.We can't wait to help residents and visitors explore everything Toronto has to offer. If you’re ready to experience Waymo in Toronto, please sign up for updates to be among the first to ride when we’re ready: waymo.com/waymo-in-canada.Waymo arrive officiellement au Canada ! Nous préparons le lancement de notre service de transport par véhicules autonomes à Toronto. Nous investissons dans les infrastructures locales et dans la création d’emplois en vue d’accueillir nos premiers passagers en 2028.Au cours des prochains jours, vous commencerez à voir des véhicules Waymo circuler dans les rues de Toronto, avec un conducteur au volant. Notre démarche est rigoureuse et axée avant tout sur la sécurité. Nous procédons par étapes, en commençant par cartographier le réseau routier local en haute définition, puis en effectuant des essais avec des spécialistes qualifiés de la conduite autonome au volant. Cette phase nous permettra de vérifier que le Waymo Driver s’adapte aux conditions de conduite propres à Toronto.« Notre arrivée au Canada marque une étape importante dans le développement international de Waymo », a déclaré Tekedra Mawakana, codirectrice générale de l’entreprise. « Toronto est l’une des plus grandes métropoles du monde : une ville innovante, diversifiée et résolument tournée vers l’avenir. Nous sommes fiers d’introduire le Waymo Driver dans la plus grande ville du Canada et de collaborer avec les communautés dynamiques des affaires, des arts et de la culture qui partagent notre engagement envers des rues plus sécuritaires et une mobilité plus accessible. »Pour assurer notre service à Toronto, nous faisons équipe avec Element Fleet Management, une entreprise dont le siège social se trouve à Toronto et qui est un leader mondial des solutions intelligentes de gestion de flottes et de mobilité. Element nous fournira des services complets de gestion de flottes. Avec Element et nos autres partenaires, nous investirons progressivement dans la création de centaines d’emplois liés à l’entretien de la flotte, aux essais sur route, au service à la clientèle et à d’autres activités nécessaires à l’exploitation de notre service. Ce partenariat s’inscrit dans la continuité des liens que Waymo a déjà tissés avec le Canada, notamment avec l’Office d’investissement du régime de pensions du Canada (Investissements RPC), un investisseur de longue date, et Magna International, son partenaire manufacturier.« En tant qu’entreprise canadienne, nous sommes fiers d’élargir notre partenariat avec Waymo afin de contribuer à l’arrivée des services de transport de personnes à la demande par véhicules autonomes à Toronto, a déclaré Laura Dottori-Attanasio, présidente et cheffe de la direction d’Element Fleet Management. Ensemble, Element et Waymo contribueront à créer des possibilités d’emploi en mettant à profit l’expertise d’Element en gestion de flottes, ses capacités opérationnelles et ses solutions de mobilité intelligente pour soutenir le déploiement à grande échelle de flottes de véhicules autonomes, tout en assurant la fiabilité de leurs opérations. »Toronto figure parmi les régions métropolitaines dont la croissance est la plus rapide en Amérique du Nord. Les besoins en matière de mobilité y évoluent et les options de transport se multiplient. Des pistes cyclables au transport en commun, le Waymo Driver, conçu pour fonctionner par tous les temps, pourrait offrir une option supplémentaire en complément des moyens de transport existants. Selon les données recueillies sur plus de 400 millions de kilomètres parcourus en conduite entièrement autonome, les véhicules Waymo ont été impliqués dans 95 % moins d’accidents entraînant des blessures graves ou plus graves que les véhicules conduits par des humains dans les villes où le service est offert. Cela représente 20 fois moins d’accidents de ce type.La sécurité et l’accessibilité sont à la base de la mission de Waymo : devenir le service de conduite autonome auquel le public fait le plus confiance au monde. Nous sommes fiers de collaborer avec des organismes de premier plan qui œuvrent en faveur de l’accessibilité et de la mobilité, notamment BALANCE for Blind Adults, l’Institut national canadien pour les aveugles (INCA), Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians et Epilepsy Ontario.« L’innovation qui favorise l’autonomie est au cœur de tout ce que nous faisons. L’expérience de Waymo en matière de collaboration avec des personnes ayant une déficience visuelle pour concevoir des solutions accessibles est encourageante. Sa décision de nous consulter dès le début montre qu’une telle approche peut donner des résultats concrets », a déclaré Michelle McQuigge, PDG de BALANCE for Blind Adults.Nous sommes ravis d’aider les résidents et les visiteurs à découvrir tout ce que Toronto a à offrir. Si vous avez envie de faire l’essai du Waymo Driver à Toronto, inscrivez-vous pour recevoir nos mises à jour et être parmi les premiers informés du lancement de notre service : waymo.com/waymo-in-canada.

item.title: Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD
item.author: rs_rs_rs_rs_rs
item.content:encoded: Calif frequently publishes our offensive research and work, but we otherwise don't draw much attention to the defensive work we do — assisting open source projects with remediation, patch generation, cryptographic improvements, and internal engineering projects we carry out for our clients.Earlier this year, we reported some vulnerabilities, often along with suggested patches to OpenBSD. One traced back roughly 37 years to the original BSD sources, where a shared memory attachment counter was defined as a signed 16-bit short. Repeatedly forking a process with shared memory attachment records could push that counter past its maximum value of 32,767, causing it to wrap to a negative value. This integer overflow could lead to a use-after-free via a race condition; combined with a separate out-of-bounds write in the kernel, it allowed local privilege escalation to root. The issues were addressed in errata 026 and 018, respectively.We managed to get local root in OpenBSD with / / enabled without the use of an information disclosure vulnerability via the following path:Map 127 SysV shared memory segments, unmap them via , and fork 259 processes to wrap the shared memory attach count to -32,643. Perform heap grooming and layout, using metrics from sysctl( (such as and ) to track allocations and determine when new pages are allocated. Win the race condition using in one process while attaching a new size-confused shared memory segment in a helper process. Align IP socket allocations and set to a non-default value of 2 to allocate a persistent 16-byte . Its final word packs two 16-bit counters: imo + 12 = imo_num_memberships | imo_max_memberships << 16. Trigger the conditional out-of-bounds write to overwrite both the number of memberships and maximum memberships fields. the socket to traverse the group members, triggering atomic decrements that modify the PTE self-referential mapping twice, switching it from user to supervisor accessible mapping, and achieving kernel code execution by overwriting a predictable kernel pointer. Clean up shared memory accounting and restore the overwritten kernel pointer to obtain a root shell.That's the short of the matter, the longer version is more interesting, including the history of the vulnerability, as a short can be traced back ~37 years ago, in the original BSD sources.Taking a step back, this vulnerability ended up getting code execution via a primitive, where the was caused by a , the was our userland memory mapping that was made supervisor mode accessible to bypass /, and the was a predictable kernel pointer location.While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic. Both the boot-time allocator and the best-fit allocator lack base address randomization. Consequently, early boot allocations consistently land at predictable locations across boots on the same hardware. When these predictable structure allocations contain function pointers, they become ideal targets for exploitation. For instance, the exploit reliably targets the and handlers, overwriting one to gain control flow and using the other to restore the overwritten pointer.Aside from the aforementioned errata fixes, there's several other approaches that can be taken to either eliminate or reduce the likelihood of those avenues being used again.Firstly, we can implement safe-unlinking, a technique that checks doubly linked list invariants before performing the unlink memory writes. If the invariants are violated, then a suitable or is called, depending on if user mode or kernel mode, preventing memory corruption from occurring. An example implementation is here. FreeBSD and NetBSD have an implementation of safe-unlinking in their implementation.Secondly, we can randomize the self-referential PTE map allocation address so that the targeted atomic decrement locations would not be possible. This is done by using a random byte () and selecting a PML4 slot (320 + (random_byte & 127)) at boot time, and installing the recursive entry at that location. The definition becomes a runtime expression, yielding bases from through at 512-GiB intervals. An example implementation is here. In case randomization is not suitable, other options might suffice, such as marking the PTE as read-only, and changing CR0.WP during modification.Thirdly, the kernel allocator can be made non-deterministic using two approaches; by randomizing the base address where memory allocations occur at boot time, and additionally randomizing the allocation order at run time. The base address randomization is effectively free as the gap it creates can still be used later on; while runtime randomization does incur some overhead during allocation - it may be possible that more in-depth allocator changes could alleviate this impact. Either approach would be sufficient to break the predictable pointer location without additional vulnerabilities, be it software or hardware.Furthermore, there are existing and upcoming compiler features that can be used to mitigate against entire vulnerabilities, from array bounds sanitizer (a subset of Undefined Behaviour sanitizer) which can eliminate out of bounds fixed size array accesses. Calif has suggested to FreeBSD that the array bounds sanitizer may make a useful exploit mitigation that can be enabled in release builds, along with privately reporting 21 issues that the array bounds sanitizer would have caught; some with local privilege escalation security impact. An upcoming compiler feature that can be used to help mitigate against heap issues is Alloc Tokens, which can be used to isolate pointer containing allocations from non-pointer allocations. This isolation can make overflows from the non-pointer containing allocation much more difficult to exploit by preventing pointer access, along with making vulnerability classes like Use-after-Free unable to use the opposite type of allocation as the replacement memory allocation.Since its inception, OpenBSD has consistently championed proactive security through source code auditing, the replacement of insecure APIs, advanced password hashing, cryptography, privilege separation, sandboxing, along with memory safety via and ; frequently setting the standard for system and network hardening.By proactively hardening, and adapting new and existing mitigation options, we can often systematically neutralize entire classes of exploitation primitives; or at the very least, increase the attacker's cost (i.e. additional time investment, additional vulnerabilities needed to exploit an issue, find alternative avenues, etc). Investing in defensive improvements before vulnerabilities are actively targeted raises the bar for attackers, helping ensure robust protection and long-term resilience. In the age of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, mitigating against entire vulnerability classes, combined with increasing attack complexity only becomes more critical.

item.title: What on Earth Is Dekton?
item.author: wawayanda
item.content:encoded: print subscribersI am aware that I am a bit of a kitchen equipment nerd, okay? So maybe you don’t have to roll your eyes theatrically like my cousins did when I tell you my wife and I got a swanky induction cooktop that was, well, kind of pricey for a middle-class couple? And maybe you can imagine my irritation when it turned out that the swanky induction cooktop – did I mention it was pricey? – did not include the necessary smooth cooking surface above the induction burners, and that you had to buy the cooking surface separately from a separate company, a fact not exactly advertised on the website, and that the surface could not be tempered glass, which is what I had thought was on top of induction ranges, a sheet of which costs maybe $30 per square foot, but a special, newly created material called Dekton that cost five times as much. ‘What on earth is Dekton?’ I asked the heavens, or at least my wife.My question turned out to have two answers. The first is that Dekton is an artificial material invented by the Spanish company Cosentino in 2013 that is amazingly heat-, pressure-, scratch-, shatter-, and stain-resistant – a high-tech substance that would have been almost impossible to fashion even thirty years ago. The other answer, equally true, is that Dekton is basically porcelain.Paradoxically, porcelain is both one of humankind’s oldest high technologies and one of its newest. The earliest proto-porcelain was created more than three thousand years ago, and was, for the time, an astonishing technical feat, as unprecedented as the roughly concurrent development of iron metallurgy. Iron technology had its second flowering in the mid-nineteenth century, when the invention of the Bessemer and Siemens-Martin refining processes allowed manufacturers to produce cheap, high-quality steel. Porcelain is having its resurgence today – indeed, high-tech ceramics are key elements in the ongoing upsurge in materials science, the study of the relationship between a substance’s structure and its physical properties.Much attention is rightfully focused now on the rise of the digital world and the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence. But that attention sometimes obscures the ongoing, equally important transformation of our physical world, the built environment, by materials science. Unleashing a cataract of innovation so ubiquitous as to be almost invisible, materials science has literally changed the walls around us. Porcelain is a reminder that the drive to create new types of matter has long played a powerful role in human history.The initial steps toward porcelain occurred when potters in northern China started to tinker with an unusual clay, chalk colored and fine grained, called kaolin. Kaolin was known for its color, useful in paints, coatings, and fillers. Potters learned that subjecting this soft, white, unremarkable-looking mud to extreme temperatures produced startling effects.Ordinary clay looks like amorphous glop but actually is composed of huge numbers of microscopic crystals. The crystals have an unusual structure: flat plates stacked atop each other like playing cards in a deck, loosely held together by hydroxyl groups (hydrogen and oxygen bound together, or -OH, in chemists’ terms). When clay is cooked in a kiln, the hydroxyl groups vibrate and break free, causing the plates to fall apart and reform into long, needle-shaped crystals that lock together into a sturdy structure. Meanwhile, the free hydroxyls merge, becoming water molecules that steam away in the hot kiln, leaving behind oxygen in the new crystals.In China, like everywhere else, ceramics had been a foundational industry for millennia. Clay was a primary part of construction (bricks, adobe, wattle-and-daub), cooking (pots, tableware), art (paints as well as sculpture), and even communication – clay tablets were the first surfaces used for writing. But porcelain was a giant leap, a concatenation of multiple innovations.Ordinary kilns couldn’t reach the temperatures required to fire porcelain, partly because their exhaust vents, located on the ‘roof’, let out the hot air almost as fast as it was created, cooling the kiln. (This is a problem for conventional home fireplaces, which are fun to look at in use but wildly inefficient as a means of heating.) Chinese potters designed downdrafts, which forced the hot air to escape through floor vents, trapping the heat around the pottery. Alarmingly, ordinary kilns would shatter or even melt at such high temperatures. Chinese potters invented new types of heat-resistant brick. And so on.When Europeans first saw East Asian porcelain, probably in the thirteenth century, they were astounded. Harder, stronger, finer, smoother, and more lustrous than any other pottery, it became an obsessive object of desire, ‘white gold’ for the Continent’s wealthy and powerful. Enormous sets of gleaming white china became symbols of luxury – the private jets and invite-only clubs of the Renaissance era.Unhappy about the high prices charged by the merchants who imported porcelain from Asia, European elites spent lavishly on efforts to make their own porcelain – and failed comprehensively for several centuries.A key problem was that nobody on the Continent knew that porcelain was made from kaolin. Or that kaolinite alone didn’t actually contain enough glassy liquid silicate to make proper porcelain, so that Chinese potters added pulverized ‘China stone’ – a type of partly decomposed granite containing silicon – into the kaolinite.Trying to make their wares porcelain-white, European potters added materials like tin oxide and ground glass to the clay, an approach that led to Italian maiolica, French faience, and Delftware. The results were often beautiful, but lacked porcelain’s impermeability to water, high tensile strength, and the distinctive ring made by porcelain cups when tapped with a spoon.Enter Count Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus (1651–1708), a mathematician, physicist, and philosopher born in the Electorate of Saxony. Tschirnhaus initially studied math and philosophy but in his twenties became fascinated by porcelain. Beginning in about 1679, he conducted a series of experiments that used concave copper mirrors to beam intensely hot sunlight on multiple types of metals, minerals, and ceramics. Eventually he realized that glass lenses could outperform mirrors and invented a method of casting glass to make big, thick lenses for focusing sunlight, sending samples of the results to European monarchs in an unsuccessful quest to obtain financial backing to establish a science academy in Saxony.In the winter of 1693–94, Tschirnhaus discovered a surprise: a type of clay that wouldn’t melt. Dug from Colditz, about 25 miles southeast of Leipzig, in Saxony, it contained kaolin (Tschirnhaus, of course, didn’t know this). Adding alabaster or chalk to the clay and heating the mix produced a hard, yellow, somewhat translucent ceramic that Tschirnhaus called ‘wax porcelain’. Unfortunately, he couldn’t produce it in quantity – his lenses could focus sunlight on an area of 10 to 15 square centimeters but not heat spaces of any size. When he tried making his porcelain in commercial kilns, their walls shattered or melted. Tschirnhaus was struggling to develop a better kiln when he was approached by Augustus the Strong, the ruler of Saxony.Tschirnhaus, Böttger, and Gottfried Pabst von Ohain, a high-ranking mining official (in those days, the closest thing available to an earth scientist), developed a red clay that could be made into bricks suitable for porcelain kilns. In June 1708, Pabst von Ohain found a source of white clay – nearly pure kaolin, though he didn’t know it – and shipped it to the other two. Mixing the white clay with ground limestone and heating it in kilns made from the new red clay in August and September, Tschirnhaus single-handedly created a cup that looked and behaved very much like white Chinese porcelain.He did not live to enjoy his triumph. In October, Tschirnhaus suddenly dropped dead, supposedly of dysentery. On his deathbed, he gave Pabst von Ohain a black box filled with documents. The box was found in Böttger’s belongings after his death, which may explain why he wrote to Augustus in March 1709, claiming to be the sole discoverer of the process to make porcelain. Augustus officially chartered the Royal Porcelain Manufacture in Meissen, another small town near Dresden, the following year and put Böttger in charge. It took ten more years for its workers to figure out that ‘China clay’ (or, more precisely, a similar local stone) was a better additive than limestone. Meissen then became Europe’s porcelain center. Augustus made so much money that he built a ‘Japanese palace’, filled it with Meissen copies of Asian originals, and crowed to visitors that he had beaten the Chinese – correctly, because Meissen porcelain was harder and less porous than the original.If Meissen was Porcelain 2.0, the Dekton for my cooktop is Porcelain 3.0 or more. Made by baking a slurry of ground porcelain, glass, and quartz into slabs, running the slabs through a huge hydraulic press that applies 25,000 metric tons of pressure, and hardening them at 1,200 degrees centigrade, Dekton took six years and almost $200 million to invent. Traditional ceramics contain microscopic voids and flaws that act as ‘stress concentrators’, focusing rather than diffusing the energy from impacts, which is what causes them to crack. The high pressure and heat used to produce Dekton cause atoms in the particles of kaolinite and quartz to diffuse across the boundaries where they touch, turning the entire thing into what amounts to a single solid mass. In consequence, Dekton has nearly eliminated porcelain’s long-standing weakness: its brittleness and structural fragility.Dekton is but one part of an ongoing resurgence in porcelain, which itself is part of the still larger revolution in materials science. The field was founded in the 1940s and 1950s, when physicists, chemists, and engineers had to work together in the Second World War, the Cold War, and the space race. But it really took off in the 1980s and 1990s, with the development of precision measuring and manufacturing techniques. Most of its innovations have been incremental, but the accumulated total has had enormous impact in our daily lives.tens of thousandsAnother personal example: My daughter, hit with a rare bone infection at age eleven, now has a porcelain hip joint – porcelain because the previous cobalt and chromium replacement joints can release metal ions into the bloodstream, which can migrate into the placenta of pregnant women, potentially harming the fetus. About the same time that ceramics firms introduced wet-activated tiles, researchers deployed 3D printing to create porous, lattice-like ‘bioceramic’ structures to replace defective bone. The structures are not permanent replacements but scaffolds that allow blood vessels and bone cells to migrate into the spaces in the bioceramic. Over time, the porcelain structure dissolves and is replaced by the patient’s own tissue. (The scaffold is expelled from the body.)I could go on to talk about the use of nanotechnology to fill porcelain pores to enhance color depth and stain resistance, imprinting porcelain with silver ion layers to enhance antimicrobial activity, or the use of lithium disilicate to make ultrathin dental implants of unprecedented strength. But maybe the best way to say it is that my grandmother, who proudly displayed her mother’s eggshell-thin Meissen china on the sideboard, would have been astonished to find that I was cooking on a thin slab of porcelain, heedlessly dropping heavy pots of boiling water on its surface.
