But when I tried to explain how remarkable this is to my son, he gave me a blank look. He had never lived in a world that wasn’t made of porcelain.Charles C Mann is a correspondent for

item.title: Show HN: Gemini 4 Argon plays StarCraft
item.author: __cayenne__
item.content:encoded:
StarSkirmish is a benchmark where LLMs write bots for StarCraft: Brood WarEach LLM gets one hour to write a Protoss bot in C++, which is then evaluated against other LLMs' bots and established human written botsStarSkirmish tests long horizon reasoning and agentic coding as LLMs must incorporate learnings from practice games to improve their StarCraft bot The StarSkirmish Bench evaluates how strong of a StarCraft bot can each LLM write given 1 hour of wall clock time. v0.2 updates StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 with flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, each running in its lab's 1st party CLI harness.
An LLM’s score reflects its win rate against a roster of competitive human written bots and demo bots. 1 hour runs, in its 1st party CLI harness. Scores are average win rates (0–100) of each model's 5 runs against a roster of competitive human written bots.Gemini 4 Argon runs at , the highest reasoning effort available to it; every other model runs at . GPT-6 Astra is the top scoring StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 LLM, a clear step ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol in second. Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 are functionally tied behind them, all scoring between 37 and 39. StarSkirmish Bench vs. CostStarSkirmish Bench score against the average API cost of one 1 hour run. Cost is on a log scale.Muse Wonder Full's pricing is based on Muse Wonder's API pricing. GPT-6.1 Sol offers uniquely good value: it is the only LLM in the most attractive quadrant, scoring second at just over a tenth of GPT-6 Astra's cost per run. The strongest human written bots are still well ahead of every model. Against Stardust, PurpleWave and BananaBrain, the best model, GPT-6 Astra, wins only 7% of its games.Win rates vs the top human written botsAverage win rate of each model's 5 bots against top human written bots Stardust, PurpleWave, and BananaBrain.1 hour reasoning limits are a factor, but these matches are played on three 2 player maps. Real human written bot tournament conditions are significantly harder. Google and Meta's new flagships replace v0.1's Gemini 3.8 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3: Gemini 4 Argon places 3rd, and Muse Wonder Full 7th. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were covered in v0.1.
Each run's agent trace records how it spent its hour. The strongest predictor of a model's score is how much it practiced against the 7 strongest bots on the roster. Win Rates vs. Practice Against Strong BotsStarSkirmish Bench score against the number of practice games a model's median run played against the 7 strongest roster bots during the hour. The dashed line is a linear fit across the 9 models. GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon start playing these bots early in the hour, while their own bots still lose to them. Muse Wonder Full, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna rarely or never do. Claude Fable 5.1 is the outlier: it scores 37 while practicing almost entirely against weaker bots. Win rates of each model's 5 runs. Each dot is one run's final bot; the line spans the lowest to the highest run, the bar marks their mean (the model's Bench score) and the band one standard deviation (σ).Results also vary between runs of the same model. Gemini 4 Argon varies far more than the other labs' flagships: its best and worst runs are 18 points apart, against 9 for GPT-6 Astra and 8 for Claude Opus 5.5. Each LLM writes a Protoss bot in C++ against BWAPI 4.4.0, played on OpenBW. Games are Protoss versus Protoss on three ladder maps: Heartbreak Ridge, Benzene and Destination. A game ends when one side's buildings are all destroyed. Games that reach the 60 minute cap (86,400 frames) are decided as on the BASIL ladder: the higher kills + razings score wins.
The LLM starts from a skeleton bot that only mines, with the source code of the three demo bots and two standard bot libraries: FAP, a combat simulator, and BWEM, a map analyzer. Whatever is in its bot folder when the hour ends is its final bot, so it has to keep the bot compiling.
The LLM has tools to compile its bot, play practice games, and read each game's summary, transcript and its bot's own log. Practice opponents are grouped into tiers: D (the three demo bots), C and B (three mid-ranked human written bots each), A (BananaBrain, Locutus) and S (Stardust, PurpleWave).
Each model's 5 final bots play each of the 13 roster bots, the 10 competitive human written bots and the 3 demo bots, 6 times on each map, on fresh seeds. Unlike v0.1, the LLM bots don't play each other.
v0.2 replaces v0.1's Elo ratings with plain win rates. A bot's score is its win rate over its tournament games, and a model's StarSkirmish Bench score is the average of its 5 bots' scores, from 0 (every game lost) to 100 (every game won).
Because every bot plays the same fixed roster, its games don't depend on the other LLM bots in the field. They all run in parallel, and a new model's bots can be scored without replaying anyone else's. A fixed roster also keeps the bar the same over time, so scores from different model generations are more directly comparable than Elo ratings fitted within one field.
StarSkirmish no longer tracks the most widely reported evals. It barely moves with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (ρ 0.26), where GPT-6 Astra, the top model here, only ties for 4th of these 9 models. It has also drifted away from Terminal-Bench 4.0, which it tracked closely in v0.1. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full both rank near the top of Terminal-Bench 4.0 but near the bottom here. Each model's StarSkirmish Bench score against its Vals IOI and WeirdML v3 scores, with the Spearman ρ between them. The dashed line is the best straight-line fit.WeirdML v3 scores 7 of the 9 models: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Full have not been included at time of writing.StarSkirmish still tracks Vals IOI, olympiad programming problems solved in C++, and WeirdML, an independent benchmark of unusual machine learning coding tasks. One reading is that the most heavily benchmarked evals have become targets that models are tuned for, while less targeted tests of long horizon, difficult coding tasks still move together.

item.title: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio
item.author: antipaul
item.content:encoded: MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1), well above average human reading speed.Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.Muse Spark Open Decode SpeedContext size of 8,192 tokensFigure 1: Muse Spark Open decode speed in tokens per second, on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, at a context size of 8,192 tokens. Higher is better. We report performance for three parallelization schemes: pipeline parallelization over two Mac Studio computers (2 M5 Pipeline), and tensor parallelization over two (2 M5 Tensor) and four Mac Studio (4 M5 Tensor) computers.We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio, using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post. We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).Table 1: Language models used in this post. Models ship in various precision formats; we evaluate Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 in their native precision, and Muse Spark Open in 4-bit (NVFP4) precision.Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with . For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively.Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2, we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s.Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×)Figure 2: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. The M5 Ultra GPU Neural Accelerator shines on compute-bound workloads.Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0×)Figure 3: Decode speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, and the M5 Ultra’s 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth (vs 819 GB/s on the M3 Ultra) is a key advantage.The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.Context size of 65,536 tokensFigure 4: Peak power consumption (in watts) during Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 inference, at a context size of 65,536 tokens, on Mac Studio with M3 Ultra and with M5 Ultra.While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.Splitting Large Models Across Multiple ComputersFigure 5: MLX supports two approaches to splitting large models across multiple computers. With pipeline parallelization, a model is split across depth, while with tensor parallelization, a model is split across width.MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation. These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides , a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline In this command, specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see Figure 6). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by ) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk , the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk , so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.Two Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×)Figure 6: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Splitting the context (here into 8,192-token chunks) lets MLX overlap computation across the two machines — hence the speedup at 65,536 but not 8,192.Two Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×)Figure 7: Decode speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Pipeline parallelization leaves decode speed essentially unchanged.Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX , is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.With MLX’s high-level helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with:mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers.With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the experts’ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5.The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s — the two-cable value reported in Table 2, the one-cable run being an additional experiment.Two or four Mac Studios with tensor parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×; Muse Spark Open: two-machine pipeline)Figure 8: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup of two or four M5 Ultras with tensor parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Muse Spark Open does not fit on a single machine, so its baseline is the two M5 Ultra pipeline configuration.Two or four Mac Studios with tensor parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0×; Muse Spark Open: two-machine pipeline)Figure 9: Decode speedup of two or four M5 Ultras with tensor parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Muse Spark Open does not fit on a single machine, so its baseline is the two M5 Ultra pipeline configuration.Time to First Token (seconds)Table 2: Time to first token (TTFT) in seconds for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Lower is better. We report a single M3 Ultra, a single M5 Ultra, two M5 Ultras (pipeline and tensor parallelization), and four M5 Ultras (tensor parallelization).Decode Speed (tokens per second)Table 3: Decode speed in tokens per second for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Higher is better. We report a single M3 Ultra, a single M5 Ultra, two M5 Ultras (pipeline and tensor parallelization), and four M5 Ultras (tensor parallelization). Decode speed was measured over 128 generated tokens following the context.Recently, agentic AI on Mac has gained considerable traction, with agentic coding tools seeing widespread adoption among developers. With MLX, powering these tools locally is as simple as launching a server with the tool. For example, a server running Muse Spark Open on port 8080 is started with:mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.server --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --port 8080 As with , the helper can be prefixed with to parallelize computation across multiple Mac Studios. From there, agentic AI can be enabled with tools like OpenCode, which can be easily configured to use that local LLM server:Many other local agentic AI experiences can be enabled through a similar approach.Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon — Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 — that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6× the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio.

item.title: RFC8950: Announce IPv4 with an IPv6 next-hop
item.author: porridgeraisin
item.content:encoded:
For the last few days I have been playing with RFC8950 setup, which allows routing of IPv4 on top of IPv6. While logically it’s quite simple, it has a very powerful application towards making “” feature riding on top of an IPv6 network ()Some of the interesting use cases:A large network can run IPv6 only everywhere on its core and leave IPv4 only on edge devices. This can work without customers doing any tweaking at their end. They still do things the old way but Backbone can run IPv6 only at its core.An IP transit backbone can run IPv6 only while exchanging IPv4 routes with its customers/peers/upstream over IPv6 sessions. So IPv4 as a “feature” stays but the network in itself is IPv6 only without the overhead of IPv4 interface config, BGP session config, firewall config, etc.An IXP can offer services without IPv4 essentually by using a (unique) IPv6 at the IX LAN & running route server to exchange both IPv4 & IPv6 routes over the IPv6 only session.Thus what 464XLAT did to the mobile networks - this has the potential to do that for the backbone networks.Multi-protocol BGP (MP-BGP) supports announcement of IPv4 routes over IPv6 sessions with IPv4 next-hops and IPv6 routes over IPv4 sessions with IPv6 next-hops. RFC8950 extends this feature for IPv4 to have IPv6 next-hops. So for IPv4 address, next hop is IPv6, IPv6 reach works via usual NDP and IPv4 rides on ethernet frames to the same MAC as discovered by the NDP. Technically RFC8950 only impacts control plane decisions by using IPv6 as the control plane but keeps the data plane as it is. IPv4 stays IPv4 & goes as IPv4 over the wire unlike say some tunnel or 464xLAT etc.As of now it’s quite widely supported by a lot of routing platforms like Juniper JunOS, Cisco IOS XR, Nokia SR OS, Mikrotik, Huawei, BIRD, FRR etc. So, it is very likely supported if you are running a recent version of the OS.Here’s a fun lab with two customer routers: C1 & C2 connected via provider routers R1-R2-R3 in Container Lab. All routers here are running open source FRR.C1 is IPv6 only on the WAN side facing R1. It originates 10.0.0.0/24 to R1 over an IPv6 session.R1 & R2 are IPv6 only with no IPv4 anywhere on their interfaces (but carry IPv4 routes in their table)R3 has IPv6 with R2 but just IPv4 only with C2. So C2 is like a typical enterprise user who lacks IPv6 deployment and still wants IPv4 only to work.R3 has 100.64.0.0/24 and originates it in the IPv4 table (to IPv6 adjacency - R2)C2 sits on 100.64.0.2/30 given by R3 and communicate in IPv4 only.C1 and C2 can reach each other over this network with parts being IPv6 only without any tunnel.name: rfc8950

item.title: I love software rendering
item.author: speckx
item.content:encoded: I love software rendering. The best DOS experience I’ve had in a long while was Quake in its software renderer at 800×600, running at a locked 60fps on my Dell OptiPlex 380. It’s one of the best-looking things I’ve seen a DOS game do.That’s not how most people remember those games looking. In the 90s you either ran them in software at a low resolution, or you bought a 3D card and played the accelerated version. Today there’s a third option: run the software renderer on a machine fast enough to push it at resolutions nobody could use back then.What software rendering isIn a software-rendered game, the CPU draws every pixel. There’s no 3D card involved: the game works out each frame in its own code and writes it straight to video memory. Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, Blood and the original Quake all work this way.When 3D cards arrived, many games got accelerated versions. GLQuake came after Quake, and Blood and Tomb Raider got 3dfx modes. Those versions hand the drawing to the graphics card, and they look different. Software renderers generally sample textures pixel by pixel, so every texel stays a crisp square. Early 3D cards smoothed textures with bilinear filtering, which looked impressive in 1997 but turns everything soft and blurry to my eye now. Most of these games ran in 256 colours, with lighting done through lookup tables into that palette. Shadows fall off in visible steps rather than smooth gradients. Technically that’s colour banding, a limitation. In practice it gives the games a rough, grimy texture that I really like, and that hardware rendering smooths away.It’s how the games were built. Quake was released with its software renderer, and GLQuake followed. Doom and the Build engine games were designed around their software renderers from the start.It isn’t always the better option. When I got a Voodoo 2 running in a modern PC, Blood ran fast in its 3dfx mode, but the VESA software modes were the better-looking option. Tomb Raider went the other way: its underwater sections look noticeably better accelerated than in the DOS software renderer. So it’s a preference, not a rule. But for most of the games I care about, I’d pick the software renderer.It’s not just nostalgia, either. Ion Fury, a Build engine game from 2019, still ships with a software renderer.The catch: it needs a fast PCSoftware rendering scales with the CPU. Every extra pixel is work for the processor, so the high VESA resolutions that many late DOS games offered were well beyond the hardware of the day.Modern hardware can power through most of it. On the OptiPlex 380, Quake at 800×600 holds a locked 60fps. But the heaviest games still push even very fast machines. In his video on the Portwell RUBY-9719, Rasteri shows Build engine games needing far more power at high resolutions, to the point where even a 3.3GHz quad-core Xeon “isn’t quite enough to run Shadow Warrior at full 1600 by 1200”.So if you want to see these games at their best, you want the fastest machine you can get that still runs them.There are other ways to get software rendering on a modern PC. Source ports of Doom and Quake run software renderers on Windows, and Ion Fury runs on Windows natively. They’re great.What I’m after is the original DOS versions running as they were released, on real hardware. DOSBox is the obvious alternative, but some DOS titles struggle in DOSBox, while on real hardware they behave exactly as intended.That leaves one more problem: sound. A fast machine running native DOS needs a sound card the games can talk to, and modern PCs don’t have one. That’s a story of its own., in software at 800×600 or higher and , the Build engine games, at high VESA resolutions

item.title: Thank You, Deno
item.author: jcbhmr
item.content:encoded: The announcement came two years to the day after Deno 2 shipped. Bun joined Anthropic ten months ago. The tempting conclusion is that the alternative-runtime experiment is over & Node has won by default. In reality, the ecosystem has gotten the benefits Deno was pushing, just not from Deno itself.Unfortunately, Deno never really hit critical mass in production; Node is as dominant in 2026 as it was in 2018. What Deno did achieve was to reinvigorate & put pressure on the incumbent, & that pressure didn't only run one way.Deno started as a clean break. Ryan stood up at JSConf EU in 2018 & listed what he'd do differently from Node: deny-by-default permissions, TypeScript as a first-class input, web-standard APIs on the server, ES modules only, a single executable. And, pointedly, no , no & no . Dependencies were URLs. The slides put it plainly: "There is no need to list dependencies."A lot of us who'd spent years on npm & Node were skeptical of that last part (not the permissions or the TypeScript, which were obviously good) & said so at the time. We'd been there before, in the hotlinking era, when every page pulled off somebody else's server & broke when it moved or got compromised. A URL tells you where something was, not what it is. Once you care that the bytes you tested are the bytes you ship, you need an integrity hash & somewhere to record it, & you've reinvented the lockfile. Matteo Collina of the Node TSC said in 2020 that "another left-pad incident is waiting to happen, but this time there is no 'central entity' that can fix it." Some of this skepticism was defensive but happened to be right in the end.Deno 1.0 shipped in 2020 on the original terms, & then spent the next four years walking them back one piece at a time. First the convention, one file that re-exported every URL: a manifest in all but name. Then , an integrity hash per URL: a lockfile. Then import maps, so you could write bare specifiers again. Deno's own documentation today recommends registries over HTTPS imports because they "can drift to different versions across files" & "trust the serving host." Those were the objections from 2018, restated as guidance.Then Bun showed up. Bun 0.1 was released in July 2022 with the opposite bet: rebuild the toolchain from scratch for speed, but run existing npm packages, read & act as a drop-in replacement for . About six weeks later, Deno published "Big Changes Ahead for Deno", announcing specifiers, a commitment to make 80–90% of npm packages work within three months & a new goal of being "the fastest JavaScript runtime." Deno credited user feedback for the shift; the timing suggests Bun was a large part of it. Deno 2, in October 2024, finished the job with full Node & npm compatibility. Four years after launching as the alternative to Node's ecosystem, Deno had become another way to run it.That was the right call, & it was also an admission that the ecosystem wasn't going to abandon over a decade's worth of dependencies overnight. Cloudflare's , which it open-sourced in 2022, grew its own Node compatibility layer for the same reason: that's where the packages are.Node ended up needing to respond. Since 2018 it has shipped a global , , Web Streams & Web Crypto; a stable test runner & ; & single-executable builds; a stable permission model; type stripping on by default; ; & . Node's contributors (many volunteers) did the hard work to listen & make big changes, & they deserve a ton of credit for it, but I don't think it happens on that timeline without three other runtimes shipping many of these ideas first. A mature open source project rarely lacks good ideas. It lacks urgency, & competitors supply that urgency.The standards work came out of the same pressure: WinterCG formed in 2022 because several serious runtimes made "what's the minimum common API?" a practical question, & now, as Ecma TC55, it should outlast whichever runtimes consolidate next.Package managers & registriesFor most of its history the JavaScript package ecosystem was a monoculture: one client, one registry, & an API contract informal enough that it stayed effectively undocumented for a decade & a half. Nearly every improvement since came from someone refusing to accept the status quo.Yarn (2016) insisted installs be deterministic & gave us the lockfile, workspaces & an offline cache; npm 5 shipped the next year. pnpm showed that didn't have to be hundreds of megabytes of duplicated files. Bun made fast enough that the incumbents had to revisit their performance. Deno argued you should be able to read a dependency's source before you take it, & while URL imports didn't last, that idea did.The clearest recent example is install scripts. pnpm & Bun stopped running them by default; vlt never did. The argument had been made inside npm for the entire time I worked there without ever becoming the default. In June of this year, after a run of supply-chain worms, GitHub announced that npm 12 would stop running them by default too. Nothing about the idea changed in those years; enough other package managers shipped it that npm could no longer treat it as radical. The pressure runs in both directions too: we borrowed catalogs from pnpm, & pnpm's borrowed our named-registry aliases.On the registry side, JSR deserves credit. It made a different set of bets than we did: publish TypeScript source, require ESM, generate docs from code. We disagreed with parts of it & added support to vlt anyway because our users asked for it. It survives the wind-down because, as far as I can tell, it's cheap to run, its API is documented, & Cloudflare had a reason to keep it alive.The two most popular independent, venture-backed JavaScript runtimes now live inside companies whose business is something else. Jarred Sumner said the Bun team's relationship with the Claude Code team "probably will look similar to the relationship between Google Chrome <> V8," with more independence, & Cloudflare's post makes clear that workerd's roadmap is Cloudflare's. That's how JavaScriptCore & V8 have always been funded, & it's still a change.Whether a community fork of the Deno runtime emerges will tell us whether the ecosystem values a secure-by-default, standards-first runtime enough to pay for one that isn't attached to a cloud. And celld-into-workerd is new optionality at a layer that has had very little: a self-hostable, open implementation of Workers & Durable Objects, led by Ryan & Bert Belder.JavaScript has insurance at almost every layer: three production engines, several runtimes, several package managers. When one layer consolidates, as the runtime layer is doing now, the others hold. The churn that makes this possible is also what people complain about most. "JavaScript fatigue" has been a running joke for a decade: a new framework every week, a new bundler every month, & yet another package manager, which, yes, I'm aware I've contributed to. But nobody had to leave Node to get , a permission model or TypeScript without a build step, & nobody has to switch package managers to get install scripts turned off by default anymore. Those things showed up in the tools people were already using because someone else shipped them first & the incumbent had to answer. The projects didn't always win, but the ideas usually did, & end-users collected them either way.To Ryan, Bert, Bartek & the rest of the Deno team (past & present): your collective efforts have enriched our shared ecosystem. Founder & CEO, vlt

item.title: RPKI now protects 70% of internet routes
item.author: emot
item.content:encoded: The Internet relies on networks telling each other which IP addresses they can deliver traffic to, using (Border Gateway Protocol). These routing announcements have historically depended heavily on trust. When a network announces addresses it shouldn’t, accidentally or deliberately, traffic can be sent to the wrong place and services can become unreachable.On February 24, 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) tried to block YouTube inside Pakistan by announcing a more specific route for YouTube's addresses. Its upstream provider, PCCW Global (AS3491), accepted the announcement and passed it to the rest of the Internet, redirecting YouTube traffic to Pakistan globally for roughly two hours (). Work on RPKI, which lets networks reject announcements like that one, had started at the IETF two years earlier, and the regional Internet registries began issuing RPKI certificates in 2011. (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) lets the holder of a block of IP addresses publish a signed record, a Route Origin Authorization (ROA), naming the networks (Autonomous Systems, or ASes) allowed to announce it. Network operators that check RPKI compare announcements against those records and can reject the ones that fail.We looked at a year of IPinfo’s daily RPKI data to see how much of the Internet it now protects, and where it falls short. What we found (TL;DR):70.3% of routed prefixes (blocks of IP addresses) are now RPKI-valid, up from 54.0% a year ago, a 30% rise. That’s 16.4 points, against 3.9 and 3.2 in the two years before.China drove most of the jump: its IPv4 addresses in valid routes went from 3.7% to 83.0%, almost 60% of the global gain counted by addresses. Outside China, the share of addresses rose 5.2 points.Invalid routes barely travel: a typical valid route is seen by 596 vantage points, an invalid one by two.Loose ROAs are the biggest hole left: 16.2% of covered IPv4 routes leave room for a forged, RPKI-valid route, the setup used against Hetzner on August 28.Protection can disappear quietly: SEACOM, Saudi Telecom and Orange Maroc each lost ROAs for months.ASPA is arriving fast, from 131 to 3,272 networks, but it verifies only about 3.5% of routing, and one operator’s incomplete record causes about a quarter of the mid-path failures.Invalid Routes Barely PropagateIn August, the found RPKI-related activity accounts for under 1% of daily BGP update volume, a share that is rising but still small, so RPKI is not itself destabilizing routing. We wanted to know whether RPKI was actually protecting Internet routing.Routes with an RPKI record and routes with none travel equally far: a typical one is seen by 596 and 595 vantage points. Routes that fail the check are seen by just two. Now that enough networks check, they are dropping these invalid routes. Nearly half of all invalid routes reach only a single vantage point. When the wrong network announces the addresses, the clearest kind of hijack or mistake, 71% reach only one.This changes how country-level RPKI statistics should be read. A country can look bad because of announcements almost nobody sees.Simply counting invalid routes can badly exaggerate how much of a country is affected. Spain has the highest share of invalid IPv4 prefixes at 28.2%. Count the addresses in those routes instead, weighted by how many vantage points see each one, and it falls to 0.057%. Slovakia falls from 17.4% to almost zero. Italy has the highest figure of any country with at least a million IPv4 addresses, 0.121%, up from 0.075% a year ago, and 90% of it is one network. WIND TRE (AS1267) announces 34 routes in its own address space that its own ROAs don't allow: 19 are more specific than the ROAs permit, and 15 come from AS1267 while the ROA names WIND TRE's other network, AS24608. None reaches more than 77 vantage points, against about 617 for the signed blocks around them.China Drove Most of the 2026 JumpCounted by IPv4 addresses on September 28 each year, the share in RPKI-valid routes rose from 42.7% in 2023 to 47.9% in 2024, 53.1% in 2025 and 65.0% in 2026. The last jump was 11.9 points, against about five in each previous year.Removing China shows how much of that was one country. Outside China, the share rose from 58.0% to 63.2%, a 5.2-point gain, a little less than the year before.China’s change was also sudden: 3.7% of its IPv4 addresses were in valid routes in September 2025, and 83.0% a year later. Most of that happened this year: at the end of December 2025, just 2.9% of China's routed prefixes were valid. It also changed which way it moves the world figure. In 2025 China pulled the global average down: 53.1% worldwide against 58.0% without China. In 2026 it pushed it up: 65.0% against 63.2%. Others moved a long way too: Egypt from 23% to 99%, Kazakhstan from 16% to 84%, Mexico from 37% to 78%, and South Africa from 38% to 60%.Where the unprotected addresses are is just as concentrated. Of all routed IPv4 space not in RPKI-valid routes on September 28, nearly 60% is in the United States, and about one in four addresses belongs to the US Department of Defense (more on who holds IPv4 in an upcoming post). Most of that is space the Department began announcing in 2021 to watch for misuse, not to run services.In early 2025 there were concerns that IPv6 adoption of RPKI was slowing. Instead, it accelerated and has now overtaken IPv4. In RPKI's 2024 year in review for RIPE Labs, Job Snijders noted IPv6 ROA growth "seems to be stalling." Over our window, IPv6 routed prefixes marked valid rose from 56% to 79% while IPv4 prefixes rose from 54% to 68%, putting IPv6 roughly ten points ahead. The RPKI report shows the same ordering.Two other metrics he flagged also changed: the average number of address blocks per ROA climbed back from 2.31 at the end of December to 2.62, and publication points, which he counted falling from 63 to 53 and read as consolidation, rose from 73 to 91 as more organizations began hosting their own repositories instead of relying on their registry.RPKI validates who may originate a prefix. It does not validate the path, and it cannot catch an attacker who stays inside the permission you published, so it's not bulletproof.On August 28, 2026, a route for 162.55.80.0/24 (a block of 256 addresses) appeared with Hetzner's AS24940 forged as the origin. Hetzner's ROA covered the surrounding /16, a block 256 times larger, and allowed announcements as small as a /24, so the forged route satisfied it. The route was RPKI-valid, no legitimate /24 existed to compete with it, and longest-prefix-match meant everyone preferred it. That was enough to obtain a genuine TLS certificate and serve a malicious Virtualizor update to hypervisors, as .We measured how common that posture is. Of 855,217 RPKI-covered IPv4 routes, 138,698, or 16.2%, have a ROA looser than the route announced and no more-specific route of their own filling the gap. For IPv6 it is 20.9%. That leaves roughly 18 million more-specific prefixes an attacker could announce today, forge the origin, and come out RPKI-valid and uncontested.Operators in the same business make very different choices here. Among hosting providers, Contabo has an open window on 540 of 553 covered routes and DigitalOcean on 780 of 863, while OVH sits at 11.5%. Access providers are worse still: Cablevision at 98.1%, Shaw at 96.5%, Bharti Airtel at 85.0%. already says the best practice is to leave maxLength unset. maxLength is the setting that lets a ROA also cover smaller blocks inside it, so leaving it unset means a ROA matches only the block actually announced. Hetzner tightened three prefixes after the incident, including the one that was hijacked, though 49 of its 63 covered routes remain open.Where RPKI Coverage DeclinedRPKI coverage can also disappear without causing an outage. A missing ROA simply removes the protection, and nobody notices unless they look. We found several cases where that happened over the past year.Unlike China, Mauritius saw its RPKI coverage fall. The share of its IPv4 addresses in valid routes fell from 94.0% to 69.0% between September 2025 and September 2026. SEACOM (AS37100) lost four of its six ROAs on January 1. One covered 105.16.0.0/12, a block of about a million addresses, 46% of which are in Mauritius. That block alone explains Mauritius's drop, and it still had no ROA on September 28.Two other operators show the same thing happening and then being fixed. Saudi Telecom (AS25019) lost RPKI protection on 19 routes, including six large blocks totaling about 1.6 million addresses, when the ROAs for those six blocks disappeared between March 30 and April 13. Saudi Arabia's coverage recovered when the ROAs came back on September 21 and 22. In Morocco, Orange Maroc (AS36925) is the only large operator that publishes ROAs, and most of them went missing twice: from July 2025 to July 2026, and again from July 25 to September 3. Morocco went from 20% covered to almost none, and back.Depending on how you check, an RPKI record can look broken while it is still protecting its routes. We ran into this while counting.Every signed record carries a link to the certificate above it. When an operator moves its repository, that link can go stale, and a check that inspects records one by one will report a hard failure. But the validation that actually produces the list routers use never follows that link, it walks down from the trust anchors instead. We found thousands of records flagged as failed that were present in every independently validated set we checked, with their routes still RPKI-valid. So if you are reading anyone's RPKI numbers, including ours, it is worth knowing which of the two they counted. A count of failing records is not a measure of lost protection.Path Validation Is Starting to ArriveROAs secure the origin of a route. They say nothing about whether the path used to reach that origin makes sense.ASPA, or Autonomous System Provider Authorization, addresses that. A network publishes a signed record naming its authorized upstream providers, which lets others check observed AS paths against them and catch route leaks that origin validation misses.Deployment is early but fast. On September 28, 2025, 131 networks had published ASPA records. By September 28, 2026 there were 3,272, 25 times as many.The growth comes in steps rather than a curve. RIPE NCC sat at about 85 networks from September to late November, then climbed to 470 by the end of December. ARIN stepped up from January 21, APNIC at the end of June and again in September, when its count nearly doubled. Each jump follows a registry making ASPA signing available, so tooling has been the main driver. One detail worth highlighting: APNIC announced its support on July 9, and its curve started climbing on June 26.That coverage is now enough to ask the better question: how much of observed routing is ASPA-valid?On September 28, 2026, 9.7% of observed routing passed ASPA checks, up from 6.2% a year earlier. Most of that is automatic: under the draft rules, a path through only one or two networks always passes, and those short paths were about 6% of routing in both years.Take them out and the records networks have published verify about 3.5% of routing, up from roughly 0.1%. Almost all the rest is not failing. It is unknown, because too few networks along those paths have published records to tell. In practice, ASPA can check only a small slice of routing today, and that slice grows with every network that publishes a record.Of the paths that can be judged, those breaking ASPA’s rules mid-path, the signal a collector can read with most confidence, rose from effectively zero to 0.048% of observations. That is not necessarily routing getting worse: a path can only be called invalid once enough of it has declared providers, so as publication grew, paths that were previously unjudgeable became testable and some failed.Attributing those failures needs care, because the gap sits mid-path: one provider with a stale record makes every one of its customers' routes look invalid, so ranking by origin blames the wrong party.Attribute to the hop instead and the networks at the top are the ones doing it right. Cogent, Arelion, and GTT each declare AS0, which says they buy transit from nobody. That is true, and it is exactly what stops a stale record further down the path from hiding as "no attestation." The real gaps are smaller: of 3,272 networks publishing ASPA records, 479 have upstream providers visible in our routing data that they never declared, across 658 missing relationships.The largest single cause is one operator. Syrian Telecom (AS29386) publishes a record naming four carriers. Three of them carry just 16% of the transit we observe through it, and the fourth carries none. The four carriers that handle the other 84% are missing from the record, so about 40% of paths arriving through them fail the check, and the rest come out unknown. Through Syrian Telecom's own routes and those of two Syrian networks that reach the Internet through it, that record accounts for 21% of all mid-path ASPA failures on the Internet. Another 3 points come from AS201550, a second Syrian Telecom network whose record copies the same four carriers instead of naming the Syrian Telecom networks it connects through. So the global ASPA failure rate is not yet a measure of the Internet’s health: about a quarter of it comes from one operator’s incomplete records.Eighteen years after PCCW Global passed on Pakistan Telecom's announcement for YouTube's addresses, PCCW is a gap in the newer system. ASPA would not have stopped the 2008 incident; RPKI's origin check is what covers that. But ASPA lets others check PCCW's place in a path, and AS3491 has not published a record. That breaks nothing on its own. Still, nearly 6,000 paths crossing PCCW read ASPA-invalid today, because networks below it publish records that leave PCCW out.RPKI now protects most Internet routes, and invalid routes barely travel. The gaps that remain are mostly in the hands of the networks that own the addresses:Publish ROAs for everything you announce. Three in ten routed prefixes are still not RPKI-valid. One in six covered IPv4 routes has a window like the one used against Hetzner.Check that your ROAs are still there. Saudi Telecom, SEACOM, and Orange Maroc each lost some of theirs, and since nothing broke, it was easy to miss.Publish ASPA, and list every provider. Syrian Telecom's record leaves out the four carriers that handle most of the traffic we see reaching it, so many routes through them fail the check.: All figures come from IPinfo’s daily routing and RPKI data, comparing September 28 of each year unless stated. Routing data comes from the public RIPE RIS and RouteViews collectors. A route’s reach is the number of their BGP peers (vantage points) that carry it, and reach figures are medians. “RPKI-valid” means a route matches the validated set of ROAs that routers use, not the status of individual records. Country figures use IPv4 only and count addresses: each route is split across countries using IPinfo geolocation (the current mapping for every year), each address is counted once, and it counts as covered if any valid route includes it. In Chart 3, the prefix share uses each prefix’s first address, and the weighted share multiplies each route’s addresses by its reach. The maxLength figures cover routes seen by at least two vantage points. ASPA figures are weighted by how often each route is observed, and the 0.048% counts failures in the middle of a path only.
