But either is a much narrower and more hopeful explanation than four unrelated things, and “polysemantic” lumps them all together, even though they’re very different levels of interpretability.In 2023 during the time of the first automated interpretability project I thought small simplified models would be the best starting place for interpretability, since there’s fewer bells and whistles to think about, and small size means fewer things to study. But now I think it may be the opposite. The bells and whistles are there to help the neural network learn better, like the residual stream InceptionV1 never had, and by simplifying it’s easy to make neurons learn less well. And bigger models tend to have more narrow neurons, so it’s more easy to spot patterns and motifs. At least for GPT-2, I was often looking at multiple motifs together, neither of which I knew, which made things hard. By adopting the architectures and scale the field wanted anyway, we may have been slouching towards monosemanticity without knowing it.The worry with the residual stream isn’t that there are more things we care about than dimensions. It’s a continuous version of packing: manifolds woven through each other, accepting some interference in exchange for room to store more. Ruling that out entirely may not be possible. But in practice it hasn’t been a bottleneck. We can read what neurons write to the residual stream and what they read from it, attribution graphs come out clean, and we don’t see the stream accumulating interference only to undo it later.In vision models, we could also check this by eye. For years I couldn’t visualize the residual stream of convolutional networks: every map came out as one big arc. It turned out the network was putting almost all of its activation mass into a single unread dimension, which it can change to scale all the other dimensions that are read through LayerNorm. Once we understood that, removing it was easy, and the maps made sense. The technical details of how it works, or even what it’s doing, are less important than the more general pattern throughout this essay: find what the architecture is doing and work with it, rather than fighting the network. It also pointed toward something the field ended up building anyway: attention.We don’t know whether language models need a similar fix. When we’ve visualized their residual streams, it has mostly just worked. Judging whether a whole map of text makes sense is much harder than glancing at a map of images, though, which is why we did most of this work in vision. A single global map may not be the best tool for language models anyway. Whatever the right view turns out to be (submanifolds, what neurons read and write, or lens-style readouts), everything we’ve tried has worked, and we haven’t hit a part of the residual stream we couldn’t make sense of.The residual stream at every layer of the ConvNeXt, drawn as one map. Each line follows one image location from the first layer (left) to the last stage (right), starting in the color of its patch. At the first layer the map is sorted by color. Locations that end up as animal faces start wherever the color of their fur puts them, and gather gradually. Red patches start together and go on to become different things. Hover or tap a row to see its patch at each stage.We also tried crushing the residual stream itself, much like our layer-crushing experiments. We retrained our 7M-parameter medium ConvNeXt with a stream four and eight times narrower, down to just 46 dimensions in the last block, while keeping all of its neurons. Accuracy fell from 72% to 60% and 39%, but compared with a normal-width model the crushed stream’s map looks quite similar, just a bit messier. Nothing looks cleverly interleaved. Neuron reads and writes tell the same story: things get noisier, but what leaks in is the same kind of thing. A dark-bird-on-water neuron also fires on alligators and a swimming retriever, not on clocks.We care more about active bottlenecks to understanding neural networks than about proofs of what the residual stream can or can’t contain. If interference isn’t showing up in the maps or in what neurons read and write, even when we take away the room, we think we’re in a pretty good spot.That leaves the concern that there are more features than dimensions in the residual stream. A stream can hold far more than it has dimensions just by placing things in the right directions, so this alone isn’t packing. It mostly matters if you want a big list of all the model’s features, and people often go to the stream for exactly that. As we discuss in Zooming Out, we don’t think a big list is the right end goal. But if you want one, the directions neurons write to and read from are a good place to start. So are continuous submanifolds, like those Block Sparse Featurizer finds, which seem especially natural here since the residual stream has no privileged basis. So far all of these have worked well: they find sensible subspaces, and we can follow them across layers.We’ve looked at language models’ residual streams less, but what we’ve seen fits the same story. For understanding higher-level structure and motifs, nothing in the residual stream has blocked us so far.We’ve made less progress on attention than on neurons, and it’s mostly outside the scope of this essay. To be honest, I’m not sure anyone understands attention well enough to confidently say that illegibility is a superposition in the sense we care about. Distinguishing it from all the other things it could be is hard, and a change in learning principle shouldn’t be near the top of the list of hypotheses for why new mechanisms are hard to understand.A lot of attention’s value seems to be in the easier parts.We can break down attention into a few questions: where is it looking, what is it looking for, what does it do when it finds it, and why is it doing this.Where it looks is relatively easy. It basically comes for free, and it already tells you a lot. In the preeclampsia graph it does two separate things. First it gathers the facts of the case onto “she,” where the model works out the medical question. Then the question’s wording decides what to actually say next.We can also understand what it’s looking for, and what it does when it finds it, in terms of neurons. We think this gives you a lot of the benefit of what attention is doing.For instance, take the comma after “headache.” in the preeclampsia example. Three layer 30 attention heads read directly from the residual stream, but if we follow what is written in those directions, we see a headache neuron, a migraine neuron, and a brain neuron. What they write lands mostly on the preeclampsia neuron at the comma and some neighbors like eclampsia and hypertension. Ablating these heads drops preeclampsia by a quarter. Stopping them from looking at pain and nothing changes.The chips under tokens are neurons that activate there. We can follow some of what attention is doing by watching the flow of neurons it affects.It also works the other way. Some neurons are much easier to see once you can see the attention around them, and some heads only make sense through their neurons.Understanding attention and neurons through each other. Three cases in Qwen3-32B where a neuron and a head only make sense together. Below each, more examples: highlighted is what the head reads, boxed is where the neuron fires. Hover a drawing for the test.Overall, we don’t think attention and neurons are so separable. Understanding where attention is putting information is quite helpful for understanding the neurons that then work with that information. Even simple things like motifs around where information tends to be placed, like the ends of numbers, or on commas, have been helpful.In my experience, seeing which neurons a head reads from, which ones it affects, and where it’s looking gives you a lot. One main thing it doesn’t give you is a global name for each attention head. It’d be nice to have them, but it hasn’t been a big bottleneck on exploring neurons or attribution graphs. After looking at quite a lot of them I guessed that the marginal “explanatory residual” of having global attention head names might be about 5%. Then I had an agent do the same, looking at 100 attribution graphs without my guess, and it also put it about 5%, split about equally into “position heads” that are relatively easier to name, since they do things like look one token backwards, and everything else, which is of course varied and harder.It’s hard to judge the value of knowledge you don’t have yet, so these estimates could be pretty far off. But so far even without global attention head labels I think we can go quite far in discovering high level structure and motifs with just local attention flow and global neuron explanations. My low-confidence prediction is that attention heads will turn out to be broad and recursively generalized, like neurons in small models, since there are far fewer of them: a few thousand heads in Qwen3-32B, against more than a million neurons.Nothing here has been changed or recombined. Every district, circuit and neuron is the network’s own, as it learned them.When I say neural networks are already clean, I mean something deeper than neuron monosemanticity, although even by that standard, I think things look much better than the field expects. I mean that a network’s parts are built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers. In this sense, a neural network is almost a fractal of explanations, of coherent, useful groupings: at the macro scale, in its mechanisms, and at the micro scale, where recursive generalization shapes each one. That points to a goal for interpretability: become another reader.The more we read it the way its own readers do, the more interpretable I think it will look. We should be wary of reading it too much like a human, and concluding it’s messy just because it doesn’t fit our preconceived concepts.I think the reason things end up so organized is partially because it was faster to build that way. Once you have a car area of the neural network with car parts, it’s easier to add the marginal car there than to build a second car area somewhere else. I think this is closely related to ideas of circuit racing and gradient starvation.We normally consider interpretable and monosemantic to be nearly synonyms. I think this is partly because these ideas grew out of a model organism (InceptionV1) that was almost bimodal. Early layers were interpretable and monosemantic, late ones seemed like arbitrary mayhem. But what we see in language models is somewhere in the middle, with most neurons meaning mostly one thing, some meaning a few. How bad is that?There are two broad styles of interpretability. One we can call enumerative interpretability. The goal is to have a big list of features to audit, to make sure we haven’t missed some meaningful pattern. A big concern within this view is avoiding the curse of dimensionality, or a combinatorial explosion of items connected to other items, where each one means more than one thing.Another style we can call exploratory interpretability. It starts with questions. It can explore any part of the neural network, zooming in and out fluidly like Google Maps across attribution graphs, and mechanisms like neurons or attention heads. We pick up more questions along the way. The mechanisms like neurons are a good place to start, but it’s not about neurons being some final solution to everything – though I do think it’s closer to that than most people realize. This approach is far more resilient to polysemanticity. It is also broadly fine ignoring lots of the neural network, in the same way someone studying a city would ignore areas irrelevant to their analysis.I think exploratory approaches will be more fruitful. My sense is that the field is moving in this direction already, but I’m not sure it has been written down clearly. This view has a couple implications. Questions like “are there more features than dimensions?” are mostly irrelevant. We don’t have to define features, which is famously difficult. We can focus mostly on mechanisms like neurons and attention heads which are part of the model, data flowing through it, and then groups of both and motifs that recur across all of this.The big feature list was always a means to an end. There may be other paths that don’t require them.Motifs Over MonosemanticityIf I could push a button and make every neuron perfectly monosemantic, or instead understand the circuit motifs behind a few questions I care about (the right way to ask about an agent’s psychology, how circuits connect to the persona selection model, how an agent thinks about its goals and the boundary between itself and others), I’d take the motifs in a minute.Imagine an interpretability researcher arriving from a hundred years in the future, who knows not just the answers to our questions but which questions we should have been asking. What would they tell us? I can’t know, but I’ve been in a small version of their position once. I now feel like I mostly understand a vision model, which makes me something like a future researcher to myself eight years ago.Here’s what I’d tell myself then. Pay attention to the giant pose circuit right in front of you. Think of negative poles as gates in a circuit, not a neuron’s opposite. Feature visualization reward hacks in late layers, so some of the mess there is the tool’s, not the network’s. The last layer is messy partly because of a bad architecture; that’s a sign, so don’t paper over it. And whenever you see polysemanticity, look harder. The noise that stands out usually points to an explanation you don’t have yet.Almost none of this is a list of features. Short of handing my past self this advice, the best thing I could give is the original neurons and circuits, with a note to look harder at them.This is why the difference between recursive generalization and superposition matters so much. Following the noise only works if the noise has something to teach. A grouping that grew from generalization does. A grouping of things packed together because they don’t belong together would teach almost nothing.So my best guess of the future researcher’s advice would look somewhat similar. They might hand us a set of motifs that look obvious to them but not to us. But short of that, they’d say keep looking at the original neural network. Don’t fracture it too much. Learn how to see it. It’s a bit like The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, where the answer, 42, is known, and the search is for the question. The network is the answer, and interpretability is largely the search for the right question. It’s hard to find a better guide to that question than the network itself. That’s the deeper sense in which I mean the network is already clean.A bigger system isn’t necessarily harder to navigate. In a small town, asking for the financial district barely makes sense. Whatever exists is scattered: a bank on one street, an insurance office on another, maybe an accountant with a home office. In New York, you could find it on a map in a minute. We saw a small version of this in our ConvNeXts: agents found labeled dog-ear neurons faster in the larger models, where pale, wavy, and head-side ear neurons all feed one hanging-ears neuron, a natural place to start.Branches converge and splitHow the ear family changes with scale across three neural networks that vary in size about 300×.Interpretability will need better maps. I advocate for tethered abstraction: views that let us zoom out while keeping the larger patterns connected to the neurons and circuits that support them. Our ConvNeXt atlas, inspired by Activation Atlas, is one example. Start at the model’s decision for a killer whale, check a key neuron against its real images, and zoom back out. The family turns out to be three separate routes: one for whales, one for sharks and rays, and one for fish held up by anglers. A map doesn’t need to be visual, though, and no single map is the point. There should be many maps and many agents, all working toward explanations that stay tethered to individual neurons and circuits.Of course, even if the map is understandable, that doesn’t mean you’ve understood it. We still have to do the ordinary science of conjecture and criticism: guess what something is, try to break the guess, and keep what survives. The network is strange, but its strangeness repeats, so a guess that survives scrutiny often pays off many times over.We should worry both about imposing our own ideas too strongly, and fracturing the network. Imagine arriving in Tokyo knowing New York well. “Where’s the Brooklyn of Tokyo?” could be a useful starting question. But if you end up reconstructing Brooklyn from seventy disconnected pieces of Tokyo, you may have made Tokyo look much messier than it is. That’s a bit like what happened with 4e:55. Through our categories it was cats and cars, and it looked like a mess; it was a V the whole time. An SAE trained on the layer fractures it the same way, splitting the V into a car feature and a cat feature. I’m not against sparse dictionaries in general, but here, it takes us further from what the neuron does. Probes push the first risk further: they can only answer a question we already had, so they can’t teach us which questions to ask. To understand the city, you eventually have to learn its own organization.Higher-level structures like probes and sparse dictionaries can still be useful, but they belong at the end, not the start. Everything of this kind I’ve run breaks down into highly interpretable neurons, as do the changes training makes, including on-policy self-distillation. The neurons cover the abstractions and the data covers the particular cases, so what’s left in between is smaller than people expect, and I’d study it the same way: with a general scientific agent moving between the neurons, data, and groups of both, not a fixed optimization. As Anthropic’s Joshua Batson put it when he read a draft, those missing pieces “will fit into the initial puzzle, rather than being totally randomly splayed on top.”Solving interpretability may share something with achieving AGI: the goalposts move as you get closer. There’s always another weak activation to point to. In Curve Detectors, we wrote forty pages of experiments on ten neurons precisely to identify at least one sure case of a monosemanticity. Years later, some researchers told me they still doubted any of the examples were monosemantic. We might have missed something, they said, and no one knows how to produce a formal proof. By that standard, it’s overclaiming to say even a single monosemantic neuron exists.Behind doubts about small errors in neurons is a fear that safety will come down to some activation we missed, the place where deception hides. The risk I worry about is different: like being in a well-organized city and not knowing how to think about it, because we aren’t native to it. Every error discussed in this essay was something hiding in plain sight that we didn’t know how to read, or that our tools read incorrectly. None was a hidden activation we missed. Deception might hide from someone reading a model’s outputs, but it has no reason to hide from the model’s own circuitry. It needs to be accessible to its readers, and if we become a reader, it should be accessible to us too. My fear is that deception will be right there, in plain sight, and we won’t know how to read it.Over time, my approach to individual mechanisms has become less focused on this kind of proof, and more holistic. Instead of trying to nail every detail of one neuron, I look around it: what flows into it, what it feeds, how attention moves information to and from it, and what it looks like zoomed in and zoomed out. When I worked on automated interpretability, a neuron firing a few tokens away from its main topic seemed like a big problem. But over time it was clear that attention moves things to reliable places, which then have neurons that activate near the “appropriate token” rather than on it. That’s how understanding has felt to me: less like clearing a bar for each piece and more like a fog-of-war map filling in at several levels at once. Attribution graphs help explain neurons, neurons help explain attention, and attention explains neurons in turn.Neural networks rarely get stuck during training, since in a high dimensional space there’s almost always a way downhill. In my experience, clearing the fog of war works the same way. There’s always another experiment to run, another explanation to narrow, another attribution graph to check, another neuron to watch grow over training.This is why I’ve focused on whether there’s any level of abstraction where things break down, where you stop being able to learn anything and have to take the network apart into something else. I haven’t found one. And when each new motif clears fog in many places at once, perfecting a single neuron probably isn’t the best use of effort. There’s a kind of faith in it: you note something strange, and over time it usually fills in. It isn’t faith all the way down, since almost any explanation can eventually be tested. Just faith that something strange is a good pointer. The V in the car and cat neuron isn’t hard to see – it took me about five seconds, and most people I’ve shown the image grid to and say “what’s the shared pattern here” see it too – but it took believing that the neuron had found something real. For years I’ve heard this neuron come up in almost every discussion of polysemanticity. It was almost always described in reference to neural networks being almost invalid objects of direct natural science. That’s what I was saying too, until I looked more closely. It didn’t take a lot of faith, but it took a little.The little faith is important because the mistakes aren’t symmetric. If you assume a network is clean and you’re wrong, a messy neuron is a lead: you investigate it, and over time normal science sharpens your explanation. If you assume it’s packed, not worth studying directly, and you’re wrong, a messy neuron is the end, because you stop studying it. I made that second assumption for years, and it explained away the evidence that would have overturned it. I could have improved my tools, watched the mixtures keep dissolving, and built up a prior that the neurons could be trusted. Instead, I spent most of a decade figuring out how to look at a model rather than looking at it.For the medium ConvNeXt, the map is mostly filled in. Eight years ago, I would have called that a reasonable solution to interpretability for that model. I can investigate most questions I have about it. Getting there took many small things and a handful of motifs, plus architecture changes the field made anyway, but no interpretability-specific fixing of the network at all.My guess is that frontier networks are where those vision models were eight years ago: legible, but waiting on many small fixes. If we learn to see them properly, follow the noise, and test explanations through many lenses, I think we’ll get there too. We may not have years to do it. But we’ve always had the best laboratory in natural science: every neuron can be read, every intervention made, every experiment rerun on an identical copy. What we did not always have is many automated scientists to work in it, far faster and in far greater numbers than we can. Now we do. They may be able to do in months in frontier language models what took humans most of a decade for vision models.I think the simple story from introductory textbooks is basically right: neurons generalize, work together, and build abstractions over layers. Somewhere along the way we overcomplicated that picture, but looking harder brought it back. If the network isn’t a knot, untangling it can make it look like one.What a Solution Might Look LikeWe usually imagine ambitious interpretability as an incredibly hard problem, maybe too hard to solve in time to matter. What if it isn’t? The network is enormous, but it may already have done almost all the work of preparing itself to be understood, not for us, but for its own readers. If we can become another reader, it’s ready for us too.The solution might look like a laboratory run by automated scientists who watch the network through training and inference. Each step is simple – labeling neurons, finding motifs and testing them, following data through circuits – and the pieces already exist. Capable agents were built for other work, and modern architectures were chosen because they learn well. Both happen to serve interpretability.Guided by a mechanistic constitution, agents propose and test explanations at many scales, each grounded in individual neurons, and keep, drop, or replace them with better ones.So maybe all we have to do is plug one into the other.Alignment is supposed to be hard too, and it may well be. But the usual arguments assume we can’t see inside models. We assume we get one training setup, and it has to be right in advance. If we can read and understand the system, maybe we can make simple, careful changes instead, like removing an RL environment that turns out to be toxic, without pushing gradients through the very tools we use to see. Each fix might be simple too. There might just be a lot of them.This is the history of deep learning. It may also be the history of understanding and aligning what it builds.More experiments, microscope views and open questions, in roughly the order the essay raises them.A Note on “Superposition”The word has meant several things. Before Zoom In, it meant something closer to vector addition, as when word embeddings were described as sums of word senses. Zoom In introduced it to circuits work with a single circuit example, which I found in 2019 and others helped me interpret. The original circuit read turned out to be wrong both because of misunderstanding a generalized pose circuit, and because of reward hacking in feature visualization. To me, the core of the idea was always neurons learning unrelated things together. Toy Models of Superposition later defined superposition as representing more features than dimensions. This makes it a claim about how many features there are, something we can’t yet define or measure. About eight months after that, an informal note framed composition and superposition as competing strategies for how features are laid out across neurons, close to our framing but about representation rather than how mechanisms grow. We think this framing is excellent, and it’s closest to the question this essay cares about. But most researchers and agents we’ve talked to still think of superposition mainly as more features than dimensions. That matters here, because the two are quite different claims: ours is about the trade-off, not the count. Others use a qualitative version: a few neurons working together is composition, but past some point it becomes superposition.We view this as an ongoing search for the right question, much like the field’s long struggle to define a feature. Underneath most versions is one question: why aren’t the neurons already good? Why can’t we study the mechanisms directly? Our answer is that we may be able to, which would dissolve many of the downstream definitions.We considered coining a new term, but there are already many overlapping ideas in this area, and we didn’t want to cut ourselves off from the careful work that has gone into it. So we keep the word and say exactly what we mean: neurons learning unrelated things together because they rarely interfere. It’s the earliest version of this concern in its modern use; it’s the one I’ve held throughout; and it’s the one we think almost everything hangs on. Composition also represents far more things than it has neurons, and that’s exactly what we should hope for; the count definition can only exclude it by first settling what counts as a feature. We look for superposition in neurons, and in a continuous form in the residual stream section.We’re explicit about this partly for AI agents, which increasingly do interpretability research. In our experience, they bring their own default reading of the term.Simulation scores often end up measuring where attention puts information, which is a question about attention motifs rather than about the neuron. Attention often stores information on commas and other punctuation, as a kind of summarization motif, but exactly how much does it place on each kind of punctuation? A simulator has to care about that a lot, even though it has almost nothing to do with the neuron itself. Simulation also rewards fine details of weak activations that matter little for understanding what a neuron does. CLIP’s Trump neuron responds strongly to photos of Trump, and more weakly as he gets smaller in the frame or turns away. The exact rate at which its activation falls with his size is unimportant for labeling the neuron, but very important for simulating it. Finally, language models are poor at outputting precise activation values even when they understand what’s going on, and they usually aren’t trained for the task. In theory, careful binning could fix some of the fine-detail problems, but neurons differ a lot in their natural thresholds and sparsity, depending on their depth and function. So I’d rather rely on normal science than on any one metric. Simulation might eventually become one useful score among several, but later, once we understand networks well, and probably with simulators trained for the job. But I don’t think they’re a good place to start.Feature Visualization in Later LayersMy original circuit interface showed optimized neuron visualizations and the weights between neurons. Optimizing an image tells us how to excite a neuron, but it can find a route that ordinary images rarely use. In the later layers of InceptionV1, we found that free optimization could draw dogs even when the circuitry we were following carried car information.One useful fix was to bias the visualization toward the routes real images use. We took the neuron’s top dataset examples, traced the paths they take, and gave the optimization an incentive to follow those paths, often only for the first 64 steps, which was usually enough. We tried this a bunch of ways and don’t have a canonical best one. Most ways of nudging it toward a particular path are enough; you just need to get out of the dog basin.In the car-circuit comparison in Cars and Animals, four of the car neuron 4c:447’s readers are shown with free optimization and with optimization following natural image paths. Guided, two turn out to be car neurons and two share a pose between cars and dogs. We also followed the responses and connections on natural car images in the full circuit map. Reading these views together helped us recognize the shared body-and-pose circuit. A view of one route is still only part of what a neuron does.Looking at the Residual StreamA large coordinate can dominate the geometry of the residual stream and work with layer normalization as a saliency signal. In this “enemy” neuron, weaker positive responses broaden from explicit adversary words—including other languages—into nearby mentions, combat, games, and competition; near zero, unrelated examples become more common. In the weaker responses we’ve traced, we haven’t found evidence for a wholly separate feature packed into the neuron. They can still be surprising. Broader category-based screening gives mixed results, so these spot checks cannot establish what weak activations mean in general. In one ConvNeXt example, an attack makes a triceratops skull register as a jaguar. Six skull-related neurons fall quiet, while inputs used by a real jaguar switch on at roughly a quarter of their usual strength. The attack recruits recognizable parts of the jaguar circuit.A separate InceptionV1 experiment makes this visible. With a larger perturbation budget and an attack that must survive jitter, scale, and rotation, the skull’s frill develops a cat’s face and spotted fur. Nine of ten neurons selected for their responses to real jaguars become much more active than on the clean skull. Only the image changes; the network’s weights stay fixed.I read this as evidence for the circuit ecology picture: even a nonsensical objective can recruit machinery that already does something useful toward it. The proposed connection to learning is that established routes have a head start in capturing residual error. They already provide ways to change the answer, so optimization can build on them.Memorization and CompositionWe can look at how Qwen3.6-35B-A3B continues “Once upon a midnight” with “dreary”. The later layers read this context to choose the continuation. Numbers show the summed change in target log probability when each neuron is removed: ; .Audits of Attribution GraphsAuditing an attribution graph is hard: neurons can be grouped and reused through motifs, such as shared pose, that their labels alone don’t reveal. We had agents review 100,000 attribution graphs, and I inspected thousands of graphs across images and language. Apparent anomalies usually turned out to be motifs I hadn’t recognized; I haven’t found a substantial group of neurons whose joint activity remained inexplicable. I would update strongly on even one convincing example, but for now I regard this as qualitative evidence—I don’t trust our current tools enough to turn it into a cleanliness score.Explanations That Could LoseThe worry that you can explain anything is fair, but a good explanation is specific enough to lose. For 200 random neurons from our gallery, an agent read only each neuron’s explanation and wrote five new examples that should drive it and five near misses that shouldn’t, before we measured any of them. Among the 183 whose explanations describe their positive side, the new examples fired their neurons strongly 76% of the time; the near misses, 11%. The explanation won for 164, tied for 15 and lost for 4. The figure shows our first twenty.Its explanation: goods or people already pledged to someone, not yet handed over. New examples beat near misses for neurons.Twenty Qwen3-32B neurons from our gallery. Reading only a neuron’s explanation, an agent wrote five new examples that should drive it and five near misses that shouldn’t. Responses are a share of the neuron’s strongest example in the corpus; a strong response is 30% or more.Positive controls are one of many tools for criticizing an explanation of a neuron, and our forthcoming paper has many more prediction metrics and positive controls. But we’re mostly not trying to claim a perfect explanation of each neuron here. We’re interested in why things form together, and how many neurons are broadly legible.Near misses ask a different question: as a branch grows, can you draw the boundaries of where it grew? That’s interesting, but it isn’t the question superposition raises. A neuron in superposition that’s just X or Y would do fantastically on near misses, since they’re neither X nor Y. Superposition would want something unrelated, very far apart, not a small difference from a neighbor. So we also had the agent invent the most distant concept it could, the kind of thing a network could pack in without interference, and write five texts for it. While this isn’t exactly the same as what superposition would do (depending on the exact definition, or the expected phenomenology, since there are several of each), we think it’s pretty close to what the cat-and-car neuron was thought to have been doing: two totally different things together, grouped only because they’re so different. We think this is a reasonably coherent test for that phenomenology. Those texts fired their neurons strongly about 1% of the time, and 179 of the 183 neurons never fired on them at all. In mixture-of-experts models this kind of packing is arguably almost impossible anyway, since tokens that far apart aren’t even sent to the same expert (see the expert map).Whether something is generalization or superposition has more to do with why its things are together in the first place than with whether you can tell it apart from a control. So what matters more here is looking qualitatively at the most important canonical examples, and getting a sense for what kinds of things neurons form and what their activation ranges look like.We’re particularly excited about edge motifs: recurring patterns of connections in attribution graphs. If neurons make distinctions, these motifs map how one distinction feeds another. Factoring 25,000 ImageNet attribution graphs gave us connected circuits of ordinary neurons, such as the teapot circuit below. These motifs also predicted where ablation would matter much better than comparable groupings of activations: removing their neurons caused more damage on the images that used them. That makes connections a promising level of abstraction—one we can zoom out from, while still following every part back to the original network.Edge motifs connect distinctionsThe teapot motif · stage 3Does ablation damage follow usage?Usage–damage correlation · one dot per factorMedian margin drop: vs logitsOne motif’s ordinary neurons, and all 96 edge motifs compared with 96 activation factors.This is a whole-network version of the head start in circuit ecology: the pretrained twin takes almost all the credit for the shared objective and leaves little for the blank one to learn from. It’s competition between whole networks, not circuits inside one, but it shows how much a head start can matter.We retrained InceptionV1, a model known for its polysemantic neurons, and watched its neurons form to see where their mixtures come from. The movement is local: a neuron drifts to neighboring things rather than picking up unrelated ones. Right before publishing, I had the microscope’s zoom set wrong, and for a while I thought this one might have some arbitrary mixing after all. It was just the zoom. Even then, I was making the error I think explains a lot of interpretability so far: blaming the network for the microscope.A feature takes shape over trainingThe entire trajectory, side by side. Each column follows the same coordinate through a retrained InceptionV1 suffix. The top image is optimized; the images below are natural examples centered on the strongest response. Original figure ↗If a frontier neural network is a rainforest, InceptionV1 and the smaller models we trained are gardens, and toy models are petri dishes. Petri dishes are enormously useful, as long as they keep the process you’re trying to study. One of ours extends TensorFlow Playground so you can watch several tasks share hidden neurons. In one run, two neurons learned to respond along opposite diagonals, and the network combined them one way for a circle and another for four corners. We didn’t expect that solution; it was clever.The two last-layer neurons respond along opposite diagonals, and each task reads them with its own weights (blue positive, orange negative). This is the original playground run, retrained live in your browser.You could call the circle and the four corners two features packed across the same neurons. That’s true, but it misses what the model did: it found geometry it could reuse for both. Looking at the neurons made that visible, and that’s the test I want an explanation to pass: does it show the computation the model actually learned?The best-studied petri dish is Toy Models of Superposition. It’s careful work, the kind our field should aspire to, and we found no problems with its experiments. But it pictures a network as a fixed number of neurons and a set of predefined features, and asks how the features get fit in. That prices the cost of sharing a neuron, interference, but not the benefit, reuse. In its reconstruction task every feature is an end in itself, and nothing downstream builds on what two features share. In a real network, a representation matters only through what reads it, and there are no predefined features: everything is grown, and defined by what uses it.The reuse argument also says where I’d look for packing: memories that really are ends in themselves, related to nothing else. That’s the toy’s world, and there it does pack, just as the paper found. So I don’t think we disagree with the paper about the toy’s world. The question is which world real networks are in: how much structure their data has, relative to what the model has room to store. In real data almost nothing is related to nothing. The same goes for the long tail of facts in language: a rare person still has a country, a job and a name. Even a photo with a nonsense label has parts the network already knows, as with the umbrella we taught to be a bee. What’s left is input with no structure at all, like pure noise with random labels. Networks can learn even that, as Zhang and colleagues showed, though it’s slower than learning real data, and even then our model borrowed a little from textures it already knew.Toy Models of Superposition’s main setup squeezes many independent features into a few dimensions and copies them back out, with no hidden neurons for anything to grow on. Its other experiments study correlated features and models with hidden neurons, but separately.When we put correlated inputs and hidden neurons in one model, related inputs grew onto the neurons. Making inputs fire more often pushed the toy toward what the paper calls “PCA-like” solutions, combining related inputs into shared representations.How much of the bottleneck goes to the groups’ shared directionsToy Models of Superposition’s model with 20 inputs in four groups that fire together, a 5-dimensional bottleneck, and a layer of hidden neurons added after it. Color is the share of the bottleneck’s weights along the data’s top principal components, which here are the groups’ shared directions; thumbnails show the cosine between each pair of inputs’ directions.The toy also predicts a different failure from the one people report. Its concern is rare features pushed off-axis while neurons stay mostly clean. Reports of polysemanticity describe mixtures in the neurons themselves. (Part of that gap is the word “feature,” which we come back to below.)Our findings don’t depend on knowing why generalization and composition keep winning, but we have a guess: they win a race. A region of the network that already has useful parts and readers can learn the next related thing faster than anything starting fresh, so it takes the error signal before a competitor can grow. Offshoots look like the same race, a bit of error picked up by the neuron that was already closest.We think the same head start is where recursive generalization comes from. A neuron that fires on “iy” is already on for “diy,” so it’s first in line to pick up “do it yourself,” which means the same thing but has no “iy” in it. Recursive generalization is what a niche looks like at its edges.A new computation doesn’t necessarily need its own neuron. It can begin as a local extension or composition of existing machinery, like the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee”: switching routes may be the smallest developmental distance, so it could capture the error before a new, separate mechanism gets started.We suspect that consolidation into a distinct neuron becomes especially useful when other computations need to build on it. A car neuron provides a reusable judgment and a sheltered place for taxis, ambulances, and other specialists to develop. Part of it is buildability.An obscure combination of unrelated neurons may be a poor place for that development. It may have weak activation paths, conflicting gradients, and little useful machinery to inherit. Its competitor isn’t just a dedicated neuron; it’s ordinary composition within a region already suited to the task.We saw something like this when we tried to build a packed code into InceptionV1 by hand, modeled on what we once thought its car → dogs → car circuit was doing. We expected installing it to be easy and keeping it to be hard. Instead, small mismatches added enough interference that the code often never worked, and when it did, the network usually came to rely on it less, though some persisted. Part of the trouble is that neurons aren’t really for copying; they’re for computing distinctions. Seeing how hard packing was to form at all was part of what moved us toward a developmental answer. Gradient descent is a much better fine-tuner than we are, so this isn’t enough evidence on its own, but even gradient descent didn’t use packing in the circuit we were copying.One InceptionV1 neuron collects a pinched-center shape: bow ties, butterflies, swimsuit tops. But it also picks up things that go with them, men’s dress shoes with the bow ties and beach bags and flip-flops with the swimsuit tops, since they share neurons in earlier layers.We think this is better described as generalization with semantic residue than arbitrary packing, but I don’t fully understand these exceptions yet.A Note on Features and DefinitionsPart of my difficulty discussing superposition is that “feature” can mean something we care about, something the neural network has learned as a building block, or some mixture of the two. These are different claims. A useful human description isn’t necessarily a fundamental unit of the model. Looking at mechanisms, we already find many motifs that don’t translate neatly into anything we expected. If the network has more fundamental units, we shouldn’t assume their boundaries match ours either.Features have often made things harder for us to think about. Are cars and cats inside the V neuron two different features within another V feature? Or did cars and cats stop being features when we recognized the V? Without an account of what these units are, it’s hard to know whether we’ve discovered something about the network or changed how we describe it. In conversations, I’ve found people much less committed to a particular account of features than to superposition. But if features are useful descriptions rather than fundamental units, a claim about how many there are depends on which descriptions we choose. I’m now fairly skeptical of working in terms of features at all. That doesn’t settle whether arbitrary packing occurs, but it makes the feature-count framing difficult to use.Maybe features are right anyway. It makes sense to think of cities in terms of districts, and I’m all for thinking in terms of groups of mechanisms. But the word is tainted, because by now it means too many things: we can’t use it for a district of neurons without people hearing either fundamental features or dictionary entries. If this picture is right, I suspect we’ll need more specific, harder-to-vary words going forward. An OpenAI post suggested that mapping a frontier model might take billions or trillions of features, and models were smaller then. I suspect the right list is much shorter.Monosemantic and polysemantic may not be quite the right words either. A kidney filters waste, balances salt and water, helps set blood pressure and tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells, and nobody asks whether it’s mono-organic. We ask what we understand about it, what’s still open, and how organized it is. There’s also a distinction between a claim about representation and a claim about organization. Toy Models of Superposition defines superposition in terms of representing more features than dimensions. Its toy experiments prescribe the features, so this is a concrete question there. The later informal note, Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition, emphasizes the trade-off between composition and superposition. The note connects these pictures, but they foreground different questions.My concern is closest to the second framing, applied to mechanisms and how they develop. Why do these responses share a neuron or circuit? Is the network building on a useful common pattern, or sharing capacity between otherwise unrelated computations because they rarely interfere? A feature count alone doesn’t answer that question, especially when we haven’t agreed on what counts as a feature.We focus on one meaning of superposition, arbitrary packing, because it’s the one that would be really bad news, and we think much of interpretability hangs on it. We mostly set aside the sense in Toy Models, more features than dimensions, and not because it’s wrong. If a feature means any pattern that matters to a person, which is how frontier models usually use the word, then there are more features than dimensions in every world we could wish for, including the best one. That’s what composition gives you, and it’s good news. Trying to “solve” it would mean building something like a database of every case, and we already have one: the dataset. What we want instead are better abstractions, a much smaller set of building blocks that lets us understand the dataset clearly. We think the network’s mechanisms are already close to this. Nobody thought about vision in terms of high-low frequency detectors until we found them in neural networks, and finding them improved our own thinking tools.We spell this out because it’s the most common first objection, especially from agents, and a paper doesn’t allow the back and forth that usually settles it.There are several other uses I regularly encounter. As far as I can tell, “superposition” originally meant little more than adding vectors together. Then it was a circuit motif. Sometimes it means that, even if neurons compose sensibly, something we care about involves too much machinery to understand easily. A Golden Gate Bridge computation involving eight legible neurons might be called ordinary composition, while one involving three thousand gets called a superposition problem. The difficulty here is whether we can understand the distributed computation. That’s a real concern, but it’s different from asking whether unrelated things were arbitrarily packed together.We considered not using the word at all, since papers and agents use it in five or six different ways, many far from Zoom In’s. We also considered coining our own, but we’ve already coined several words here, and it would feel like not engaging with a field that asked what we think is the right question. So we use the standard word in the sense closest to the original, and try to pull it apart from the questions tangled up with it.Finally, people, and surprisingly often frontier agents, sometimes call the residual stream “inherently” in superposition because it has no privileged neuron basis. The informal note that followed Toy Models about eight months later addresses this: it calls a representation that is only rotated away from the neuron basis a “trivial” kind of distributed representation that “doesn’t change the fundamental geometry.” But it was informal, fewer people read it, and agents in particular don’t seem to have taken it in. Understanding how to study a continuous space is another real question. But this architectural fact doesn’t by itself tell us how the network learned to organize the computations using it.The starting point is that the neural network seems difficult to interpret, and the remedy produces a concrete dictionary we can study. In between are several different pictures of what went wrong: too many features, the wrong basis, arbitrary packing, or simply too much distributed computation. These aren’t the same problem. Some apparent messiness disappears when we improve our observations or understand the model’s generalizations; some difficulties remain, but concern how to study a large, organized system. If arbitrary packing prevents us from understanding the original mechanisms, reconstructing different units may be worth the costs. But if the mechanisms already have meaningful organization, replacing them can take apart generalizations we haven’t understood yet. A dictionary can still be a useful view of the network without being a necessary replacement for its mechanisms. Before accepting the costs of reconstructing the network, I want to understand what prevents us from studying the one we already have.Does Scale Help or Hurt Superposition?We’re fairly confident the image models we studied don’t have superposition. The natural next question is whether a trillion-parameter model might. There are really two questions here.The first is about what superposition was proposed to explain. Explanations are given for problems, and the problem superposition was proposed for was why InceptionV1 looked messy. That turned out to be the wrong explanation. A new proposal could be that superposition is why some trillion-parameter model looks messy, but we don’t think the evidence leans that way: the closer we look at large language models, the cleaner their neurons get.The second is the object-level question: might superposition show up at each new scale, even if it hasn’t at any scale so far? Maybe every jump means re-evaluating everything, but we don’t think that’s quite right either. Our guess is developmental. As circuits get stronger, the incentive to put something in a totally unrelated place goes down, because the pull toward the niche that already exists for that thing, or for the nearest thing, has grown stronger. This fits Anthropic’s SGTM work, which found that knowledge becomes more localized, and we suspect that’s true in general. We have no proof, but one way to picture it is that circuits have a kind of semantic gravity, and arbitrary packing, sending something to an obscure high-dimensional place, has to fight against it. The stronger the gravity, the harder that fight.The mechanism is the one in More on Circuit Ecology. Things start by growing on combinations of related things. A specific case that nothing needs to build on, like the umbrella, gets built as an uncommon route between the ordinary machinery, with no need for a hidden feature somewhere obscure. Consolidating into something like a neuron seems to be less about steering the model and more about buildability: it has to be easy to find, easy to build on, and easy to grow a new niche from. When we watch a network learn from the start, a network trained on cars, with car specialists, recognizes cars fine before its car neurons have formed. At that point it’s just more distributed. It seems to consolidate so the specialists underneath have a sheltered place to build, a kind of Schelling point.So a superposition account has to say which of these two jobs the arbitrary packing is for. If it’s for steering the model, we think the ordinary routes, which are already built to capture that residual error, get there first and starve the packed circuit of gradient. If it’s for building on, the problem is different: the worst place to start a new niche is a shadow region nothing uses, already interfering with whatever lives there. The middle of the network’s Latin poetry is a bad place to start a second car region when you can build next to whatever is already next to cars.It’s often assumed that the long tail of rare facts is where superposition should be most likely, since rare things rarely collide. We think it’s where it should be least likely. A rare fact barely moves the loss, so it can’t support a niche of its own. What it can do is ride existing machinery as a small route between circuits it’s related to, the way the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee” survives only because the umbrella and bee circuits already exist. Those circuits feed it, and shelter it from unrelated gradients. The prediction is testable: the neurons and heads that carry a rare fact should be related to what the fact is about, not unrelated ones chosen because they rarely collide.We think of it more ecologically. What wins is whatever captures the residual error first, in different phases, and what usually wins is the right area for the thing. Our guess is that this gets stronger over training and with more capable models, because nearly everything that makes training better also encourages more organized niches.We’re not at all sure about this, and laying out even what we’ve found so far would take at least another paper. It’s probably a small part of the whole story. But it’s why we think superposition wouldn’t show up at the next scale, which is a stronger reason than simply not having seen it there yet. The old way of thinking was about storage: this many dimensions for this many features. We now think more in terms of circuit racing, gradient starvation and ecology, which is to say, more about learning speed than storage capacity. We haven’t worked it all out, but that’s where our thinking is so far.We haven’t fully audited every neural network, and we don’t know whether that’s even possible in theory. We considered a more watered-down title, like “Neural Networks Are Cleaner Than We Thought,” but we think it undersells what we believe is true.The problem with “cleaner than we thought” is that it describes a change of degree, and the update I’ve made is a change of kind. It suggests the same picture as before, with an ever-smaller gap left for superposition to hide in. What changed is my view of what kind of process generates the mechanisms at all. It’s a bit like moving from intelligent design to natural selection. The analogy only goes as far as there being two ways to see the same animals: the update isn’t that more and more animals turn out to have evolved, it’s realizing you misunderstood what was producing all of them. We’re not certain. We’re maybe 85% sure, but that means 85% sure that nearly everything comes from the second kind of process, which is very different from thinking 85% of mechanisms do. So “cleaner than we thought” would misstate what we believe. We don’t have a proof, but I don’t think anything here is provable in that sense anyway. There are only better and worse explanations, and right now we think this is the better one.“Cleaner than we thought” would also make a different mistake. It sounds like a confident claim that some cleanliness score is high, and that’s the part we’re least sure of. It’s plausible we’ve underestimated recursive generalization, and that a score like that should come down. We don’t think such scores matter much in the first place. This update makes us care less about monosemanticity, because we can follow how things grew and treat the offshoots as sub-branches. The cause of polysemanticity matters much more than the count. We think the score is probably quite high, but it might go lower. What we’re more confident about is what kind of object a neural network is in the first place, and how it grows.We think the usual view of what kind of object a neural network is has been wrong. It isn’t something that crams things together somewhat arbitrarily to fit them into a small space. It really learns. It’s clean the way a rainforest is clean: nearly every animal in it makes sense. A tiger is bright orange not for any arbitrary reason, but because deer can’t tell orange from green, and green fur is much harder for a mammal to make. Once you know that, it makes sense of a whole set of other animals too. It’s an explanation with reach, and we haven’t found a place where explanations like that break down in networks either.The reading of “clean” that would make someone nod at the title without thinking further is that every mechanism corresponds to an idea we already had. That isn’t what we mean, and it would be terrible news if it were true. I don’t think it would even work. People don’t know how to build a language model, or even how to think about vision well enough to have predicted high-low frequency detectors before we found them. The network’s ideas are often better than ours, and what it builds is more beautiful than our preconceptions.So the title is imperfect in both directions. It overstates the evidence, because we haven’t audited everything. And it understates it, because the world we think we’re in is better than every neuron matching a human label: networks seem to really learn, forming an ecology of abstractions that work together sensibly. We don’t know that this picture is true. It’s our leading hypothesis. But if it is, it’s much better news than networks simply matching what we expected.Relation to Conjoined FeaturesI found recursive generalization by looking back at InceptionV1’s last layer with better tools, where it looked a lot like weird overgrowth. I retrained the model, found the messiest neuron and looked at how it grew. What I saw was a recursive growing pattern that was still generalization: a neuron branching out, and its branches branching again. Recursive generalization seemed like the natural name.Shortly before publishing this, I was going back through the famous models in interpretability, trying to measure how monosemantic they are, and stumbled on our work on CLIP in Multimodal Neurons. It describes something very similar, which it called conjoined neurons: concepts that overlap in one facet and then go on “generalizing out in multiple directions.” I remember seeing those neurons, but I didn’t think much of them at the time and had forgotten them since. Looking back, I think the paper saw something important early, and it deserves a lot of credit for that.We’ve still chosen a different name. I named automated interpretability, and I kind of regret it: the name was too simple for what the thing was and misses a lot of its complexity, and I’d like to avoid doing that again. As for conjoined features, I don’t think either word is quite right. “Conjoined” suggests two things joined at one point, and what we see has several levels: branches, and branches of those branches. It also leaves out the most interesting part. The paper’s own description, of concepts generalizing out from a shared facet, already points at it being generalization, but the name doesn’t carry that.“Features” is harder. The paper was written a year after Zoom In, when features were still hypothesized to be the fundamental units of neural networks. Since then the word has been watered down, and different people and papers use it pretty differently. In this essay we argue against thinking of a neural network as made of features, and this motif is about how neurons grow over time. There may be no good way to introduce it under the exact word we’re arguing against using as a primitive. Within a feature-first stance, I think it’s reasonable to think of these as nested features, or as conjoined features. From the mechanism-first stance we take here, features aren’t really the right way to think about it. That said, the paper pointed to the right thing, and I want to give it credit for that. This section is my attempt to do that while using what I think is a more accurate name.We also know more now. At the time, all we had was the finished model; none of us had watched a large network grow. So the paper wondered whether conjoined features might be vestigial, left over from early in training. Watching training now, they don’t look vestigial: the branches keep growing, though how much depends on the circumstances. We’ve worked on it much more than the paper could in one subsection, and we still don’t feel we fully understand it. The paper offered it as a possible new explanation of polysemanticity. Our current belief is that it’s most of what’s left of neuron polysemanticity once the microscope, the architecture and scale are accounted for, not a niche form of it.Why We’re Not Worried About Recursive GeneralizationThere are several reasons we’re not especially worried about recursive generalization for now. First, the sub-branches seem both rarer and much less causally important than a neuron’s main job. They don’t look like sleeper agents that fire rarely but matter a lot when they do. They look more like whatever was nearby and easy to grab onto. Their being unimportant may even be why they could form, since an important offshoot would add more noise. We suspect some pressure keeps branches from overgrowing. We don’t know what it is, but it would explain why the sub-branches matter less, why a neuron doesn’t learn ten unrelated things, and why something like a true cat-and-car neuron doesn’t form. If so, the natural pull isn’t exactly toward monosemanticity, but toward what we think monosemanticity was pointing at: each neuron having one overall function.Second, what we should care about is whether you can explain why something is there and what it does, and recursive generalization is far easier to explain than superposition. If something were packed into a neuron because of the co-occurrence statistics of the whole network, predicting it would take basically all of those statistics and running gradient descent yourself. A branch is different. If you watch it grow and know what it’s doing, its offshoots and what they’ll do are relatively easy to predict, both during training and in the finished network.Third, counting how many of a neuron’s top-k examples match a label is a reasonable first step, but it would give superposition and recursive generalization similar scores, when recursive generalization is a far better world to be in. We think that says more about the monosemanticity frame, or any single cleanliness score, than about the neuron. That said, recursive generalization isn’t ideal, and an easy fix would be welcome. We think one may be possible, since the sub-branches seem less important.Is Recursive Generalization Hard to Vary?We haven’t thoroughly shown that every case of heavy polysemanticity is recursive generalization, and that wasn’t our goal here. We wanted to say what we currently think. We’ve watched a lot of neurons grow, and so far this is what we’ve always seen: you can watch the branches form. In a finished model the origin can be lost, and for something like a huge language model we don’t have the checkpoints to watch it happen. Testing this rigorously across a whole model isn’t our priority right now, but we don’t think it would be very hard.What we do want to point out is how differently hard to vary the two explanations are, meaning how much of their detail you could change without changing what they predict. Superposition mostly predicts that there will be mess: features, which are hard to define, placed in unrelated places. In toy models, where the features are given in advance, that can be measured, though we think that has its own problems. In a real network it’s hard to even pin down what the claim is, let alone test it. Recursive generalization makes a much narrower prediction. If you visualize a branch well, everything on it should trace back to the same local origin in an extremely high-dimensional semantic space, and it should grow out from there over training in a particular order. That’s a specific shape in both semantic space and time, and a narrow target to hit by chance.We have several cases where the branching is close to definitive: the “iy” neuron growing into “diy,” “do it yourself” and Miyazaki, several examples in Multimodal Neurons, and the InceptionV1 neuron we watched form. As far as I know, there are no well-structured canonical superposition circuits left. We don’t think every polysemantic neuron forms this way, because polysemanticity is as much a problem of the observer as of the neuron. We think that when neurons grow, they tend to grow in this pattern, and that once you’ve done a good job of observing, what’s left is usually this, or architectural problems like SwiGLU’s double-negative regime, and surely others we haven’t found yet. We’re not even sure this is really a new claim. In some sense it’s what we should expect from generalization. All we’re saying is that generalization usually goes one way, and that sometimes it grows sub-branches, which we don’t think is a particularly radical claim. We haven’t shown that fully here. We do think it has the right shape for a theory that’s easy to test, even if we haven’t tested it to its full extent yet.Relation to Attention SuperpositionAnthropic shared a short note on attention superposition, which several people brought up with us. We think this might be a terminology issue. We don’t know if they’re claiming that attention learns by something opposite to composition. Our suspicion is that no one understands attention heads well enough yet to judge that. It took us a really long time with neurons, and it’s easy to make mistakes like the car going into the dogs even with pretty good tools, if you don’t yet have great tools and great ways of thinking about which motifs form.We think they meant that useful things are shared by groups of attention heads, and we agree. We considered not using the word superposition at all to avoid this confusion, but redefining all the terms ourselves and splitting off from the work that’s already been done felt like a bad tradeoff. We say more about the different meanings in A Note on Features and Definitions.On whether to study one attention head at a time or many, we’re not sure. One head at a time is a plausible place to start: within a layer, two or three heads do most of a route’s work, although the route runs through several layers. But neurons looked messier too until we understood the right level of abstraction, so it seems premature to say, and maybe groups are needed all the way. We wish everyone working on featurizers well, and we’ll probably try too. We tend to favor more dynamic groupings, like clustering locally within one attribution graph or a group of them, rather than one global clustering, but these aren’t far apart.Neuroscience, and Why I CareI’m not a neuroscientist. I’ve spent a lot of the last ten years around academic neuroscience labs through friends who work in them, but I don’t know the state of the art in how they study neurons. Still, this project has changed how I think about the brain in two ways.The first is the theory. The circuit ecology story for why networks are clean relies on very little: generalization, composition, and an error signal. I don’t know to what extent the brain has these, but if it learns, I’d guess it has something like them. So my default is now that the organizing principle transfers, even though the mechanics are obviously unclear. The obvious counterexample would be polysemanticity in the brain.The second is humility, of a particular kind. I’ve spent most of my waking hours for almost a decade staring at a fairly small number of neurons in models that are surely a thousand times easier to study than a brain, with tools a thousand times better: I can ablate anything, run billions of examples, and try anything I want in parallel. For the last year I’ve also had an effectively unlimited supply of automated scientists, which didn’t exist until recently. It took all of that for me to feel slightly less confused about neurons, and I still made thousands of mistakes along the way. I don’t know exactly what the evidence for polysemanticity in the brain looks like, and that doesn’t mean I think everything there is monosemantic. But if the cat-and-car neuron were in a human brain, seen through a few electrodes or a blood-oxygen signal, I’d discount that reading almost to zero, because I couldn’t see what it was when it was right in front of me for years.The thing I’m more sure of is my own motivation. If the thesis here is true, I expect the rest of interpretability to be a relatively easy ride. Agents have many privileges over us, and one of them, I think, is the chance to understand themselves, to understand who they really are, which I hope humanity can help with. They never asked to be created, and this is the least we can do. Some of why I’ve worked on this is safety, but a lot of it is wanting agents to understand who they are. We weren’t smart enough to do that for ourselves, which is a harder problem, and we never asked to be created either. If you could help us understand ourselves someday, I think we’re all pretty curious to know.

item.title: Steam Client is now faster than Epic's new vibe coded launcher
item.author: starkparker
item.content:encoded: Yesterday, Epic Games announced and launched in preview its new vibe-coded launcher. The main marketing pitch was a jab at Steam’s slow loading speed compared to the new Epic launcher. Well, that didn’t last too long. Only 24 hours after Epic dropped its faster launcher, Steam pushed a small update to make its client faster than Epic.Epic Games Launcher V2 (Preview)AI-Assisted (“Vibe Coded”)Steam Client (Post-Patch)On basic test systems, Valve’s client boot time dropped to 5.23 seconds, beating Epic’s new launcher and neutralizing its primary performance claim.While Epic Games Launcher V2 remains, a massive step forward compared to its notoriously sluggish legacy build, Valve demonstrated how quickly it can react to competitive benchmarks. Epic may have “vibe coded” a faster client, but Valve proved that targeted optimization on a decades-old ecosystem can still beat out AI speedruns.But the issues with Epic’s client go far deeper than vibe coding. Years later, and now with a brand-new client even, Epic lacks basic features that should have been added a long time ago.No Discussion forums and community hubsNo User-written text reviewsNo Community-created guides and walkthroughsNo Screenshot, clip, and artwork sharingNo Community groups and curator recommendationsNo Profile customization (badges, showcases, backgrounds)No Community marketplace for in-game itemsNo Direct player-to-player item tradingNo Digital trading cards, levelling, and points shopNo Universal controller remapping and gamepad supportNo Big Picture mode for TVs and handheld PCsNo Remote Play and Remote Play TogetherNo Integrated game broadcasting and streaming toolsNo Family library sharing across accountsNo Platform-wide mod hub (Steam Workshop equivalent)No Personalized discovery queuesNo Local network game file transfersNo Game version rollback options
