item.title: AdFection: Targeted ads turned into a pipeline for zero-click mercenary spyware
item.author: jcomp
item.content:encoded: Devices at international news network Al Jazeera were infected with mercenary spyware from Candiru (rebranded as “Integrity Labs”) via targeted online advertisements. We provide the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection.The malicious advertisements were purchased by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate advertising company, but which we found operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners.Discover-Tech operates a platform called that enables its mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered — a form of zero-click attack.Analysis of four billion Discover-Tech bidding records shows that during a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries.Discover-Tech’s ads also covertly directed millions of devices to contact Candiru’s servers, likely for large-scale tracking and reconnaissance. Discover-Tech is linked to mercenary spyware and intelligence threat actors beyond Candiru, including Intelos and Bindecy. A separate threat actor we call is using Discover-Tech’s infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across numerous mobile carriers to link device advertising IDs with phone numbers, mass-deanonymizing internet users. We will detail our findings concerning this threat actor in a separate forthcoming report.Discover-Tech has appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served ads via major networks such as Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. Discover-Tech has also leveraged the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target users within the European Union.Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report.We call on regulators to investigate whether Discover-Tech and Candiru/Integrity Labs violated applicable laws, and make recommendations to lawmakers, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection-style attacks and espionage. We disclosed our findings to ad vendors and industry organizations. Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi took action to disconnect Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem. Other ad vendors we found to be involved in Discover-Tech’s operations did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. We are also actively working with vendors to mitigate ’s mass-deanonymization attack.This section provides an overview of the online advertising ecosystem, and summarizes our findings about Discover-Tech.The Online Advertising Ecosystem is Ripe for AbuseWhen a user sees an ad on an app or a website, it is likely the result of a real-time auction, where advertisers bid on the chance to show that specific user that specific ad. So-called Real-Time Bidding (RTB) auctions, which are hosted on ad exchanges operated by companies including Google, take place hundreds of billions of times a day. In less than a second, the user’s device initiates a bid request, advertisers submit their bids, and the ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. Besides an image or video, an online ad can also contain code that runs within the app or browser that shows the ad.Both advertisers and publishers of apps and websites use ad vendors that act as their intermediaries in these auctions. Advertisers typically buy ads via a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), and a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) sells ad inventory on websites and apps.Malicious actors make use of two interrelated facets of the online advertising ecosystem:The advertising ecosystem collects a lot of data and enables individual-level targeting: When a publisher of an app or website wishes to show ads, they add code from an SSP to their app or site. This code collects and shares granular information about the user and their device with ad exchanges to solicit for the ad slots. This information can include device identifiers and characteristics, precise location, and IP address data, as well as data about the app or website, and specifications about the ad slot. The DSP or advertiser then examines this information and decides whether they wish to bid on the impression in order to show an ad. The auction system isdesigned to enable targeting single individuals based on their mobile advertising ID, cookie ID, IP address, and other identifiers.The advertising ecosystem allows many different third parties to run code in apps and websites: It is tempting to think of an online ad as, simply, a video or image. However, ads themselves maycontaincode from the advertiser, DSP, and other parties, and run it in the app or browser while the ad is shown to the user, for example to track users, ad impressions, and clicks. Code run by advertisers, DSPs, SSPs, and other third parties within apps and websites is often referredto as “tags”, “pixels”, “SDKs”, or “third-party tracking” more generally.Exploiting Advertising Tech for SurveillanceThe totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable. A company with access to auction data cantrack users without their knowledge as they move around in physical space, or switch between cellular, Wi-Fi, and VPNs, by observing how bid requests tied to a specific identifier change location or IP address over time. In fact, the surveillance industry sells access to so-called ad intelligence (ADINT) platforms that leverage this sort of data, often combined with third-party tracking data. In recent years, several investigations and media reports haveuncoveredvendors that sell ADINT to defense, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies.Zero-Click Spyware Delivered via Targeted Ads: AdFectionBeyond passive data harvesting, malicious parties can also exploit this infrastructure to target certain individuals based on user data included in ad auctions and then run malicious code on their devices. Advertisers or DSPs may run HTML and JavaScript code when an ad is shown to the user. That code retrieves additional JavaScript code, which may, in turn, load further code, such as a browser exploit to install spyware. Since the code can contain identifiers for the user or their device, arbitrary JavaScript code can be sent precisely to a single user’s device. Our research in this report indicates that this architecture is indeed abused to facilitate the delivery of zero-click targeted spyware, and that the simple display of a targeted ad is enough for infection.There hasbeen some reporting about the intersection between spyware and the advertising ecosystem. However, the specific ways mercenary spyware companies plug into the ads ecosystem to target particular users have remained largely secret. This report exposes zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads, which we call, and is the first technical demonstration that mercenary spyware is being distributed via targeted advertisements.Discover-Tech is a Bridge Between Mercenary Spyware Companies and the Advertising EcosystemWe present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse, including the automatic delivery of mercenary spyware when ads are displayed to a target and the mass profiling and deanonymization of users.The company serves as a bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem. In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose. Its platform, Controlium, allows malicious actors to precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking, where their devices can be automatically infected when an ad is displayed to them.Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem. As we detail in this report, Discover-Tech ads are used to infect and profile on behalf of mercenary spyware vendor Candiru. We also detail connections between Discover-Tech and another mercenary hacking company, Bindecy, as well as connections with Intelos, a mercenary ADINT firm.What is Discover-Tech and How Does It Operate?Discover-Tech is led by its CEO Dekel Boni, who has a background in digital advertising. Eric Banoun, whom Haaretz describes as “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel”, joined the company’s board of directors soon after it was founded in 2020 and remained there until 2025. Between 2020 and March 2026, Discover-Tech’s shareholders included a company linked to Sara Hamou, who has managed the corporate network of the spyware group Intellexa.Discover-Tech appears to place advertisements using several techniques. Firstly, the company operates a platform called which interfaces with online ad vendors including Google, Yandex, Vungle (Liftoff), and Sunteng. Secondly, separately from MyDSP, it purchases ads via the ad vendors Eskimi and Comcast-owned Beeswax (Freewheel).A large number of ads placed by Discover-Tech contain a tag pointing back to what the company refers to as a “” (also called a “getAd server”). This tag causes the ad, when rendered, to connect back to Discover-Tech, submit advertising identifiers for the user (either a cookie ID or a mobile ad ID), and automatically execute any JavaScript code returned. The NOAS server decides, apparently based on a combination of the source IP address and the advertising identifiers, whether the target is eligible to receive any JavaScript. If so, then code is returned. If not, a 0-byte response is returned. The NOAS server is a key part of Discover-Tech’s strategy, allowing Discover-Tech to avoid directly sharing malicious code, or even pointers to malicious code, with the companies who serve and display the ads.As detailed in , Discover-Tech appeared on several lists of “certified” and “approved” ad vendors maintained by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe from the year 2020 until 2026. These listings helped make Discover-Tech appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and facilitate its participation in the digital advertising ecosystem at scale.As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Google, which collaborated in the investigation, terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms. Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform, Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review, and Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains.Report Overview: Exposing Discover-Tech’s AdFection Pipeline In this report we provide an overview of the different types of ad abuse facilitated by Discover-Tech, the company’s ad targeting systems and practices, as well as its partners and corporate network.In , we show how Candiru works with Discover-Tech to conduct AdFection attacks, and describe one such attack: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with Candiru’s mercenary spyware. In , we examine Controlium, a Discover-Tech platform that provides a control-panel style interface enabling mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads.”In , we examine links between Discover-Tech and mercenary spyware companies Candiru/Integrity Labs and Bindecy. We then outline their relationships with other mercenary surveillance companies, including advertising intelligence (ADINT) vendor Intelos, and an ADINT vendor we refer to as , which is building databases linking users’ mobile advertising identifiers to their phone numbers.In , we analyze Discover-Tech’s malicious advertisements land. We identified a Discover-Tech server that published almost four billion ad bidding records. These records show that Discover-Tech ads were served in almost 200,000 different Android apps, iOS apps, and websites in many countries. We also highlight specific countries and government networks where Discover-Tech’s advertisements had impressions.In , we use technical analysis to examine how Discover-Tech deploys ads, tracks users and exchanges user identifiers with other ad vendors, including with Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad system Xandr.In , we present our research on Discover-Tech Ltd, its corporate network, key persons linked to the company, the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology, and its connection to the wider advertising ecosystem.In , we summarize what is known about the mercenary surveillance firms Candiru, Bindecy, and Intelos, and we further examine their activities and corporate networks in the context of the findings presented in our report.In , we explore how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, including Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, Sunteng, and Xandr (Microsoft).In , we discuss the implications of AdFection for user security and human rights.In , we provide recommendations to lawmakers, regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to mitigate and block threats from AdFection-style attacks.The Citizen Lab sent requests for comment to 13 companies; their responses are included in full in the ‘Correspondence with Companies’ section.2. How Discover-Tech’s AdFection Zero-Click WorksThis section provides the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click spyware attack via targeted ads in the wild: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with mercenary spyware. We refer to this type of attack as. Using network analysis, infrastructure fingerprinting, and analysis of implant behaviour, we connect Discover-Tech’s infrastructure with the distribution of Candiru’s mercenary spyware.What AdFection Looks LikeThe instances of Candiru AdFection via Discover-Tech ads all share similar characteristics. First, Discover-Tech wins a bid, and one of their ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device. The user may see this ad, such as in , though in some cases the ad may render in the background.When the website or app receives the ad, it renders it, requesting JavaScript from a Discover-Tech server embedded within the ad. In most cases, the user who sees the ad is selected for targeting, and the server will JavaScript to be executed. Nevertheless, the ad will still gather data from the user’s browser and submit it back to Discover-Tech, which can include cookies set on the webpage including the ad, as well as the device’s public IPv6 address.Confirming the Targeting of Al Jazeera with Candiru Spyware via Discover-Tech AdsIn 2024 and 2025, international news network was targeted in a series of zero-click attacks that we link with high confidence to Candiru’s spyware delivered via Discover-Tech’s ads. At least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in these attacks.Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Infected devices first show contact with domains from Discover-Tech infrastructure, indicating an ad impression. Next, the devices show connections with a Candiru validator server. The validator server performs an initial check of the device before it is further profiled and infected. Ultimately, an infected device communicates with a Candiru Command and Control (C&C) server. This temporal signature is illustrated by .Fingerprinting Candiru ServersWe developed a fingerprint for Candiru validator servers. Both and returned banners that matched the following regular expression on Censys. We refer to this as :We found hosts on Censys matching between August 2022 through July 2026, though we note that in May and June 2026, this behaviour gradually began being retired. In all, we found 305 distinct domain names on 319 IP addresses, though to save query costs we only searched one historical Censys snapshot per month. The set of 305 validator server domains we found includes ones publicly attributed to Candiru by Sekoia, as well as Recorded Future.We also identified a separate fingerprint for the C&C servers used in the attack, . Four of the servers matched it (, insightenterprisells[.]com, , ). We could not locate a response in Internet scanning data for the other three.Attribution of the Attack to CandiruAl Jazeera isolated a Windows DLL file from one of the compromised devices which contains hardcoded Command & Control servers matching Fingerprint C1. The sample is available on VirusTotal.Candiru spyware sample SHA256: 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8This sample hard-codes two C&C servers that match : and . The functionality broadly overlaps with the functionality of the Candiru chain from our 2021 report. For example:Both samples use a COM hijack for persistence, though make use of different DLLs.Both samples obfuscate strings using a 48-byte repeating XOR key, though the samples have different keys. Both samples also have an interesting quirk where obfuscated strings contain a “dummy” null-terminator character that is not deobfuscated (the deobfuscation with the key would be nonsensical), and is instead silently discarded. The only function of this dummy null-terminator appears to be to ensure that the right-size chunk of memory is allocated to hold the XOR-decrypted output.The configuration within both samples hardcodes the same ordered list of domain names to fetch to check network connectivity: http://www.google.com and http://www.microsoft.com.The combination of the COM persistence hijack, the use of a distinctive 48-byte repeating XOR obfuscation technique with a “dummy” null terminator, and the specific hardcoded network connectivity check leads us to conclude with high confidence that this sample is a newer version of the Candiru attack chain that we captured in 2021.3. Exposing Discover-Tech’s Controlium: Malicious Ad Targeting PlatformThis section examines Controlium, a platform that provides a control-panel style interface allowing mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads” that deliver malware. Discover-Tech published the full source code for Controlium’s frontend on the app’s login page, which allowed us to review and reconstruct the user interface.Discover-Tech provides its customers with access to a platform called that appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements. Customers can use Controlium to select a user for infection or profiling based on their mobile advertising identifier (iOS or Android), browser identifier (MyDSP or Beeswax cookie ID), and/or IP address. Discover-Tech’s malicious ads (referred to as “controlled ads”) sometimes also contain branding of companies that are closely linked to Discover-Tech, or branding from apparently unwitting third-party companies, including Amazon and AliExpress. We have no evidence that these ads were purchased by Amazon or AliExpress.As is standard for many web apps, the entirety of the source code for the Controlium frontend is included on the app’s login page. We visited the login page in a web browser and saved the page to disk to obtain a copy of the frontend. We modified our copy of the code to remove any communication with any external servers, and to reveal all available screens in the UI. We then opened this version in a web browser to explore the app’s user interface. In our analysis of Controlium, we downloaded only publicly accessible resources without circumventing any access controls. Most data associated with Controlium, such as information about Discover-Tech’s customers and their operations, is intentionally protected with an authorization token. However, we were able to obtain data on Controlium user logins from an unauthenticated API endpoint (see below: ‘Unauthenticated Endpoint’). We also assess that it would have been possible for a hacker to spoof a valid authorization (see below: ‘Authentication Vulnerability’), although we did not test this.Attribution to Discover-TechWe found the Controlium platform available on the following websites:Additionally, several strings in the Controlium code directly reference Discover-Tech:Furthermore, if a user tries to access a particular endpoint in the app called “/jsConfig”, the app displays the following message, which is a possible reference to Discover-Tech’s CEO Dekel Boni:Finally, an unauthenticated API endpoint (see below: ‘Unauthenticated Endpoint’) shows frequent login activity from users whose names overlap with Discover-Tech employees on LinkedIn.Controlium: Examining Admin ModeAn account designated as an “admin” on the Controlium platform can configure a number of different parameters for customers of the platform. First, an admin may grant a customer access to the web interface, or the API. It also appears that the Controlium product can be “white labeled” with a different logo, and that access can be restricted to specific IPs.Next, admins may add restrictions on what type of campaigns a customer may run. These restrictions control which combinations of user IDs and IP addresses they are allowed to bid on, and which “URL Types” they can access.Customers can have certain “OpSec” restrictions placed on their ad bidding, which appears to be an effort to ensure that customers are not bidding too frequently or too broadly:There is also another type of “OpSec” called “Ad URL OpSec”, which we explore more in Section 4.Customers can be further restricted based on how many campaigns they can run daily or monthly, or restricted based on a “Domains Whitelist” or “Apps Whitelist”, which appear to control on which domain or within which mobile apps ads can be bid on. As is customary for licensing of an attack platform, customers can be restricted to only bid on ads in certain countries via either an allowlist or blocklist.Controlium: Examining Customer ModeThe exact steps a user or customer would need to take to use the platform are not clear. The Controlium user interface includes a number of modules and forms that provide, in part, overlapping functionality to set up ad campaigns and monitor ad data.Controlium users can create a “tag”, which defines a combination of an ad image, a landing page, a “NOAS URL” (see below: ‘A Look at the NOAS Server’), and URLs for logging impressions and clicks.Users can select a DSP to use for delivering the ad. The available options include Beeswax, Eskimi and Discover-Tech’s own MyDSP. When selecting MyDSP, they can also choose whether to use the Google or Yandex ad exchange.Controlium’s “OP Creative Upload” module allows users to upload and configure advertising content (e.g. an ad), and then upload the data to a DSP. Users can attach a tag to the ad either by defining a landing page, a NOAS URL and URLs for logging impressions and clicks, or they can paste a “Custom Tag” generated by the “Tag Generation” module.The available DSP options include “MyDSP WW”, “MyDSP Yandex RU”, “Beeswax (Palm 3)”, “MyDSP Google (Palm 3)”, and others. Users can also select several “Add Ons” including “Infinite FIFO”, “Detect Zuid”, and “User Agent”.Another module labeled “Campaigns” allows Controlium users to associate “Ad URLs” to selected “controlled ads”, which can be served either in mobile apps or on websites, according to Controlium’s source code. As shown in the screenshot, the module allows users to define target “User IDs” and select a “URL Type”.The URL types available for selection include “Ad URL”, “Test URL”, “Script”, “User Agent”, “Monitor”, “Pixel”, and “De-anon”. We are unsure what most of these options mean, but we think that for “Ad URL”, the NOAS server returns JavaScript adding a 1×1 iframe to the page pointing at the specified URL, and “Script” may be designed to allow arbitrary JavaScript to run. Any URL is delivered via the NOAS Server (see below: ‘A Look at the NOAS Server’).Authentication VulnerabilityWhile the data associated with Controlium’s customers and their operations are nominally protected with an authorization token, it appears that it would be easy for a hacker to spoof a valid token. We did not attempt to exploit this issue, as we believe doing so would have constituted unauthorized access to Discover-Tech’s systems.The underlying issue stems from Discover-Tech’s improper use of Okta’s product. When a Controlium customer authenticates with , a JWT is returned to their browser. This token is digitally signed by , and contains information about scopes and expiry that the backend server should validate. However, Controlium ignores this token and instead passes a separate object as a token to the backend server. The object simply contains unauthenticated metadata about the user, such as their name and email address. Controlium encrypts this information with a secret key published in the Controlium platform.Interestingly, the code to use the JWT as an authorization token was present within the Controlium platform, but was commented out in lieu of the vulnerable code.During our analysis of the Controlium platform, we observed that the source code mentioned an endpoint called “/csv-download”, which accepted start and end date parameters. When we sent normal HTTP GET requests to this endpoint without any password, special headers, or authentication token, we received logs showing which users had logged in to Controlium, and from which IP addresses. We successfully exported authentication logs for 128 days and identified 120 distinct usernames logging into the Controlium instances on and . We further delve into this data in Section 4.A Look at the NOAS ServerWe were able to elicit code from NOAS servers by testing “dummy” User ID values. For example, we observed that a visit to:Yielded the following content:We also found that we could task a NOAS server for a similar Discover-Tech app published on called “Mini Platform C”.We input a User ID, “test123” into this form, and an AD URL, “https://example.com/”, then we observed the tasking by visiting this NOAS URL:The first time we visited it, the URL returned this:Subsequent visits returned nothing.This version of “Mini Platform C” does not appear to support any other options besides “Ad URL” for tasking the NOAS server. A similar version of the “Mini Platform C” app is also available on the site events-ui.discover-tech[.]io. The JavaScript code for both app versions is available on archive.org (1, 2).Additional Customer Mode FunctionalityThe Controlium platform provides several additional modules, according to our analysis of the app’s user interface and source code.Two Controlium modules named “Targeting” (also known as “Targeting Config”) and “cTargeting” (also known as “Upload Audiences”) allow users to upload digital identifiers referring to single or multiple targets, including mobile advertising IDs for Android and Apple devices, Beeswax user IDs, MyDSP user IDs and IP addresses. The same ads also attempted to unmask the phone number (MSISDN) of mobile users who were served the impression. The MSISDN leaks exploit various issues, including widespread problems with so-called “zero-click login” technologies, which aim to facilitate frictionless authentication and purchases for users on their mobile devices.One way “zero-click login” operates is that mobile providers select certain websites for “HTTP header enrichment,” so that when plaintext HTTP requests pass through the provider’s mobile gateway, an HTTP header (like X-MSISDN) is added to the request that provides the user’s phone number to the website. As an alternative to HTTP header enrichment, third-party services may work directly with the telco to facilitate this “zero-click login”. There appear to be widespread bugs with this allowlist matching, as well as bugs or security issues in third-party enrichment providers. While mainstream web browsers such as Chrome are moving towards blocking any non-HTTPS requests, it is likely that the app ecosystem will still embed webviews that permit non-HTTPS content.We taxonomized the issues into five types, exploited by attackers across numerous mobile providers in more than 30 countries in North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia, and disclosure to companies is in progress. Once the disclosure process is complete, we will release our subsequent report delving into technical analysis and attribution of these attacks.Notably, ’s infrastructure links to both a mercenary adtech vendor and a U.S. government contractor. It is rare to see such direct overlaps between mercenary vendors and U.S. government or intelligence contractors. We assess that this attacker has been exploiting MSISDN leak issues since at least 2019, fronted by a variety of mercenary adtech companies. Uncovering Discover-Tech’s Billion-Bid Scale Ad TargetingTo understand the scope of Discover-Tech’s activity, we analyzed nearly four billion ad bidding records that were publicly exposed on a Discover-Tech website. We found that Discover-Tech ads were displayed in over 70,000 mobile apps, and over 120,000 websites between March and June 2026.We found two world-readable Apache Druid instances running on Discover-Tech’s website . The endpoint contains bidding data for Discover-Tech’s MyDSP platform, which is connected to several upstream ad providers including Google, Yandex, Vungle, and Sunteng. The endpoint appeared to contain additional bidding data for Discover-Tech’s use of Sunteng. These instances did not contain any information about Discover-Tech’s use of Beeswax or Eskimi DSPs. Discover-Tech appeared to shut down both instances in August 2026.There were no instances of cookie IDs, advertising IDs, or GPS coordinates recorded in the Druid data. In this period, Discover-Tech’s MyDSP bid on 3,770,286,576 impressions, and appeared to win 441,954,291 (11.7%). About 76.7% of the bids were for ad impressions in mobile apps, and 23.3% for impressions in the web browser.The database shows a total of three advertisers, with nine total combinations between advertiser and an advertiser domain name. How Discover-Tech Deploys Ads in the BrowserIn this section we show how, beyond targeting users of mobile apps, Discover-Tech deploys a range of techniques to deliver ads and track users while they browse across websites. This involves Discover-Tech running its own code in the user’s web browser, both while deploying ads to users and independently of showing them ads. We explore Discover-Tech’s “Banner Tester” tool to show how the company generates tracking tags and pixels attached to ads, including code that connects to a NOAS server, which we identified as a vector for spyware delivery. We also document how Discover-Tech engages in “ID syncing” with other ad vendors, and how it leverages IAB Europe’s “Transparency and Consent Framework” to appear GDPR-compliant, even while facilitating unwanted and malicious activity.An ad displayed to a website visitor consists of an image or video to be shown and a link to be clicked, but canalsocarry HTML and JavaScript code that connects to one or more domains in order to track users, ad impressions, clicks, and other activities. This code is typically referred to as an ad tag. A related concept, a so-called tracking pixel, also describes code running in the web browser that connects to third-party ad vendors. Ad vendors use additional tracking code for user ID syncing by exchanging user identifiers with each other in order to identify, profile, and target website visitors across sites and vendors.Our analysis of ad tags, tracking pixels, and ID syncing activities associated with Discover-Tech’s ad delivery is based on an analysis of publicly available code, browser testing and ad transactions archived by the web investigation tool urlscan. While ads displayed in mobile apps similarly carry code that connects to ad vendors, this section focuses on Discover-Tech ads displayed in the web browser.Discover-Tech’s Ad and Tracking TagsWe found two versions of another app related to Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform named “Banner Tester” published on the sites and . One version of the app generates tags for the “Target” platforms “Default” or “Mini Platform C”. The other version can generate tags for production, staging and testing environments, according to its source code. The process of “ID syncing”, often also referred to as “cookie syncing”, addresses this lack of a universal user identifier. Research shows that digital advertising firms and data brokers use sophisticated forms of ID syncing to identify, profile and target web users across vendors. They achieve this by constantly exchanging user identifiers with each other, storing them in the browser and retrieving them again while users visit different websites that embed third-party tracking code.We found evidence showing how Discover-Tech engages in ID syncing with Comcast’s ad system Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad platform Xandr.Discover-Tech appears to use its domain for ID syncing with Yandex. The requests contain the parameter “bee_sync_partners=dtech”, which indicates some kind of business relationship between Discover-Tech and Beeswax.These ID syncing activities typically take place during website visits even when a user was not served a Discover-Tech ad. We are unsure how exactly Discover-Tech uses its browser ID syncing capabilities. Generally, being able to synchronize and correlate user identities across vendors is considered a precondition for individual-level ad targeting in the web browser. The Controlium platform, as examined in , offers to upload lists of Beeswax identifiers for ad targeting in its “cTargeting” module, among mobile advertising IDs, IP addresses, and other identifiers, based on our analysis of the source code.We conclude that many websites make constant requests to Discover-Tech’s domains and in the background. These requests serve the purpose of ID syncing with Beeswax and Yandex, and Discover-Tech’s domains receive, in addition to user identifiers, at least the website visitor’s IP address and information about their browser and operating system.Discover-Tech’s Tracking PixelSeparately from Discover-Tech’s large-scale ID syncing on many websites, we found JavaScript code for a “tracking pixel” that was loaded during recent visits to only a few sites including , , and Discover-Tech’s corporate website, (all three archivedonurlscan).These sites loaded versions of the tracking pixel code, both broadly similar, from the following URLs:Based on our analysis of the source code, the tracking pixel serves the purpose of storing, retrieving and synchronizing user identifiers across Discover-Tech, Beeswax, Xandr, and Yandex. Once loaded on a website, the code stores user identifiers associated with Discover-Tech, Beeswax, and Xandr in the user’s web browser in order to retrieve them again during subsequent visits to websites that load the same code.The code is designed to initiate the ID syncing process by sending Discover-Tech’s user identifier to Beeswax and Yandex in order to receive corresponding Beeswax and Yandex identifiers. Additionally, the code retrieves the user’s Xandr identifier. Request chains archived on urlscan show Discover-Tech’s tracking pixel in operation, including ID syncing with Yandex and the retrieval of user identifiers from Beeswax and Xandr.When the tracking pixel code detects that a website visitor is located in a region where the GDPR applies, based on geolocating the user’s IP address, it uses IAB Europe’s Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF) to process user “consent” signals for the three TCF vendors Discover-Tech Ltd, Xandr Inc, and BeeswaxIO Corporation. This demonstrates how Discover-Tech utilizes its listing as a registered and approved ad vendor by IAB Europe, as discussed in .The code also clearly maps the acronym “ZUID” to Xandr’s user identifier. As detailed in , several Controlium modules refer to an option labeled “Detect ZUID”. We are unsure how Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform exactly utilizes this identifier. As the “Detect ZUID” option is among a few “Add Ons” that can be activated when setting up an ad campaign, it may serve the retrieval of Xandr user identifiers either for ad targeting or for tracking targets. Xandr (Microsoft Advertising) did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided.Generally, the purpose of Discover-Tech’s tracking pixel is unclear. As a large share of Discover-Tech ads are designed to lead users to the site when clicking on those ads, the tracking pixel loaded during the site visit then correlates a target’s Discover-Tech user identifier with their Beeswax, Xandr, and Yandex identifiers.Records archived on urlscan show that the MyIPInfo website loaded a version of the tracking pixel from another domain associated with Discover-Tech in the past:7. Discover-Tech and Its Corporate NetworkDiscover-Tech has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the digital advertising industry for years. In this section, we further investigate Discover-Tech, key persons affiliated with the company, related companies, and the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology.Adtech with a Background in SpytechDiscover-Tech purports to be a typical digital advertising firm, offering a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), which facilitates the delivery of targeted ads. On its website, it claims to have “unrestricted access to top-ranking apps with 1+ billion daily active users” via a “worldwide ad exchange”. In addition to its DSP, Discover-Tech offers “monetization” solutions to mobile network operators and mobile device manufacturers, which we discuss further below.Israeli company records we reviewed link Discover-Tech’s website, , to the company Discover-Tech Ltd registered in March 2020, with Dekel Boni listed as its initial director and sole shareholder. In the two months after its incorporation, Eric Banoun, who is a major figure in the Israeli surveillance technology industry, joined Discover-Tech’s board of directors, and the shareholder base was expanded. From April 2020, the company’s shareholders included Dekel Boni, Guy Lants, Yaniv Basil, Zfanya Leib, Sergei Bartashevich, and Chaia Services Ltd, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. Eric Banoun left the company’s board of directors in January 2025 and Chaia Services Ltd ceased to be a shareholder in March 2026. As of July 2026, Discover-Tech is directed by Dekel Boni and owned by Boni, Basil, and Lants.Eric Banoun co-founded the cyberespionage firm Circles, a close NSO Group affiliate, and Senpai Technologies, which is part of the Intellexa consortium. We could not access corporate registration information on Discover-Tech’s shareholder Chaia Services Ltd. However, a Haaretz investigation reported that one of Chaia’s directors was Sara Hamou. Hamou managed Intellexa’s corporate network and was sentenced to eight years in prison (pending appeal) by a Greek court for her role in the Predatorgate scandal. Eric Banoun was listed as a director of a similarly named U.S.-based company, Chaia Services Tech LLC, which was dissolved in 2025.Based on the links to Eric Banoun and Chaia Services Ltd., we conclude that Discover-Tech was linked to the spyware industry for almost six years, according to Israeli company records and other publicly available information.Discover-Tech’s other shareholders, including Dekel Boni who is now the company’s sole director, have a background in digital advertising, previously working for adtech firms like Digital Turbine and Taptica, accordingtotheirLinkedInprofiles. Boni lists himself as Discover-Tech’s CEO, Guy Lants as its “Director of Product”. Yaniv Basil lists himself as the company’s “Chief Technology Officer” between 2020 and 2023.Ad Vendor Registrations with Google and IAB EuropeDespite information about Discover-Tech’s links to figures in the spyware industry that could be readily obtained from a review of corporate records, major advertising industry organizations added the company to several lists of “certified” or “approved” ad vendors, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitated its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale.As discussed in , Google listed Discover-Tech among its “Ad Manager Certified External Vendors”, “Ad Technology Partners”, and “Ads Personalization Providers” from 2020 until 2026. The advertising industry association IAB Europe listed the company on the “Global Vendor List” for its “Transparency & Consent Framework” (TCF), also from 2020 until 2026. Candiru: Prior Investigations, Abuses, and DiscoveriesCandiru is a mercenary spyware threat actor known by multiple names, including SOURGUM and Carmel Tsunami by Microsoft.First Candiru Abuse Discoveries: 2021On July 15, 2021, the Citizen Lab published the first report exposing Candiru. That investigation included identifying a Candiru victim and recovering a copy of Candiru’s Windows spyware. We then worked with Microsoft’s Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC) to analyze the spyware, which led to the identification of two zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-31979 and CVE-2021-33771). We also identified over 750 websites linked to Candiru’s infection infrastructure that masqueraded as a wide range of civil society entities ranging from media organizations to Amnesty International.Microsoft’s own investigation into Candiru, published simultaneously with our report on July 15, 2021, identified at least 100 spyware victims across ten countries. Microsoft reported that the victims included journalists, opposition politicians, dissidents, and activists. On November 16, 2021, ESET reported on a series of watering hole attacks observed in 2020 and 2021 targeting websites in the Middle East with what they described as a “strong focus on Yemen.” They attributed the attacks to Candiru.Further Investigations and Abuses: 2022-2025In 2022, the Citizen Lab again found Candiru spyware targeting victims among Catalan civil society groups in Spain. In that investigation, we identified signs of a live Candiru infection on a Catalan university network, and successfully worked with system administrators to identify the victim, isolate the device, and extract the active spyware. The targeting we observed as part of this campaign included emails masquerading as official Spanish governmental messages about COVID.On July 21, 2022, Avast published a report revealing that Candiru was using a Chrome zero-day exploiting WebRTC (CVE-2022-2294), and found evidence of targeting of users in multiple countries in the Middle East.On December 22, 2022, Meta disclosed that it disrupted around 130 Facebook and Instagram accounts used by Candiru to send infection links amongst themselves to “test phishing capabilities.”In the summer of 2024, during the parliamentary election campaign, Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Daniel Freund was targeted with Candiru’s mercenary spyware, according to the European Parliament’s security services. On August 5, 2025, Recorded Future’s Insikt Group investigated Candiru infrastructure and identified multiple Candiru clusters linked to Hungary, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, and Azerbaijan, among others. On September 2, 2025, Sekoia published an investigation into Candiru’s spyware, highlighting how Candiru and similar companies leverage complex jurisdictional structures to avoid discovery.On November 3, 2021, Candiru was added to the United States Commerce Department’s Entity List for malicious cyber activities. The entity listing noted that Candiru was added because “they developed and supplied spyware to foreign governments that used this tool to maliciously target government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics, and embassy workers.” Legal Actions Against Candiru and UsersIn October 2024, Daniel Freund filed a criminal complaint with the assistance of German digital rights NGO GFF against Viktor Orbán and unnamed persons over his targeting with Candiru.On April 30, 2025, the NGO Sentinel Alliance filed a caseagainst multiple Spanish governmental entities, NSO Group, and Candiru over the mercenary spyware attacks targeting Catalan civil society.Candiru’s 2025 Acquisition by Integrity Partners In April 2025, Israeli media reported that U.S.-based Integrity Partners acquired the operations of Candiru for $30 million in a bid to bypass the U.S. Entity Listing. Research by Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified Candiru as having been rebranded to “Integrity Labs” (אינטגריטי לאבס בע~מ) in December 2024. The current status of the acquisition is unclear.Candiru/Integrity Labs did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided.9. Discover-Tech’s Relationship to the Digital Advertising IndustryThis section explores how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, and notes that Discover-Tech achieved “certified” and “approved” status by Google and the major advertising industry association IAB Europe.Our analysis indicates that Discover-Tech deployed ads via Google, Yandex, and other ad vendors including Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, and Sunteng. In addition, both Google and the advertising association IAB Europe have listed Discover-Tech as a “certified” and “approved” ad vendor since the year 2020, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitate its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale.As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. These vendors, which Google also refers to as “allowed vendors” and “certified companies”, “undergo a business review,” the nature of which is not specified, so they “can serve third-party ads on the Google Ad Manager platform”. Google claims to “conduct a thorough certification process” for “vendors that are certified for third-party ads” and ensure they “meet Google’s requirements for third-party ad serving”. A listed vendor is “permitted to make third-party calls”, which may include tracking pixels. Google emphasizes that it might pause the delivery of ads when it detects “non certified vendors”. Being listed is crucial for a company that wants to interface with Google.Google also listed Discover-Tech among its roughly 1,000 Ad Technology Providers, who can receive data on website visitors and app users in Europe. In Google’s own words, these vendors “agreed to comply” with its “data usage policy” and “have shared certain information that is required by European regulations policy”. Website and app publishers “need to list these partners for [their] users.” Until 2025, Google referred to these vendors as “certified ad technology providers,” but a later redesign of the page dropped the term “certified.” In addition, Google listed Discover-Tech in its global list of roughly 1,700 ads personalization providers, which may participate in ad auctions based on “user consent”. The list contains “domains which can be attributed to the provider.” For Discover-Tech Ltd, the domains and are listed.Discover-Tech Ltd was added to all these lists in 2020. Google, which collaborated in this investigation, removed Discover-Tech from its ad vendor registries and terminated the company’s access to its ad exchange platforms as of the first week of October, 2026. Discover-Tech Ltd was also listed in the Global Vendor List (GVL) maintained by the European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), a key digital advertising industry association. The GVL contains roughly 1,000 vendors that are “registered and approved” by IAB Europe. These vendors can participate in IAB Europe’s “Transparency & Consent Framework” (TCF), which promises to enable ad vendors to comply with European data protection and privacy law when processing personal data for digital advertising purposes. While the TCF’s ability to enable lawful data processing iscontroversiallydebated, a GVL registration has become a de-facto requirement for an ad vendor to participate in digital advertising, display ads and receive data in Europe. IAB Europe added Discover-Tech Ltd to the GVL on July 2, 2020. As a result of this investigation, Discover-Tech was removed from the GVL on October 8, 2026. According to IAB Europe, it takes “reasonable steps to vet and approve” vendor applications, including the “identity of the party or parties controlling the vendor” and the vendor’s ability to “adhere” to a number of TCF policies, and then monitors their compliance with those policies. The TCF is the basis for passing user “consent” signals for personal data processing across the digital advertising supply chain, from users to publishers to intermediaries (like SSPs, DSPs, and ad exchanges) to advertisers, including in bid requests and tracking pixels. Most ad tags and tracking pixels that connect to third-party vendors require “consent” signals, including in some jurisdictions outside Europe and the U.K. like California. Google, Xandr, and most larger ad platforms require TCF compliance. While severalstudiesfoundthat vendors are too often ignoring “consent” signals, an ad vendor that is not listed in the GVL, and thus cannot pass any signal, can hardly interface with other ad vendors in reliable ways.While the vendor lists maintained by Google and the IAB Europe help a company appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and are the basis to participate in the digital advertising ecosystem in a reliable way at scale, they appear to be largely based on self-attestation by vendors. They are also the basis for most of the “consent” popups shown to European web and app users every day. Discover-Tech Ltd’s inclusion in those lists potentially means that, for almost six years, hundreds of millions of Europeans were presented with a consent request that, if the recipient clicked “Agree,” could be construed as authorizing Discover-Tech to process their data under the GDPR.As of October 2026, Discover-Tech is additionally listed in a registry operated by the “Trustworthy Accountability Group” (TAG) created by major U.S. advertising associations and the IAB, which aims to increase trust in the digital advertising industry, eliminate fraud and fight criminal activity including “malware threats targeting the digital advertising supply chain”. The Verified by TAG badge held by Discover-Tech, which the company also displays on its website, is used across the industry to “determine trust and transparency” and let prospective partners know that a company has taken “actionable steps to verify their identities and adopt rigorous standards to fight online fraud, piracy, malware, and lack of transparency”, according to the TAG website.Advertising Firms Involved in Discover-Tech’s TargetingOur analysis of ad bidding data in indicates that Discover-Tech targeted users by participating in ad auctions handled by Google, Yandex, and other ad vendors including Vungle and Sunteng. Discussion: AdFection Shows that Online Ads Are a Cybersecurity and Privacy CrisisThis report provides the first-ever technical evidence of zero-click mercenary spyware attacks delivered via targeted advertising. We also confirm that AdFection was used to infect devices at international media organization Al Jazeera.These attacks were facilitated by Discover-Tech, which presents itself as a legitimate advertising business but actually serves as a bridge between mercenary spyware companies and the advertising ecosystem. Discover-Tech not only helps companies like Candiru use ads to mass-profile unwitting phone users, their ads directly enable these companies to silently infect selected targets’ devices.The combination of advertising intelligence and the delivery of spyware is extremely concerning, for several reasons. First, both the digital advertising and mercenary spyware industry are very poorly regulated, with the latter featuring numerous firms notorious for deception, a lack of transparency, and even unlawful activities. To see entities from those two industries forming an alliance should be a wakeup call to regulators and policymakers around the world. Dozens of reports by numerous organizations, including the Citizen Lab, have shown incontrovertible proof of the harms caused by mercenary spyware vendors on civil society around the globe. With the addition of the type of advertising intelligence capabilities we have documented, those firms’ capabilities will now be supercharged.Second, the combination of advertising intelligence and spyware infections provide government security agencies with highly invasive systems that span both mass highly targeted types of user surveillance. As we show in this report, millions of devices were likely unwittingly profiled as a form of preliminary reconnaissance to enable targeting with spyware tailored to those device’s specific characteristics. Ominously, many of these infections took place without any visible indication of tampering or other clues that might have alerted them to the compromise. Also ominous is the fact that the services of Discover-Tech appear to span multiple regions around the globe. It is not known at this time exactly which governments are capitalizing on these new capabilities, but if past evidence is any indication it seems highly likely that some proportion of them are abusing those capabilities to target individuals outside of strictly criminal or national security purposes.ADINT: Journalism in the CrosshairsThe use of spyware to target the media directly interferes with the ability of the free press to hold power to account. It also threatens the privacy of journalists’ sources, and can chill reporting. Foreknowledge of movements, reporting topics, meetings, and sources does not just help powerful interests try to frustrate coverage and reporting, it can put people at physical risk. This is especially true for a news organization with reporters, freelancers, stringers, fixers and sources working in conflict zones around the world. Investigations into mercenary spyware operations have repeatedly surfaced targeting against the media, including in the context of governmental and cartel killings of reporters. Journalists have been confirmed spyware targets, from the Citizen Lab’s earliest findings of Pegasus spyware in Mexico almost a decade ago, to cases across Africa from Angola to Morocco and Togo, to Jordan, Serbia, El Salvador, andItaly, among many others. Organizations like Reporters Without Borders provide helpful overviews of the scale of the threat which, as Access Now points out, is sometimes coupled with laws designed to authorize government access to journalists’ communications. The International Federation of Journalists, meanwhile, has a recent overview of how spyware is situated within a broader set of digital threats against journalists. Recently, reporting from the Committee to Protect Journalists outlined the dangers posed to journalistsfrom ADINT-style tracking. The combination of this tracking with zero-click mercenary spyware targeting presents an even more serious danger to journalists’ safety.This investigation should also serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat. This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members. We urge news organizations to immediately seek expert assistance and ensure that their systems are protected against these attacks to the fullest extent possible. We provide some guidance in Section 11, however we urge all news organizations to systematically review their security posture (and logs) for signs of AdFection style spyware targeting and infection.The Advertising Industry: A Dangerous Lack of Due Diligence Our findings also reveal a troubling lack of due diligence within the digital advertising industry that helped enable this inappropriate activity. Discover-Tech, which presented itself as a legitimate ad vendor but served as a bridge between the online advertising ecosystem and the spyware industry, has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the online advertising ecosystem for years. Multiple ad vendors let the company utilize their systems. The two key industry organizations, Google and IAB Europe, have helped Discover-Tech appear as a legitimate ad vendor from the year 2020 until 2026, despite information about the company’s links to figures in the spyware industry being readily accessible in corporate records. Our findings show that the digital advertising industry is ill-prepared to prevent malicious actors from exploiting its infrastructure for the distribution of spyware via targeted ads.Advertising Industry: Prioritize Security, Stop AdFectionThis case should serve as an alarm to the advertising industry that business as usual is no longer acceptable. The online advertising industry must get serious about tackling the distribution of mercenary spyware via targeted ads, alongside other malicious advertising practices including financially motivated fraud and cybercrime. Technical and organizational measures currently implemented by the industry, such as the SafeFrame specification or standards for supplychain transparency are insufficient or not even adopted in a meaningful way.Fix a Broken Digital InfrastructureMore broadly, the distribution of spyware via targeted ads depends on the way digital advertising – and the web economy at large – currently operate.Many mobile apps and websites containtrackingsoftware operated by dozens of third parties, which themselves may include code by additional third parties within apps and browsers. Also required for the targeted deployment of spyware, ad targeting at the individual level depends on uncontrolled data sharing via RTB auctions and third-party tracking.Automated ad selling and buying via RTB, which connects large numbers of publishers, advertisers and intermediaries across opaque supply chains, is designed to minimize human intervention. When combined with a lack of oversight and accountability, it is generally prone to abuse. This is further aggravated by the assumption that at least some ad vendors benefit from malicious and fraudulent advertising. Leaked internal documents from Meta reported by suggest that Meta estimated that it earns between five and ten percent of its annual revenue from running fraudulent ads. Industry sources suggestthat ad fraud accounts for one fifth of all online advertising spend. AdFection: A Threat to States, Civil Society, and Everyone ElseThe distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large. Two major U.S. security agencies, the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), have warned already in 2018 and 2020 that adversaries may leverage malicious ads to deploy malware on devices, and thus both recommended that government agencies and other organizations use ad-blocking software.Given the current threat posed by Discover-Tech’s AdFection vectors, and the evidence of wide-scale targeting, we judge that the most feasible protection is for defenders to block targeted ads at the gateway. This defensive recommendation (see ) holds until the industry has shown that it is reliably able to block all AdFection style vectors.At the very time that state actors may be employing offensive cyber attacks, malicious ads can be deployed via apps and websites used by defense personnel, political leaders, and people maintaining critical infrastructure alike, creating national security risks for those very same states. The same structural deficits that endanger civil society, journalists, and opposition figures are potentially exploited by both foreign adversaries and cybercriminals, creating systemic risks for everyone. These security risks make it apparent that there is an urgent public-interest need to reform digital advertising.The same risks apply to the private sector and to civil society. Indeed, as prior research has made clear, a large number of governments will use these potent capabilities to undermine political opposition, stealthily target journalists and lawyers, and target refugees, immigrants, and other vulnerable populations. The mercenary spyware industry is already notorious for widespread harms; fueling that industry with digital advertising capabilities will multiply those harms immeasurably.11. Recommendations: How to Stop AdFection AttacksThe AdFection attacks and espionage described in this report impact millions of people in dozens of countries. Existing laws and self-regulation by the industry failed to catch or prevent them. In this section, we provide guidance to regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection and ADINT-style espionage.Advertising Vendors: Time to Get SeriousThe advertising industry uses terms like “certified” and “approved” to try and convey a veneer of effective self regulation. However, the industry appears to perform no meaningful due diligence on participating vendors, instead improperly relying on self-attestation where vendors check a box on an online form. This process allows widespread privacy abuses, including failing to prevent mass espionage via targeted ads.Ad vendors must significantly level up their cybersecurity and threat detection capacity to effectively cut off malicious advertisers across the supply chain. They must rigorously and regularly vet, screen, and audit their business partners and hold them accountable for their own supply chains. This type of more robust due diligence applies in particular to key industry organizations and dominant players who must introduce rigorous and regular audits for companies listed in ad vendor registries which they maintain and provide to many other actors in the supply chain. Business partners from countries with opaque corporate registries or where known malicious actors operate deserve specific attention.Technical and organizational measures to be taken must include both vendor-specific and industry-wide efforts. Cybersecurity agencies and other regulators in the U.S., Canada, Europe, and other regions must support these efforts by investigating risks, calling out shortcomings and taking action to ensure the implementation of effective measures by the advertising industry.Detect and block malicious ads: Ad vendors must radically increase their capacity to identify AdFection-style attacks in real-time, alongside other forms of malicious advertising such as ad fraud, across their supply chain. Develop better threat sharing and clearinghouses for sharing information about malicious actors and recklessly permissive jurisdictions.: Implement mandatory know-your-customer, including due diligence and recurring vetting for all partners and other firms who transact over the provided ad and data services. Major advertising organizations must introduce mandatory third-party audits for “certified” or “approved” vendors. Ban vendors in problem jurisdictions: Adopt a default-deny policy for vendors operating in jurisdictions known to be highly permissive of abuse, or without accountability mechanisms.Fix systemic vulnerabilities: Implement industry-wide measures to improve ad delivery security and to introduce full supply chain transparency, and support their adoption.We urge regulators to take immediate action to ensure that advertising platforms and partners stop facilitating AdFection-style attacks, and secure their populations from the security, cybersecurity, and privacy threats posed by the advertising ecosystem.Investigation and EnforcementImmediately investigate Discover-Tech and Candiru: Our research showed large-scale data collection from millions of devices involving Discover-Tech and Candiru. The data was apparently collected for the purposes of AdFection. We urge competent authorities in all jurisdictions to investigate whether the rights of their citizens, as well as applicable privacy and security laws were violated. It is unlikely that Discover-Tech is the only enabler of AdFection-style zero-click attacks. Authorities should more closely scrutinize the advertising ecosystem to determine whether other companies are leveraging it for espionage and spyware delivery, and determine whether they have violated applicable laws and regulations.Enforcement and sanctions: Use all necessary domestic enforcement and sanctions authorities to discourage AdFection abuse. These measures can include the use of sanctions and entity-listing powers against firms that deploy mercenary spyware and conduct espionage via targeted ads, the companies that enable them, and the individuals who work in the AdFection domain.Legal and Regulatory ImprovementsCommission investigations: Enlist the assistance of cybersecurity agencies and regulatory bodies to evaluate the security, privacy, and national security risks from the current advertising ecosystem.Tighten privacy regulations around ad tracking and targeting data: Evaluate legislation to remove personal data from RTB auctions and work with international partners to adopt similar measures. Real regulation of the advertising industry: It is time for regulators and lawmakers to develop frameworks based on mandatory oversight with clear enforcement mechanisms and penalties for violation. Independent audits and KYC: Require that the advertising industry implement third-party audits and know-your-customer standards for all their business partners, as well as companies included in “certified” vendor registries. Develop meaningful penalties for failure to comply or misrepresentation.Securing National Infrastructure Requires Blocking Ads and Tracking on Official DevicesMandatory ad-blocking on government devices: Issue policy guidance aligned with relevant cybersecurity agencies (e.g., CISA and NSA in the U.S.) recommendations requiring ad-blocking software on edge devices, and ad-blocking at the gateway for all government-owned devices. (See, for example, U.S. Senator Ron Wyden’s letter to the CIO of the U.S. Department of Defense, as well as Senator Wyden and Rep. Harrigon’s joint letter to the Inspector General of the U.S. Department of Defense).: Mandate the disabling of unique advertising IDs on all government mobile devices (such as through MDM), and issue guidance and policy recommendations for personal devices used in governmental spaces.Ban browsers that facilitate data harvesting: Evaluate the security risks of browsers with impossible-to-disable tracking, and consider provisionally banning them from governmental networks and devices.Defenders: Ad-Blocking Is A Cybersecurity Best PracticeAdFection attacks demonstrate that online advertising is now a vector for zero-click spyware infection into your organization. Taken together with research showing that data from targeted advertising is already being used for mass espionage, and potentially for corporate espionage, this makes it clear there is currently no consistently safe way to expose your users and networks to targeted ads. You can directly block Discover-Tech’s methods by blocking advertising identifiers, however we suspect that the AdFection attack surface may be larger, requiring more systematic measures. Block ads and tracking on devices and at the gateway: Where possible, block online advertising at the gateway to your organization, and on work-issued and edge devices. Opting out of ad targeting (such as through MDM) on company-issued devices is also advisable. We also encourage you to develop guidance and easily actionable tools to help your personnel protect their devices.Transition towards browsers with less tracking: Browsers with built-in anti-tracking features, ad-blocking, and support for the Global Privacy Control (GPC) will improve your security posture and protect your IP. We encourage defenders to monitor traffic linked to advertising impressions for signs of malicious requests.Protecting Yourself from AdFectionAdFection is a complex threat, and if you face elevated risk because of who you are or what you do, we strongly recommend seeking expert help. However, there are certain actions you can take to reduce some AdFection risks.Increase your overall security by following personalized instructions from the Security Planner.Consider using a privacy-respecting browser that blocks tracking and data-harvesting.Consider using an ad-blocking service on your network, such as at your home router, or use a trusted commercial VPN service that offers ad-blocking.Our investigation found that an attacker that we call used Discover-Tech ads and a number of additional vendors to deanonymize users at scale since at least 2019. As these efforts rely on the exploitation of widespread security issues across numerous mobile providers, disclosure to providers is in progress. We will release a subsequent report delving into technical analysis and attribution of these attacks once the disclosure process is complete.Based on our findings, we believe that further research would be fruitful with respect to:customers and victims of the ad-based spyware deployment capabilities provided by Discover-Tech and the companies linked to it, including Candiru, Bindecy, and Intelos;additional vendors and vendor networks that deploy ad-based spyware; and,technical, organizational, regulatory, and political measures that effectively prevent the distribution of spyware via digital advertising.This report is part of an ongoing series of investigations we are doing on surveillance technologies that rely on digital advertising. We will be publishing subsequent investigations that explore areas for further research we have flagged in this report.Correspondence with CompaniesDiscover-Tech Ltd, Candiru (Integrity Labs), Bindecy, Intelos, Xandr (Microsoft Advertising), Sunteng, IAB Europe, and Affle did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided.On October 11, 2026, we received a response from Adtimizer Ltd.
