Ad Vendors Involved in Discover-Tech’s Ad OperationsGoogle dominates the digital advertising ecosystem in the U.S., Europe, and other regions. It operates a massive ad exchange and systems for ad sellers (Ad Manager, AdSense, AdMob) and ad buyers (Google Ads, DV360). Its “Authorized Buyers” program allows third-party ad vendors to deliver ads by participating in ad auctions on Google’s ad exchange.Yandex, although much smaller in revenue, similarly dominates the digital advertising ecosystem in Russia and some other regions. It also providesboth an ad exchange and systems for ad sellers and buyers.Beeswax, Owned by Freewheel/ComcastBeeswax is a major US-based ad buying platform, since 2021 owned by Comcast’s ad platform FreeWheel. It offers a Demand-Side Platform (DSP) that helps advertisers and other ad vendors deliver targeted ads to users by participating in ad auctions. Its “bidder-as-a-service” product is considered highly customizable and imposes fewer restrictions on its clients than other DSPs.The FreeWheel website states that, by using Beeswax’ ad buying platform rather than other DSPs, clients could “access the full, unfiltered stream of RTB events, in much the same way [they] would if [they] were building a bidder from scratch”. Clients can augment the stream of ad bidding data they receive, for example, by “mapping” users to “rich profiles”, and they can use custom bidding algorithms and targeting attributes.While this appears to offer great flexibility to clients to an extent that may come close to operating their own DSP, FreeWheel takes care of the integrations with ad exchanges and Supply-Side Platforms (SSPs) that help app and website publishers sell ads. As of July 2026, the FreeWheel website lists integrations with 36 “supply partners” including Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Index Exchange, and many others.Beeswax is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google lists Beeswax as a certified ad vendor and among its “common” European ad technology partners which Google will use by default when publishers do not set up a custom list of ad vendors. For its ad serving and third-party tracking, Beeswax uses the and the cookie identifier (devicedisclosure.json).Eskimi, a White-Label DSP Based in LithuaniaEskimi is a digital advertising group based in Lithuania with offices in Greece, Turkey, Japan, United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Nigeria, and Kenya, according to its website, eskimi.com. Its ad buying platform Eskimi DSP, which allows its clients to target 1.5 billion “profiled users” across 60 ad exchanges, according to the company, is also offered as a “white-label” version that “enables agencies, ad networks, and businesses to offer ‘Eskimi DSP’ under their own brand”. Eskimi also provides a data management platform (DMP) that “collects and stores data” it receives from 50 ad exchanges, amounting to two2 billion profiles, according to a 2025 version of the company’s website. Its website and Lithuanian company records show that it is incorporated as “UAB Eskimi”, also known as “UAB Aktyvus sektorius”.Eskimi is much lesser known than Beeswax. Except for two paidposts, we did not find any articles discussing the company on digital advertising trade press sites like Adweek, Digiday, and AdExchanger. Eskimi was, however, prominently discussed when US-based data broker Datastream Group told U.S. Senator Ron Wyden that Eskimi was the source of 3.6 billion location data records revealing the exact movements of millions of people, including U.S. military and intelligence personnel, as reported in a joint investigation by German netzpolitik.org and other outlets. This investigation has helped spark extensive debates about ad surveillance.While German netzpolitik.org found several additional links between the analyzed data and the company, Eskimi denied that it was the source of the data. Google told 404 Media that Eskimi is “part of Google’s Authorized Buyer program and must abide by our policies”. It added that it “regularly audits its Authorized Buyers program participants”. Eskimi is closely linked to the location data broker Redmob, which claims to sell data on one billion people across 150 countries according to its website, redmob.io. While Redmob is incorporated in Dubai, netzpolitik.org found that Eskimi and Redmob share the same CEO, who responded to their questions about Eskimi from a Redmob email address.Vungle, Liftoff’s SSP, and Ad ExchangeVungle was a mobile advertising firm that merged with the U.S.-based mobile advertising firm Liftoff, which went public in June 2026. Since the merger, Liftoff offers several Vungle-branded products including a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) named Monetize, which helps app publishers sell ads, and the mobile ad exchange Vungle Exchange, which helps marketers buy ads served in mobile apps.Both the SSP and the ad exchange rely on the Vungle SDK, which is a piece of advertising and tracking software embedded in many Android, iOS, Amazon, Windows, and Unity apps. The Vungle SDK is embedded in 150,000 mobile apps used by one billion people across 150 countries, which also describes the number of users that can be targeted via the Vungle ad exchange, according to the company.Guidelines for the Vungle ad exchange contain a rule that asks clients to “refrain from” using the platform for the distribution of “malware, spyware, and files that can harm or gain unauthorized access to a device or user information”. We did not find an explanation of how the company monitors and enforces this rule.Vungle has been controversially discussed in several papers and reports on mobile tracking and privacy. The Norwegian Consumer Council found in 2020 that Vungle received GPS coordinates and other personal data on users of Grindr and another mobile app, seemingly without a legal basis under the GDPR.As of July 2026, Liftoff’s “Monetize” and “Vungle Exchange” products are listed as approved TCF ad vendors by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google lists Liftoff’s DSP and Monetize products as certified ad vendors and it lists Liftoff among its “common” European ad technology partners that Google will use by default when publishers do not choose a custom list of ad vendors.Google has been deeply interconnected with Vungle from its inception. Google Ventures was an investor in Vungle’s seed, series A, and series B funding rounds. The Norwegian Consumer Council pointed out in 2020 that Google’s mobile advertising system AdMob “provides Vungle with access to extra features that allow Vungle to bypass data filters, and thus send more data to its partners than what would ordinarily be possible through Google’s regular advertising tools”. As of July 2026, Liftoff’s Vungle product Monetize is listed among a few “premium bidding partners” in Google’s mobile advertising system AdMob and among a few “ad sources” for AdMob’s advertising services on Android and iOS.Sunteng, a Chinese SSP, DSP, and Ad ExchangeThe Chinese digital advertising firm Sunteng provides ad buying and selling services for both advertisers and publishers, as well as a “programmatic marketplace”, i.e. an ad exchange, according to its website, sunteng.com. The site also refers to the company as “Shunfei Technology”. The link to Sunteng’s DSP offering leads site visitors to biddingx.com (“BiddingX”), an entity that promotes itself as China’s largest DSP. Sunteng appears to operate also under the brand Bidex (bidex.cn), which focuses on “overseas programmatic”, i.e. on digital advertising services for non-Chinese clients. We assume that Sunteng, Shunfei, Bidex and BiddingX are part of the same Chinese group of companies with offices in Singapore and the US. Sunteng claims to process 50 billion ad bid requests a day across 10,000 mobile apps and 60 ad vendor partners, and it lists Eskimi as a partner.As of July 2026, Google lists biddingx.com (“Shunfei Infomation Technology Corporatio” [sic]) as a certified ad vendor. IAB Europe listed bidex.cn (“Sunteng Hong Kong Holdings Limited”) as an approved TCF ad vendor until December 2025 (vendor list).Xandr, aka Microsoft AdvertisingXandr, formerly known as AppNexus, has long been a major player in digital advertising. After Microsoft acquired it from AT&T in 2022, it became part of Microsoft Advertising in 2023. While Microsoft shut down Xandr’s ad buying system, the “Invest” DSP, in early 2026, it continues to offer Xandr’s ad selling system, the “Monetize” SSP. Ad buyers who used the former Xandr DSP were “handed” to Amazon DSP, according to trade press reporting.As shown in , Microsoft’s user ID syncing in the browser via the domain , whichassigns a Microsoft user ID to people who visit the sites of ad sellers and maps it to user IDs assigned by other ad vendors, appears to remain operational as of June 2026. Xandr has long been operating massive identity databases. In 2020, when Xandr was still owned by AT&T, it reportedly operated an identity graph linking 5 billion identifiers.As of July 2026, Microsoft’s ad system Xandr is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google’s list of certified ad vendors contains four records for Xandr. Google also lists Xandr among its “common” European ad technology partners which Google will use by default when publishers do not choose a custom list of ad vendors.Adtech vendor, ad vendor. Advertising technology intermediary such as a Demand-Side Platform (DSP), Supply-Side Platform (SSP) (both defined below) or ad exchange. Designated space or position on a website or mobile app reserved to display an ad.Demand-Side Platform (DSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps advertisers buy ad placements across many different websites or mobile apps in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by ad exchanges.Supply-Side Platform (SSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps publishers of websites or mobile apps sell ad slots in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by an ad exchange, which is often operated by the same ad vendor as the SSP. Automated marketplace operated by an adtech intermediary that hosts real-time auctions which facilitate the selling of ad slots and the buying of ad placements across many publishers, advertisers and intermediaries like DSPs and SSPs. Ad exchanges are often operated by SSPs. Automated high-frequency auctions hosted by ad exchanges where advertisers (or DSPs on their behalf) bid on ad placements offered by website and mobile app publishers (or their SSPs). When a user visits a website or uses an app that sells targeted ads via RTB, the publisher’s SSP initiates a bid request that transmits data about the user and the ad slot to several DSPs, who submit bids on behalf of advertisers. The ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. RTB auction record that describes an ad slot and the user who currently visits a website or uses a mobile app. Bid requests are initiated by publishers and sent via an SSP and an ad exchange to several DSPs, which place bids in order to show ads to specific users on behalf of advertisers. Bid requests typically contain personal data about users in order to facilitate targeted advertising.Mobile Advertising ID (MAID). Unique identifier for a mobile device used for advertising and tracking purposes, assigned by the device’s operating system such as Google Android or Apple iOS. While users can reset or delete mobile ad IDs in the settings, they are activated by default. Advertising and data companies use mobile ad IDs to link user data across contexts and vendors in order to track, follow, profile and target users. Unique identifier for a user’s web browser, typically stored and retrieved in the browser by third-party code operated by adtech vendors during website visits.Appendix C. Domains linked to Discover-Tech and ControliumWe assess that the following domains are – or have been – linked to Discover-Tech and Controlium:According to our analysis, Discover-Tech operates – or has operated – the following NOAS servers as part of its Controlium platform:Additional NOAS domains that appear to be associated with Discover-Tech:We assess that the following additional domains are – or have been – associated with Discover-Tech’s ad tracking or targeting:

item.title: An Apology
item.author: cdrnsf
item.content:encoded: We launched an AirTag silencing tool recently. We have always made products we want for ourselves, and this was no different - we wanted it for AirTags on our bikes. (Some of us here have bikes more valuable than our cars.)In retrospect though, this also has the side effect of aiding someone with bad intentions to track someone that wouldn’t get phone notifications.We have removed the product and will use our patent on it to prevent anyone else from making one in the future.

item.title: The Double Headed Stack Allocator
item.author: g0xA52A2A
item.content:encoded: When programming high performance applications, such as video games, you learn neat tricks for writing fast code that makes the most of limited resources.Memory allocation is a huge topic for performance critical code that needs a variable amount of memory.When you hear “stack allocator” you might think of “alloca” which lets you allocate memory from the actual program stack. That is super useful in a pinch, but that is not what today’s post is about. Another name for the type of stack allocator we are talking about today is “bump allocator”.Around 2010 I was working at Surreal Software (Midway Seattle) on an open world game “This is Vegas” which unfortunately was cancelled when Midway went out of business.On that project, one of my duties was animation programming. Animation worked by having a state machine for sets of bones, where each state was a tree of animation blends. When states changed, they would blend out from the old state into the new state to preserve continuity.There was a lot of blending going on, and it used a large number of dynamic memory allocations for these animations to be evaluated and blended on the CPU. These allocations were all transient though and only needed to exist for part of the frame. Furthermore, these allocations had to happen per frame, as things could change drastically from one frame to the next, as to which characters were being animated that frame – based on the camera frustum for example. The allocator showed up as a hot spot in profiling this section of code.To solve this problem, we implemented a “stack allocator” where allocation is just an integer add, and deallocation is even cheaper.To do this, you allocate and keep some amount of memory that is the maximum amount you will need, like say 1MB. This is your stack. You also keep an integer “tos” variable to know where the top of the stack is.When you want to allocate memory, your memory is the memory at the top of the stack, and you add the number of bytes you want to allocate to the tos variable so that the next allocation comes after yours:In a real implementation, you would also want to know how big the memory was, so that you could handle the tos hitting the end of the memory – by returning null, or asserting, or something else.When you are done with the memory, you just set the tos variable to 0.In our case, we set the tos to 0 after animation blending was finished and we had copied the results into the buffers that were heading to the vertex shader for skinning. If you were using a stack allocator more generally for all transient memory allocations during a game’s frame, you may set it back to 0 when the frame starts.The result was night and day. Allocation no longer took any measurable time in the profiler, because allocation was an integer addition, and freeing all memory was a single integer assigment. It doesn’t get faster than that.One thing to note is that as written, this allocator does not call destructors or destructors. Using placement new for constructors would be easy enough. Calling destructors would be harder, as it would have to be a manual process, which is error prone. You might be able to use some RAII pattern, but stack allocators work best for simpler types.Another great thing about stack allocators is that they can work in multi threaded environments. If the tos variable uses atomic addition, multiple threads can allocate from the same stack allocator. This can be nice in a fork/join situation on the CPU, or for a complex algorithm running on the GPU.You can also do “partial deallocations” with stack allocators. For instance, if you had some recursive process where each level needed dynamic allocation, you could remember where the tos was when that level started, and set it back to that value when that level of processing finished.The Double Headed Stack AllocatorA few years later, I found myself at Blizzard on the StarCraft 2 team. My boss James Anhalt was (and still is) a really smart dude who introduced me to shader toy, and shared a bunch of really cool techniques that have been previous blog posts. He told me about double headed stack allocators as a solution to a memory fragmentation problem he had hit in the past.Imagine that you had a streaming world game where as the player ran around the world, old level geometry would deallocate, and new level geometry would allocate and stream in from disk.At the same time, imagine the player character could shape shift into different forms – and each time they changed forms, the old form was deallocated, and the new form was allocated and streamed in from disk.A challenge is, when you have these two systems allocating and deallocating random amounts of memory, on their own timelines, your memory is going to get fragmented.Lets walk through a simple example. Let’s say you have 100 MB total memory for the level (red) and the character (green). The level allocates 20MB, then the character allocates 30MB, then the level allocates 20MB and the character allocates the final 30MB.Now let’s say that the player runs to a new section, so the old level data memory is freed. The new level data only needs to make a single 30MB allocation. We do have 40MB memory free, but it isn’t in one chunk! We only have two blocks of 20MB. So even though the new level data is smaller, we can’t allocate space for it. This is memory fragmentation, and it’s a big problem in memory constrained environments.So, James told me what they did in this type of situation was to have a chunk of memory like a normal stack allocator, but the level data had a tos which grew upwards from 0, and the character data had a tos which grew downward from the end of the memory. You knew you were out of memory when they crossed over each other and the level tos was greater than the character tos.Let’s see how that works:This made it so when the level data needed to change, it could reset the level tos back to 0, and reallocate the memory it needed, without any fragmentation whatsoever. Similarly, when the character freed its memory, it would reset its tos back to the end of memory, and could then reallocate the memory it needed, also without any fragmentation.Once again, these allocators work fine in multithreaded environments, even when each thread might allocate from either side. Atomic add to the tos indices is all you need.You might ask “why not have two stack allocators instead of a double headed one?” The main benefit is when you are memory constrained and know that the size of one stack allocator is enough to serve two systems, but the proportion of memory that goes to one side vs the other is flexible. In a game situation like described above, that means some levels could use more memory, but in those situations, the character would need to have reduced memory usage. A bit of a contrived example but hopefully you get what I mean.Storing Variable Sized Objects In A Finite RegionThere is a variation of this when you are trying to store a number of variable sized objects in a fixed amount of memory, but you want random access by index. An example may be that you want to send network packets of a specific size for efficiency reason, and you want to that memory to encode a variable number of variable sized network commands in it. You want to be able to easily iterate through the messages, but you want to support them having variable sizes too.What you do is have a double headed stack allocator where one stack is for the dynamic allocations, and the other stack is for an array of integers that are an offset in the memory to the dynamic allocations.Let me show you what I mean with an example. Starting with an empty double headed stack allocator:You want to allocate 24 bytes. Stack 0 has a tos of 0, so that is where you write your 24 byte object. You add 24 to stack 0’s tos and it is now 24, where the next free region of memory is. You also allocate an integer from stack 1 and write 0 there, as the offset for where this first item lives.Next you want to allocate 14 bytes. Stack 0 has a tos of 24, so that is where you write your 12 byte object. You add 12 to stack 0’s tos and it is now 38. You also allocate an integer from stack 1 and write 24 there, as the offset for where this second item lives.you also have to somehow keep track of how many objects there are. You could have a separate integer keeping count of how many offsets there are in the offset table, or maybe you could have a sentinel value in the offset table to indicate where the end of the offsets are. Perhaps ~0 (all 1s in binary) could be the sentinel value.Just like the other stack allocators we talked about, this one can also work in a multi threaded environment. You might be tempted to make the two updates transactional – like with a compare and swap loop – but it isn’t needed.Lastly, this configuration allows you to remove items, or move them around in memory, which is another way of reducing fragmentation – you just need to update the offset table to match reality when you do so.

item.title: The engineering that allows articulated buses to bend
item.author: CharlesW
item.content:encoded: Every day, countless people around the world board a bus to travel to a destination. These buses come in all shapes and sizes, from comfortable coaches to towering double-deckers. One of the best ways to increase a coach’s passenger capacity without adding height is to build the bus in at least two sections, adding a pivot point near the middle. The articulated bus is a common sight everywhere, but how they actually work, especially when they have a rear engine, is far more clever and interesting than you might think. A lot of these buses put brilliant engineering in plain sight.America’s largest train museum, the Illinois Railway Museum (IRM), hosts a special event each year to celebrate the transit bus, one of the greatest forms of public transportation that does not ride on rails. IRM is home to America’s largest collection of preserved buses, and most of the over three dozen trolley buses and motor buses in the museum’s hands do run and drive. This vast collection makes IRM the only railroad museum in America with a regular bus service. You might think it’s weird for a train museum to preserve so many buses across three warehouse-sized barns, but buses and trains complement each other in functional public transportation systems. One helps the other.I have not missed a single Bus Day since I started coming to the Illinois Railway Museum in 2022. This year’s Bus Day was the 11th running of the event, and in my experience, each Bus Day has been better than the last. This time, for example, there was a practical buffet of 13 buses to ride throughout the whole day.One of those buses was King County Metro No. 4020, a 1987 MAN SG-T310 articulated trolley bus. This unit usually gets to stretch its legs on every Bus Day, and it’s a favorite among visitors because everyone loves a fun “bendy bus.” As my wife published posts about our Bus Day at IRM, some followers and readers asked a curious question: Just how do articulated buses actually work?The answer to that question is more exciting than it would seem at first glance. Yes, a lot of bendy buses work exactly how you probably think they do. But others require quite a bit of clever engineering that you might not notice until after you read this.Over A Century Of BendingLet’s start at the beginning: the dawn of the articulated bus, because it’s important to see where we’ve come from before I show you where we are now.The articulated bus came early on in the development of the transit bus. Some of the first known internal combustion buses were built in the mid-1890s, and while those units were small, they wouldn’t be for long. As technology progressed, builders figured out how to stuff more people in a single bus. This was great for efficiency. It was cheaper and more practical to stuff one bus full of people than it was to run multiple smaller buses. Mechanics had fewer buses to work on, the transit district had fewer drivers to hire, and there were fewer engines to fuel.However, a rigid bus can only get so long before making it any longer leads to diminishing returns. Super-long buses can carry more people, but have a harder time navigating city streets. Building up may also not be possible, as a double-decker bus might interfere with overhead infrastructure or fail to fit into tunnels.The solution was simple. Builders began assembling buses in two distinct sections. The second section of the bus would connect to the rear end of the coach’s front section through an articulating joint. The earliest example of an articulated bus I could find is this Dutch Ford Model T, which was built in the early 1920s. Check out how the interior of the rear section is paired with the front using an accordion-like central section:This wasn’t the only way to do it. An even simpler method to increase bus capacity was to make a single-unit bus or truck tow a trailer that had seats in it. A good example of this type of bus is the Officine Meccaniche bus truck from 1930, which is pictured below.The interior of the trailer was not connected to the main unit in any way. As a result, the trailer had its own entry doors. Often, buses like this had a conductor to signal to the driver when the bus was ready to get underway.Of course, I cannot talk about towed buses without talking about the very fun trailer bus. Those weirdos are little more than tarted-up semi-trailers with seats and windows. But they aren’t really articulated buses, so I will talk about those buses on a different day.Articulated bus history starts getting really interesting in the late 1930s. Over in Italy, Alfa Romeo produced the pioneering 1937 Alfa Romeo 110 AM-Macchi. This bus, which Curbside Classic said carried up to 180 seated and standing passengers, had a novel way of articulation. Unlike today’s articulated buses, which articulate horizontally and vertically like a trailer, the Alfa Romeo had only vertical articulation. Having the center section articulate up allowed the bus to drive up grades without getting stuck.In 1938, the city of Baltimore put America’s first articulated bus into service. The Twin Coach Super-Twin was similar to the Alfa Romeo in that it articulated only vertically. To permit sharp turns, Twin Coach, like Alfa Romeo, designed a rear-wheel steering system. While extremely weird, there was some logic to this. Per Twin Coach, because its bus articulated only vertically, the bus floor is straight from front to rear.The Twin Coach’s articulation was more of a transitional technology. After World War II, bus builders largely switched to the more modern articulation system that we know of today. Here’s America’s first fully articulated highway bus, the 1946 Kaiser built for the Santa Fe Trail Transportation Company.How To Make A Bus ArticulateToday, there are generally four ways to achieve an articulated bus. Two concepts that I explained earlier, the trailer bus and the bus that tows a trailer, remain in operation today. Trailer buses can still be found in Cuba, and they’re glorious in their simplicity:Meanwhile, over in Munich, Germany, the Münchner Verkehrsgesellschaft runs the Busanhänger (bus train), which is a bus that tows a separate trailer that is also a bus. These were built in just 2022 by Sono Motors:Here in America, you’ll generally find two kinds of articulated buses. The first, and older type, is the puller. In puller designs, the front section of the bus is a complete vehicle. The engine will usually be located towards the rear of the front section and under the floor. Only the rearmost axle of the front section (typically the middle axle of the whole bus) is powered.Built from 1980 to 1986, these buses feature a Cummins 855 cubic-inch NHHTC straight-six mounted under the floor near the middle axle of the bus. That engine drives the middle wheels through either an Allison HT740 automatic or a Voith D864.2 automatic, both featuring four speeds.Puller buses usually connect to their rear sections through a somewhat complex articulation joint.This unit consists of a front and rear subframe that connect to the front section and the rear section, respectively. They meet in the middle, where they ride on a ring of bearings. These bearings allow the front and rear sections to turn relative to each other. In other words, it functions like a joint. In a puller configuration, the rear section of the bus straightens itself out as the front section pulls the bus forward. It’s like a semi-truck trailer, but with a few extra steps. These joints tend to be made out of materials like welded steel or cast iron.From here, a bus builder will place a turntable on top of the articulation joint, bellows to seal the bending path between the two bus sections, and flexible cabling to provide power to the rear of the bus.The benefit of the puller bus is that it’s technically a simpler design. The rearmost axle isn’t powered, and the articulation joint needs fewer components to get its job done. Anecdotally, some bus drivers I’ve spoken to prefer puller buses in snowy situations, since the powered axle is ahead of the articulation joint. Articulated buses also have a limited amount of vertical flexibility, permitting them to climb city streets.However, puller-type articulated buses have one main drawback, and it’s that, generally, the floor cannot be lower than the engine that lives right in the middle of the bus. Some puller-type articulated buses manage to have a low floor by moving the engine to a side of the bus and having the lower floor go around the engine.The Van Hool AG300 has this design, and while it has a low floor, the large engine takes up a vast amount of space that could be used for seating. Check it out:How A Rear-Engine Articulated Bus WorksThe preferred solution to this problem is to place the engine at the very rear of the bus, where it won’t gobble up valuable passenger volume. Yes, a rear-engine bendy bus!Here’s where the engineering gets really fun. In a rear-engine articulated bus, the front section of the bus now becomes the “trailer,” and the powered rear section of the bus pushes the whole bus forward. Transit departments all across America have buses like this, and you’ve likely ridden on at least one. You can usually tell that you’re on a rear-engine articulated bus because you’ll find the engine’s exhaust and vents right there at the rear.If you’re experienced in towing a trailer of any kind, you know that having the trailer overpower the tow vehicle is a bad idea. That’s a great way to jackknife your whole rig. Yet, articulated transit buses easily glide through their cities without crumpling into an L-shaped mess.How rear-engine articulated buses achieve this has a lot to do with the articulation joint. Much of the core design of a pusher bus articulated joint is the same. You still have the two plates meeting at a circular bearing in the middle. But now, there’s more.One of the biggest additions to the articulation joint of a pusher bus is a set of dampers. The dampers provide hydraulic resistance, slowing down the rotation speed of the sections. Newer joint designs feature semi-active dampers that utilize an array of sensors and a control unit. The bus tracks its speed, steering angle, and articulation angle.If the control unit detects that the bus might become unstable, the dampers can become firmer to further restrict movement. If the control unit fails, the articulation joint still has passive damping, and if the driver turns sharply enough, there are bump stops at the end of the articulation joint’s travel. Likewise, the articulation system can work in tandem with the drive-by-wire system to cut throttle when things are getting a bit too spicy. Having the active system allows the joint to be stiff during high-speed driving, and more relaxed in low-speed cornering.Here’s an example of how a HÜBNER system intervenes based on bending angle:Pusher buses then use similar copolymer-based bellows and flexible power systems as a puller bus does. Some of these systems are designed to be universal, so they could be installed on just about any articulated bus, no matter if it’s a diesel, a hybrid, natural gas, electric, hydrogen, or something else.There are even articulated buses out there that have two articulation joints, essentially creating a long snake of a three-section unit. These buses (example below) tend to be rare and are often used more like trackless trams, as their sheer length limits their maneuverability.As for how driving an articulated bus is different from a rigid bus, the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority has a neat video explainer from a driver (click here if you do not see the embed):A lot of this technology has been around for a long time. HÜBNER says it’s been making articulated bus bellows since 1952. JOST, another German maker of commercial vehicle parts, says it made its first ball bearing turntables in 1952.Meanwhile, FG Fahrzeugwerkstätten Falkenried GmbH claims to have invented the damper system for today’s low-floor articulated buses in 1975. One of the first rear-engine articulated buses to use this technology was the 1978 Mercedes-Benz O 305 G:All of this history and engineering is essentially hiding in plain sight, or right under your feet. When you’re riding these buses, you can’t see the articulation joint hard at work to keep the bus comfortable and under control. You might not have even noticed that many “bendy” buses have rear-mounted powertrains.For decades, the articulated bus has proven itself to be the right kind of bus for when a transit district wants to increase available passenger volume but without deploying more buses. Articulated buses also work on the routes where a tall double-decker bus just won’t work. Of course, they’re also a subject of curiosity for transit enthusiasts, too.The next time you’re on a bus during your morning commute, think about the century of advancements that led to that bus ride. It all started with wooden carriages slowly getting people to their destinations. Now, the buses of today are marvels. Also, be sure to thank your bus driver and the mechanics, because without them, your commute wouldn’t go nearly as smoothly as it does.Top Graphic Image: Author

item.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
item.author: gmays
item.content:encoded: Today, we release , a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B.LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.What changed since LFM2-24B-A2BLFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion, which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens. has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads. turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B)SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode)Table 1: LFM2.5-24B-A2B benchmark performance*.LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.Fast inference everywhereLFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem: — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput — High-performance GPU serving framework — Cross-platform inference across diverse acceleratorsAll runs were collected on Pipette, the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2BLFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls.Video 1: Local Hermes Agent with LFM2.5-24B-A2B creating a morning briefing about trending models on Hugging Face and responding to follow up questions.The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out our local agent guide for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice.Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on Hugging Face.For API inference, you can also sign up for Liquid Console where you'll receive $2 in credit to get started. The model is priced at $.10/1M input tokens (at $.05 for cached input) and $1.00/1M output tokens.With LFM2.5, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are: — Download, fine-tune, and deploy. See our model license. — Native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and Nvidia hardware — From base models for customization to specialized audio and vision variants, one architecture covers diverse use casesWe can't wait to see what you build.For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX:Liquid AI, "LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents", Liquid AI Blog, Oct 2026.*All the models were evaluated with vLLM and the following generation parameters: temperature = 0.6, top_p = 0.95, no max output tokens (bounded by the model's context window).: temperature = 0.001, max output tokens = 4096.: temperature = 0, max output tokens = 1024; user simulator: GPT-4o-2024-08-06, temperature = 0, max output tokens = 1024.: temperature = 1.0 (vLLM default; the agent sets no temperature), max output tokens = 8192.: official user model (GPT-5.2, low reasoning effort) with default BM25 retrieval, temperature = 0, max output tokens = 16384 per turn. temperature = 0.6, top_p=0.95, max_turns=40 (no of browser actions allowed), no max output tokens (bounded by the model's context window)): temperature = 0.6, max output tokens = 32768.

item.title: We’re releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for dreamers
item.author: emschwartz
item.content:encoded: TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity.To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally.On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers.Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards.Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love () was multimodal all along!Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the , , or even ! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve.As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot.TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: trueCheck out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/imagesWe’re introducing another new type as well: . It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support.We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for (spoilers).Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/boxSize matter, apparently 💅We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod.We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to:TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: trueCheck out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-lengthWe love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases.We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under ! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to. Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support.Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but we’re well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. will be updated to in a week. will be available for a while. We intend to give 60 days warning before is formally deprecated, and 30 days for . We’ll release a deprecation policy prior to this.As you all know, we dislike public benchmarks. However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers. We’re trying something new out here: we’re going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all.This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, don’t expect them to be consistent.Don’t believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases.We’re including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers.This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models.Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi we’re releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment.

item.title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke
item.author: sunshowers
item.content:encoded: Update 2026-10-15: I wrote a followup to answer questions and concerns.Here is Anthropic describing (archive link) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights. The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.)I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.)But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke.Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse.

item.title: Fancy Curl Sites
item.author: adunk
item.content:encoded: March 18, 2026 (Updated: October 14, 2026)So a good while ago I added a fun of my site, meant for viewing in the terminal. Try running these commands!curl nytpu.com/gemlog/2026-03-18 # or curl nytpu.com (sorry Windows users, not my fault that ANSI escape codes are disabled-by-default in . And not my fault that in Powershell you have to use instead of because Powershell inexplicably aliases that to .)I posted about it a bit on the Fediverse, but otherwise didn't elaborate much on it becuase I figured it was fairly self-explanatory. But I've had a handful of people ask me how I did it, so I decided it might actually be worth it to write a post about how I did it (…like seven months late).I should note this idea came from trinkey's () and strongsand's () curl sites, I didn't come up with it myself. Even though I did go about it quite a bit differently from them, all credit for the very cool idea goes to them. (UPDATE: unfortunately neither of their curl versions are functional anymore as of 2026-10-14.)First, since it's the more interesting part, actually generating the ANSI-marked-up files to send to the clients. I entirely hand-wrote the index page and about page.Note that I believe trinkey and strongsand generate theirs on-the-fly with the ratatui library (or similar), which is probably more convenient; hand-writing it seemed more expedient to me though.I had the main escape code—, i.e. — in a Vim register to easily paste when needed, and then the Wikipedia page for the main graphics codes open to reference the specific escape codes. And, yeah, that's about it. I experimented to decide on consistent styling I liked, and just referenced the Gopher version of my pages when crafting the marked-up curl pages.Now, the notable thing about my version is that I have curl versions of the entirety of my blog, rather than just one or two pages being available. This is entirely due to a convenient coincidence: over four years ago I implemented outputting ANSI-marked-up plaintext in my custom markup language I use for my blog, Gemroff. Originally it was just to allow convenient previewing of drafts in the terminal while writing; but it was trivial to plug into my static site generator to immediately get Curl versions generated.This is the main thing that makes it hard to say since it was only easy for me because I use an entirely custom markup language and static site generator and I happened to make the right design choices years ago—e.g. my SSG also happened to already have support for multiple, modular output formats instead of solely HTML like other SSGs, since I tri-host my site on HTTP, Gemini, and Gopher.However, offering nothing but a few hand-written pages for fun is a completely acceptable way to set up a site like this anyways, since it's just a neat gimmick and no one's likely to actually use it more than a few minutes of browsing.Finally, the last step is actually presenting the Curl version of your site to any user agent containing , which for me was just a few changes to my Nginx config, with other servers it'd presumably be equivalently simple. The main feature I wanted was an override header () so you could still get an unmodified HTTP response like someone casually running Curl likely wanted, and I wanted everything to be served statically still.And… that's really it! As I said, when I first set it up it seemed fairly self-explanatory to me, but it is very non-orthogonal to what people normally do with either web servers or ANSI escape codes so I can see where people's curiosity/confusion came from. It would be neat to see more sites doing this trick around! acksually I'll have you know that my markup language has had an explicit markup element for emdashes since November 2022. And believe it nor not: LLMs are trained on shit copied from actual authors, so LLMs wouldn't be using emdashes if they weren't already used in human-written works.And what, am I supposed to avoid having twenty parentheticals a paragraph, to where I feel the need to use emdashes to vary it up? Unthinkable!

item.title: Things to know when you get cancer
item.author: jjmaxwell4
item.content:encoded: index I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation.AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note.You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups.You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines. You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case.If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is.Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion.I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time.Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation. Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors.Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings. The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). The rest of the HN comments are worth reading too.
